articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.standfirst: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
paragraphs: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.
9 November 2026
Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.
Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems
Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.
But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."
There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"
Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.
Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".
"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.
Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.
But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.
The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.
With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.
The alternative is to build.
Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.
Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.
All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.
And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.
And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.
I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".
Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.
Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.
"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.
Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.
Foreign investment, then - just not from China.

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.
Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.
And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.
If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

articles.title: Californians reject wealth tax for billionaires
articles.standfirst: Proposition 40 targeted Californian billionaires with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income.
paragraphs: California voters have voted to reject a wealth tax on its billionaires.

The ballot proposal would have levied a one-time tax on the state's mega wealthy to help fund healthcare. It took nearly a week of counting votes after the midterm election to determine a projection on the measure.
There are about 200 billionaires in the state, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, reality television star Kim Kardashian and media mogul Oprah Winfrey.

Proposition 40 targeted Californians with a wealth of more than $1.1bn (£800m) with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income. It failed amid divisions among Democrats and labour unions.
Had it passed, experts believe it would have been the world's first wealth tax targeting billionaires.
The tax would have raised about $100bn to make up for federal funding cuts to healthcare in California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.
Those who backed the measure had argued it would help ensure that the ultra-wealthy were contributing their fair share and helping backfill gaps in the state's budget.
The wealth tax faced fierce opposition, including from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, as well as California Governor Gavin Newsom and labour unions.
Newsom, whose tenure as governor is coming to an end, had expressed concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

Some billionaire critics of the measure spent millions trying to crush it, with a handful even moving out of the state to evade the possible tax. Brin gave more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the tax, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Dave Regan, head of the union that led the charge for the measure, said on election night that the billionaires' efforts to block the tax created "a lot of confusion and a lot of second-guessing among people who really in their hearts know what the right the thing to do is".
Regan, who is president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, pledged to seek a billionaire tax once more in 2028.
The measure had odds stacked against it, with two other propositions on the ballot that would have effectively reversed it, even if it passed.

California, home to some 23 million registered voters, has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy. It is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world, but also has one of the highest wealth gaps.

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.standfirst: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
paragraphs: PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world"
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

articles.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
articles.standfirst: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.
paragraphs: Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson apologised for the "hard news" of 850 job cuts
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

articles.title: Holiday hunger bill to face final Stormont hurdle
articles.standfirst: The new law would would help poorer families with food costs during school holidays.
paragraphs: Community and voluntary groups have been publicly supportive of the Holiday Meal Payments Bill, with some staging a demonstration at Stormont on Monday
A proposed law which would help poorer families with food costs during school holidays is to face its final hurdle in the Northern Ireland Assembly on Tuesday.
Some parents and charities have welcomed the Holiday Meal Payments Bill, which was brought forward by Sinn Féin's Danny Baker.
It would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals, which would be made outside of term time to help with the cost of food.

But Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) Education Minister Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation, warning it will immediately cost his budget £25m to £30m a year at a time when all departments are struggling financially.
The Holiday Meal Payments Bill was brought forward by Sinn Féin' assembly member Danny Baker
Baker said he was motivated to introduce it by some of his experiences of breakfast clubs and meal schemes in youth work.
"There was a young boy, about the same age of my youngest, around seven years old," he explained.
"He was filling his wee pockets up and we caught on to this.
"To cut a long story short, he was bringing home food for his siblings because there just wasn't enough food in the house."
Baker said all ministers had choices to make and the legislation alone could not solve child poverty, but would act as an "early intervention".
Children are eligible for free school meals if their family's household income is below £15,390 a year.
Northern Ireland is the only UK region without government-funded holiday food support, after the Department of Education (DE) ended its £27-per-fortnight holiday meal grant in 2023.
Baker's legislation was introduced in the Northern Ireland Assembly in March and has been scrutinised by members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) on a number of occasions over the past nine months.
Louise McCullough is a mum-of-three who cannot afford to work full time because of the cost of childcare
Community and voluntary groups have been publicly supportive of the bill, with some staging a demonstration at Stormont on Monday in a bid to urge MLAs to get it over the finish line.
Louise McCullough, a mum-of-three from east Belfast, was among those who spoke at the event.
She said her children receive free school meals and that she would be directly affected by the legislation.
"There are so many working families who need this, it will change their lives and be massively impactful," she told BBC News NI.
"I can't afford to work full time because of the cost of childcare, and the cost of living.
"We have to do what we can and schemes like free school meals make a difference but so much more needs done... if you can't find money for hungry children what are you doing?
"Our government should be scaffolding our families properly."
Edel Diamond is from the South West Belfast Foodbank said the new law would make a big difference to the families she comes across
Edel Diamond from the South West Belfast Foodbank said organisations like hers had been "filling in the gaps" to help struggling families.
"We shouldn't have to - it's incumbent on our executive to put these initiatives forward," she said.
"This will make such a difference to families we're seeing daily."
Paul Givan challenged supporters of the bill to identify which educational services should be cut in order to fund the holiday hunger payments
Paul Givan said his department does not have enough money to cover meal costs outside of school terms.
Speaking to the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme ahead of the vote, he warned other education services would have to be cut to fund meal payments.
"The problem with [Baker's] private member's bill is that this funding doesn't come from the Department of Finance," Givan said.
"It is a Sinn Féin private member's bill with a Sinn Féin finance minister that are literally picking the pocket of the Department for Education to pay a welfare payment."
He warned it will "require an annual commitment of nearly £25m to £30m" and challenged supporters to identify which services they would cut to pay for it.

"To take the funding out of special educational needs and maintenance programmes in schools in order to make a welfare payment to people that are entitled to free school meals is not a responsible decision," Givan added.
Last month, his department tabled amendments that would have given him power to delay its implementation, but these were rejected by a majority of parties.

Ulster Unionist leader Jon Burrows said his party would not support the bill, saying that it was "undermining" the executive's case for asking London for additional funding to solve its budget impasse.
Although the DUP and UUP are set to vote against the bill on Tuesday, Sinn Féin is expected to have enough support from Alliance and SDLP MLAs to ensure the bill passes.

articles.title: Headteachers say families will struggle after another rise in school dinner prices
articles.standfirst: The price of a school dinner in a primary school will have risen from £2.60 to £3.40 since the start of 2026.
paragraphs: The latest increase means that the price of a paid for school dinner in a primary school or special school will have risen from £2.60 to £3.40 since the start of 2026
A headteacher has said she believes "families are going to struggle" as the price of school dinners is to increase for the second year in a row.

The price of meals for pre-school, primary and special school pupils will go up by 30p, for post-primary pupils will they will rise by 15%. It follows an increase of just under 20% introduced by the Education Authority (EA) in January 2026.
Áine Leslie, principal of Malone Integrated College in Belfast, said this will put further pressure on families who are already worried about the cost of living crisis.
But the EA said that the amount parents would have to pay was still well below the average cost of producing a school meal, estimated at over £5.20.

The latest increase will come into effect in January and means that the price of a paid for dinner in a primary school or special school, for instance, will have risen from £2.60 to £3.40 since the start of 2026.
Pupils eligible for free school meals will not be affected.
The rise in school dinner prices is not the only measure introduced by the EA in response to what they describe as "an exceptionally challenging financial position".
There will also be a change to some menus in schools, replacing baked desserts with cheaper alternatives.
Principal of Malone Integrated College, Áine Leslie, said she believes "families are going to struggle"
At Malone Integrated College about 55% of pupils have free school meal entitlement and there are also a lot of parents who are on lower incomes.
When the prices of school meals increased earlier this year, Leslie said she remembers "sitting with the head of the cafeteria and heartbreakingly decide how much to put up each item".

"I think the cumulative effect of this will be immense, particularly families who have multiple children, both at a primary school and a post-primary school, and trying to make ends meet, it's going to become incredibly difficult," Leslie told BBC News NI.
"I can't imagine what it would be like for families trying to budget that moving forward, as well as planning for Christmas.
"I firmly believe families are going to struggle at Malone.

"I do believe that there will be some families and some young people who will be worried about the stigma attached to this, and won't voice their concerns and won't ask for help. And as an integrated school, that's really sad for us.
She added: "I think it's going to be quite cutthroat for families.

"Already, we have some of our children, particularly in junior school talking about Christmas and how they've had discussions with their families that things are going to be much more scaled down this Christmas, just with the general cost of living crisis.
"And then this is only going to amplify the situation even more for young people."
Leslie added that not having a healthy, balanced diet or going without food will be a "barrier to learning".
Education Minister Paul Givan said he was disappointed and concerned about the price rises but added it was due to underfunding of the education sector as whole.
"I don't want this to be introduced but it is a result of the Education Authority not having sufficient funding," he told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme.
He said education often bears "the greatest burden" during cost-saving exercises and he argued his department should receive a greater share of Stormont's budget.
Givan also said the "inadequate" funding that Stormont receives from Westminster was "bearing down on a huge number of public services in Northern Ireland".
Stormont ministers are yet to agree a budget, despite weeks of talks with Secretary of State Sir Chris Byrant, who has repeatedly said there is "no more money".
Christos Gaitatzis is the principal of Omagh High
Christos Gaitatzis is the principal of Omagh High and described the increase of 15% on a school meal as "excessive".

"What is the price index at the moment – is it 3,4, 5%? I would imagine that would be the reasonable increase that you would put on anything, so they are going three times the value - to me it is unreasonable," he told BBC News NI
Close to 30% of pupils at his school are on free school meals.
"You would expect that the cost for a child every week, when a price of a meal is close to £5, we are talking about £20 a week, £100 a month – that's a significant cost for lunch," Gaitatzis said.
"So other measures have to be taken by the families in order to make savings, for example pack lunches – then would that diet be balanced?

"We're talking about a society where the importance of nutrition provided by schools has significant impact on your mental and physical health, so you effectively deter these families and children having these nutritious meals by putting the price up.
"Clearly this will have an overall future impact on the health of the kids."
The commissioner for children, Chris Quinn, says children should not have to pay the price for the financial crisis in education
Northern Ireland's commissioner for children and young people said he was ''flabbergasted" at the change.

Chris Quinn said what makes the move "particularly difficult to accept is that it comes shortly after schools were directed towards energy-saving guidance advising people who were cold to wear more clothes rather than turn up the thermostat".
"I strongly advised the Education Authority to remove that guidance and made clear that responsibility for financial pressures in education should not be transferred to children and families."
The commissioner added: "Children did not create the financial crisis in education and they should not be expected to pay the price for it.
"School meals are not a luxury. For many children they are an essential part of the school day, and these increases will hit hardest those families already struggling with the cost of living."
Payments to schools for school milk are at risk.
The EA currently pays milk subsidies to about 500 schools.
It is to seek funding from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs.
The EA is also planning to offer more parents payments to transport their children to school rather than paying for taxis.
At present, some parents receive payments if their children are eligible for free school transport but no private providers, like taxis, are available.
Charges for EA music lessons for pupils are also set to rise again, and some schemes run in schools will no longer be funded.
The authority, however, has not specified what is at risk.
The EA said it was being asked to deliver important services to young people "with insufficient funding".
It said it hoped to save £20m by introducing the measures on top of £30m saved this year.
It added that costs, such as providing energy for schools, continued to rise.
"These were difficult decisions which sought to balance our commitment to children and young people alongside the requirement to live within the funding allocated for the year."

articles.title: Independent bookshop closing after rise in bills
articles.standfirst: The Chicken and Frog in Brentwood says business rates and electricity bills have risen dramatically.
paragraphs: The Chicken and Frog bookshop initially managed to survive the Covid-19 lockdowns and subsequent cost-of-living increases
An independent bookshop described as being a "haven" for families and neurodivergent children has announced it will close after 14 years.
The Chicken and Frog says it will leave Brentwood town centre in January after a huge increase in its bills and business rates.
Owner Natasha Radford, aka "Mrs Chicken", also says the town's footfall has been so low that at times she has gone a whole day without a sale.
The 53-year-old said she had been busy since announcing the news, with customers coming in for a hug and a farewell.
"It means the world because running your own business is difficult. It becomes all-consuming," said Radford, a former teacher.
"So, to know that we've had a positive impact on people's lives... it's huge."
Customer Stephanie has enjoyed taking her children to events at the shop
The shop's absence will leave behind more than just empty bookshelves, as it runs workshops and provides a sensory space.
Stephanie took her neurodivergent child to the shop and said the news was "truly heartbreaking" and that it would be an "immense loss" to Brentwood.
The 36-year-old teacher described it as an "incredible haven" of "knowledge, support and community".
"Natasha and her husband treated everyone who came into their shop as a close friend and went above and beyond to help," she said.
"Her love for children and their wellbeing was felt in every part of that shop and every club and session she ran."
Radford said her profit margins were thin, and a book she typically bought in at £4.05 would then sell for £6.99.
The business did not get the "deep discounts that the big boys get", she explained.
On top of that, she said her electricity bills had tripled since first opening, and that what she paid annually in business rates had increased from £2,868 in 2024 to £8,435 this year.
The amount many businesses are paying in rates has increased because the government reduced its temporary 75% "relief" discount to 40% in April 2025.
Rates are also dictated by market rental value, and Radford pointed out that this disproportionately affected a town close to London like Brentwood.
Natasha Radford has brought her teaching background to her business on Brentwood's Crown Street
Radford said communities felt "fragmented" and allowing hubs to close was a "massive oversight" by the government.
An HM Treasury spokesperson told the BBC that the autumn Budget gave High Street businesses "more breathing space".
Traders will now only pay business rates once their rateable value reaches £18,000 - up from £12,000.
However, the spokesperson accepted that some areas were "more expensive than others", meaning certain shops would not benefit.
Rental value was a "commercial decision" between landlords and businesses, they added.

articles.title: New chief outlines main issues facing Isle of Man
articles.standfirst: The chief minister says connectivity and food storage were among his top government priorities.
paragraphs: Ard-shirveishagh Chris Thomas has outlined his priorities surrounding connectivity
The chief minister of the Isle of Man has said reliance on imports, risks of transport disruption, and pressure on household finances are among the main challenges facing the new government.
The warning came after recent storms disrupted sea and air connections, and questions over how prepared the island is for more prolonged supply problems.
Chris Thomas outlined plans to strengthen food security and connectivity, but said emergency preparedness was not among his top five priorities.
The chief minister, ard-shirveishagh in Manx, said: "It is a serious issue. We need to improve connectivity through the airport and through Douglas Harbour."
He said ensuring "the firms that bring our supplies to us... can get to the island will be a big focus for this government".

He acknowledged that more needed to be done around emergency planning and public information, adding the government had held workshops on the issue in 2025 and would look to improve communication with residents.
One area of focus was reducing the island's reliance on imported food through greater support for local agriculture, Thomas said.
He said one of his first meetings in the role was with the Manx National Farmers' Union, with discussions focusing on maximising local production and reducing supply risks.
He also highlighted the need to improve storage and warehouse capacity.
Thomas said there was "substantial building going on" on Cooil Road in Braddan, to "optimise the amount of storage we have".
But the island's ability to maintain supplies remained closely linked to the reliability of its transport connections, he said.
He said: "We had the worst possible situation at the end of October where we had some runway lights out on our airport and we had storms at the harbour."
Improvements were needed at the airport, including air traffic control services, to help provide more reliable and affordable routes, he added.

The ard-shirveishagh said sea connectivity was another priority, with the government facing ongoing questions about the Steam Packet's vessels and the suitability of the new vessel for Douglas Harbour.
He confirmed that the purchase of another vessel remains on pause until harbour issues, including the need for dredging, have been addressed.
Thomas said putting more money back into people's pockets would be central to the government's approach, pointing to the increase in personal tax allowances introduced in the February budget.
He argued that creating a "smaller, smarter, more efficient, more effective" government would help reduce pressure on taxpayers while allowing people to retain more of their income.
He also acknowledged the impact of international events on fuel and food prices, and said the government needed to focus on tackling the underlying problems affecting people's lives.
While he encouraged residents to take sensible steps to manage their own risks, he said household stockpiling was not something he wanted to make a major government priority.

articles.title: The top Canadian cities in 2026
articles.standfirst: On average, Canadian cities outscore the US on Human Capital, Governance, and Quality of Life, but lag marginally on Economics and Environment.
paragraphs: Driven by a strong economy and favourable quality of life measures, Canada’s major cities continue to offer significant benefits to the world’s highest-skilled workers. On average, Canadian cities outscore the US on Human Capital, Governance, and Quality of Life, but lag marginally on Economics and Environment where three of the bottom four scores in North America belong to Canadian cities. This partly reflects the country’s seasonal weather fluctuations, which drag on their Environment scores.

The majority of Canadian cities are set to grow at a slower rate than US cities over the next five years, with the exception of oil-rich Edmonton and Calgary. However, the Canadian cities tend to average higher on Quality of Life score, with a more even income distribution, higher life expectancy, and lower crime rates.

In our 2026 Global Cities Index, Toronto is the top-ranking Canadian city overall, placing 20th in the world out of 1,000 cities. As Canada’s premier centre for business, finance, culture, and art, it performs best in the Economics and Human Capital categories. It is an economic powerhouse and continues to boast some of the most robust employment growth rates in the region, with migrants attracted to its buoyant jobs market and high-wage sectors. Lower immigration targets announced by the federal government in 2025 have slowed the pace of growth compared with 2022–2024, but the city is not alone in Canada or the wider Western world in facing demographic challenges.

Canada’s other major cities also score highly in our index, and like Toronto, they tend to have their strongest results in the Economics and Human Capital metrics. Vancouver ranks 24th globally and second in Canada, above US powerhouses such as Miami and San Diego. This is largely due to the city’s tech and business services sectors, which have underpinned Vancouver’s steady economic growth over the past decade and attracted workers and businesses from around the world. In fact, many US tech firms have established offices in Vancouver to more easily recruit talent from overseas. Unlike some other Canadian metros, Vancouver also performs well in the Environment category. It boasts very good air quality, and the city has historically been proactive in implementing well-defined energy transition and climate adaptation plans.

Montreal, Canada’s third-ranked city, places 62nd globally. Its economic outlook is slightly cloudier than Toronto’s and Vancouver’s, but the city still scores in the top decile globally thanks to its large economy, high life expectancy, and skilled workforce. In fact, Montreal is a key hub for education and innovation in the country and globally: it is home to McGill University, a global leader in medical research, and is also a hub for AI research and video game development, attracting skilled professionals from around the world.

In a similar vein, Calgary (fourth in Canada, 69th globally) and Ottawa-Gatineau (fifth in Canada, 104th globally) are regional bright spots with strong Human Capital scores. Ottawa-Gatineau has high levels of educational attainment thanks to its large government and public policy-adjacent sectors, while Calgary is home to many corporate headquarters and leads the country in population growth thanks to high incomes and easy access to national parks.

Calgary’s Albertan neighbour, Edmonton, is a place we have designated as a ‘City to Watch’ in the coming years. While not quite at the same level as Canada’s other major metros, partly due to its dependence on oil refining, Edmonton is a city we believe is primed to move up the rankings at pace, through a process of self-reinforcing economic growth and business development. It is among North America’s fastest-growing urban economies, recording strong gains in GDP, employment, and population. And this robust economic growth will have positive downstream effects: disposable incomes in the city, which are already higher than the national average, are set to rise at one of the fastest rates in Canada, boosting consumer spending.

House prices are still relatively affordable in Edmonton too, which cannot be said for many other Canadian cities. Residents of Toronto and Vancouver in particular typically spend a larger portion of their income on housing than residents in nearly every other city in the world. High housing costs have pulled down the Quality of Life scores for several Canadian cities, and is an enduring challenge for local and provincial governments around the country.

The other key challenge currently facing Canadian cities is the trade war with the US. The volatility around the USMCA renegotiations and broader uncertainty have stymied business investment in the country and harmed the economies of export-producing cities. The oil exporters Edmonton and Calgary have largely been spared as Canadian oil exports have targeted non-US markets with the aid of the Trans Mountain Pipeline and shipping from Vancouver. However, the manufacturing sectors of Toronto, Montreal, and Hamilton have been hit hard, both directly and through the higher cost of input materials. In our index, Hamilton ranks very similarly overall to Detroit and Pittsburgh, two cities with a similar industrial heritage and exposed to the current uncertainty.
To explore the full rankings and see how other cities perform, visit the 2026 Global Cities Index site.
Access detailed city analysis and forecasts with a free trial of our cities and regions services.

articles.title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
articles.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury has been convicted of fraud after pocketing £284,000 of taxpayers' money over three years.
paragraphs: Kashim Chowdhury fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money
Aleesha Adams joined a video call with Kashim Chowdhury in May 2023.
He'd been on sick leave from his job at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for nearly three months and Adams, his line manager, wanted to put a plan in action to ease him back into work.
At the start of the call, Chowdhury was coughing and waving tissues up to the camera in an attempt to show how ill he was. But what really caught Adams' attention was how pale he looked.
She noticed white powder had started separating from his forehead. "He was sweating, it was like rubbing off, so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck," she told his trial.
She claimed he was wearing white make-up to look sick. Something he denied in court.
Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.

That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.
In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.

Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.
But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs until September 2023 when he left the Civil Service.
He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of Civil Service databases, such as payroll, every two years to look for anomalies.
On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".
Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.
He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.
He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box.

Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.
He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".
But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system.
Chowdhury sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box
However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?

Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.

Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said.
"That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."

There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.

Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.
But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.
In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.
While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.
His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.
Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.

Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.
But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.
In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.
A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.
An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management.
"Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said.

"But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."

A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost £285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions.

"This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."
The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers".
Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.

He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.
Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.

The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered £500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months.

Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her £2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.

At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.
Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.

articles.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.standfirst: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.
paragraphs: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

articles.title: Civil servant who secretly held five jobs found guilty of fraud
articles.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury had secretly held multiple public sector jobs on full-time salaries.
paragraphs: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury juggled multiple public sector jobs
A civil servant who secretly held multiple public sector jobs on full-time salaries has been found guilty of nine counts of fraud.
Kashim Chowdhury, from east London, had five government jobs that overlapped in the spring of 2023. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.
The prosecution accused the 56-year-old of ''deliberate, intentional dishonesty'' and of ''exploiting the system''.
After seven hours of deliberation, the jury unanimously found Chowdhury guilty of eight counts of fraud by false representation and one count of fraud by a failure to disclose.
The judge said Chowdhury faced a ''very significant custodial sentence''. He added he was refusing bail because of the significance of the crime and for Chowdhury's own wellbeing.
"This was sustained and deliberate dishonesty," said Sarah Melo, specialist prosecutor at the CPS Serious Economic Organised Crime and International Directorate.
"He knew he could not legitimately hold multiple full-time positions at the same time, but continued to conceal what he was doing."
A Defra spokesperson said Chowdury "abused the trust placed in him as a public servant", adding that it would use all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending.
The judge said Chowdhury faced a ''very significant custodial sentence''
Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight full-time public sector roles that overlapped and earned him £350,000 in total.

The prosecution told the court that on application forms he provided inaccurate information about his employment status and failed to disclose to government departments that he was already a civil servant. Once he secured the roles he didn't tell his employers he was working elsewhere.

He was allowed to work entirely from home because he told his employers he was caring for his mother, whom he lived with in east London. She had dementia and was diagnosed with terminal cancer in 2023.

But rather than reduce his workload to look after her, he kept taking on new jobs. In the spring of 2023, when his mother was a few months away from death, he had jobs at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the Department of Health and Social Care, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office.
During this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Chowdhury said he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment in the past. He was made redundant from a job at the Department for Education in 2013 and was given a diagnosis of PTSD.
He said he had not been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".
But the prosecution barrister, Lucy Organ, told the jury: "He's lied to you in evidence, he's lied to you under oath, which demonstrates the level of deceit he has descended to."
A succession of his managers told the court about his poor performance. Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney who managed Chowdhury at Defra.

He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time". McCartney said that during video calls Chowdhury had his camera switched off blaming technical problems. McCartney said this went on for four to five months.
But McCartney said that because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job and remained there for two years.
Chowdhury told the jury he had not worn make-up during a work video call

The prosecution argued that he used sick notes to cope with his impossible schedule. In March 2023, he was on sick leave from four of the organisations he worked for. But he kept working at the Home Office and did not tell them he was ill.

His line manager at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023. By this point he'd been off sick for three months and she wanted to make a plan to get him back to work.
She told the jury that at the start of the call he was coughing a lot and waving tissues up to the camera. She also told the jury that he had been wearing white make-up to try to look ill.
Adams told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."
Chowdhury told the jury this was a smear and that he had not been wearing make-up.
After the call, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it he blamed a technical error.
Adams grew suspicious. ''I believed he was lying,'' she told the jury. She escalated her concerns up the chain at the UKHSA.
But his fraudulent behaviour went on for several more months until he left the civil service in September 2023.
He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of civil service databases such as payroll every two years to look for anomalies.
Chowdhury has also been accused by his siblings of bullying their mother into increasing his share of the family home days before she died.
In a case at the High Court, Chowdhury's two brothers and sister allege that he put "undue influence" on Faijun Nessa to sign documents that meant he would inherit half of her home.
The four-storey, six-bedroom home in east London has been valued at £2.1m.

His siblings say their mother could not have understood what she was signing because she was "desperately unwell". In January 2023 she was given a terminal diagnosis of stage four metastatic colorectal cancer.

The claimants also allege that Mrs Nessa, who was nearly blind and could not speak English, was unaware of what she was signing because the documents were not translated into her native Bengali at the time they were signed.
Kashim Chowdhury denies the claims. That case is ongoing.

articles.title: State Tax Rates on Long-Term Capital Gains, 2026
articles.standfirst: Savings and investment are essential for individuals’ and families’ financial security and for long-term economic growth. Policymakers should therefore consider reforms that can help mitigate—rather than add to—tax codes’ biases against saving and investment.
paragraphs: When taxpayers sell capital assets like real property or corporate stock, net earnings on those sales (capital gains) are generally subject to taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., and net losses (capital losses) can generally be deducted when calculating income tax liability.

One major shortcoming of current capital gains taxation is that the tax basis, or the purchase price of an asset, is not indexed for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin. As a result, capital gains are measured in nominal dollars, with the original purchase price subtracted from the sale price without any adjustment for the value of money over time. This means taxpayers are taxed on a combination of real gains and fictitious income that does not reflect an actual increase in purchasing power (although the tax code provides some accommodations, such as for qualifying sales of owner-occupied homes and properties transferred to heirs). In some cases, this lack of inflation indexingInflation indexing refers to automatic cost-of-living adjustments built into tax provisions to keep pace with inflation. Absent these adjustments, income taxes are subject to “bracket creep” and stealth increases on taxpayers, while excise taxes are vulnerable to erosion as taxes expressed in nominal dollars, rather than rates, slowly lose value. can be significant enough that taxpayers owe taxes on what appears to be a capital gain on paper, but is, in real terms, a net loss.

The federal tax code partially addresses this shortcoming through the preferential treatment of long-term capital gains. Long-term capital gains, defined as net gains on assets held for more than one year, are taxed under a separate rate schedule with lower rates and different brackets. Depending on a taxpayer’s overall taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. , long-term capital gains are taxed at rates of 0 percent, 15 percent, or 20 percent.

At the state level, accommodating the effects of inflation is less commonly seen. Thirty states and the District of Columbia overtax capital gains income simply by subjecting capital gains to the same rate schedule that applies to ordinary income.

Three states—Maryland, Minnesota, and Washington—expose some capital gains to higher rates than those that apply to ordinary income. Specifically, Maryland adds an additional 2 percent capital gains surtaxA surtax is an additional tax levied on top of an already existing business or individual tax and can have a flat or progressive rate structure. Surtaxes are typically enacted to fund a specific program or initiative, whereas revenue from broader-based taxes, like the individual income tax, typically cover a multitude of programs and services. to the state income tax due on income exceeding $350,000; Minnesota taxes most capital gains at ordinary rates but levies an additional 1 percentage point tax on net investment income exceeding $1 million; and Washington imposes a 7 percent rate on capital gains income up to $1 million and an additional 2.9 percent excise taxAn excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. on capital gains income over $1 million.

Eight states, like the federal government, apply lower effective individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source rates to long-term gains than to ordinary income, either by applying lower statutory rates or by offering an exclusion for a portion of otherwise taxable capital gains, while Missouri exempts capital gains from its income tax. Eight states avoid this dilemma by forgoing an individual income tax altogether.

It is worth noting that several states provide targeted preferential tax treatment for certain types of capital gains, often providing exemptions for qualifying capital gains from investments in certain industries. For example, Colorado offers a subtraction of up to $100,000 to farmers for capital gains from sales of qualifying agricultural real property, while Maine offers a subtraction to certain housing organizations for a portion of capital gains from the transfer of certain properties to be used for affordable housing. While these types of provisions vary considerably from state to state, their existence indicates that policymakers recognize that taxing capital gains the same as ordinary income can disincentivize investment and create economic distortions. However, these provisions are often very narrowly targeted, offering tax advantages to only a small subset of taxpayers.

At the state level, taxing long-term capital gains at lower rates or excluding a set percentage of capital gains income (for all taxpayers and for all types of capital gains) helps offset the fact that capital gains taxes apply to nominal, not real, capital gains. Therefore, more states should reconsider their treatment of long-term capital gains, either by applying a lower statutory rate to capital gains income or excluding a certain percentage of otherwise taxable capital gains. Additionally, states should also ensure they provide robust and timely deductions for capital losses.

Even when lower rate schedules or exclusions are granted, capital gains taxes represent a form of double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. on investment income. To illustrate this, consider an individual who decides to save for the future by purchasing shares of stock in a company. Unless the shares are purchased through tax-advantaged investment accounts—like a 401(k) or IRA, where invested income is taxed only once, either on the way in (Roth accounts) or on the way out (traditional accounts)—the investment is made using ordinary wage or salary income that has already been taxed under standard federal and state individual income tax rate schedules.

Under favorable circumstances, the value of that investment will grow over time. The growth reflects corporate earnings that have already been subject to corporate income taxes, reducing the amount of income ultimately distributed to investors. Years or decades later, when the investor sells their shares and realizes a capital gain, the same underlying income will be taxed again under the individual income tax.

While preferential rates applied to long-term capital gains reduce this burden, they do not eliminate it. Moreover, the burden can be compounded by the fact that capital gains are measured by nominal rather than inflation-adjusted dollars. Thus, taxpayers may owe tax not only on previously taxed earnings but also on inflationary gains that do not represent a real increase in purchasing power.

When evaluating the tax treatment of investment income, state policymakers should consider all layers of taxes on those earnings, including corporate income taxes, and understand how the failure to inflation-index the tax basis, combined with most states’ failure to adjust rates accordingly, results in the widespread overtaxation of capital gains income in the United States.

Savings and investment are essential for individuals’ and families’ financial security and for long-term economic growth. Policymakers should therefore consider reforms that can help mitigate—rather than add to—tax codes’ biases against saving and investment.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Nicole Fox is a Policy Analyst with the Center for State Tax Policy at the Tax Foundation, where she serves as a resource to policymakers in their efforts to modernize and improve the structure of their state tax codes.
