articles.title: Devolution to Cumbria
articles.standfirst:
Devolution to Cumbria ellie.slee.lamb Fri, 06/11/2026 - 13:33 England On 6 May 2027, voters will elect the first mayor of Cumbria. 7 Explainer Esme Barlow Hall Harriet Shaw Akash Paun Institute for Government Yes Barrow-in-Furness in Cumbria Devolution Local government Local elections Regional economic growth Levelling up Economy Transport Burnham government North West
No

The first mayor of Cumbria will be elected in May 2027, leading a new combined authority for the region. The mayor and combined authority will hold powers over skills, transport, planning, housing, health, public safety and economic development1 Cumberland Council, ‘Devolution’, Cumberland Council, (no date), retrieved 6 October 2026, www.cumberland.gov.uk/your-council/devolution   across the two local areas of Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness.  

Who are the candidates for mayor of Cumbria? 

David Allen, Cumbria’s current Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, is Labour’s candidate for the election.2 Labour Lakes and Dales, ‘Dave Allen selected as Labour's candidate for Cumbria Mayor’, Labour Lakes and Dales, 27 February 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.labourlakesanddales.org.uk/campaigns/2027-mayoral-election/2026/02/27/dave-allen-selected-as-labours-candidate-for-cumbria-mayor 

Mike Starkie, previously the independent mayor of Copeland from 2015 to 2020 and Conservative mayor from 2020 to 2023, is the Conservative candidate.3 Kieran Molloy, ‘Former mayor of Copeland running in mayoral elections 2027’, The Westmorland Gazette, 23 August 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.thewestmorlandgazette.co.uk/news/25520126.former-mayor-copeland-running-mayoral-elections-2027 

Libby Bateman, a former Cumbria county councillor, is the Liberal Democrat candidate.4 Libby for Cumbria, ‘About me’, Libby for Cumbria, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.libbyforcumbria.uk/meet-libby 

Mark Borthwick, an environment policy researcher, is the Green candidate.5 Penrith Town Council, ‘Green Party Announce Candidate for Cumbria Mayor Elections in May 2027’, Penrith Town Council, 18 September 2026, retrieved 19 October 2026, www.penrith.town/news/green-party-announce-candidate-for-cumbria-mayor-elections-in-may-2027 

Reform UK has not yet announced their candidate. 

What is the history of devolution to Cumbria? 

A coalition of Cumbrian local authority leaders previously called for a devolution deal in 2015. Local authority leaders, including the then leader of Cumbria County Council and all of the county’s major council leaders, collectively called for a devolution deal through the Cumbria Deal proposal.6 hitehaven News, ‘Cumbria Deal: An ambitious bid to win “devolution” for county’, Whitehaven News, 10 October 2018, retrieved 15 October 2026, www.whitehavennews.co.uk/news/17119836.cumbria-deal-an-ambitious-bid-to-win-devolution-for-county 

This proposal argued that Cumbria’s assets such as nuclear expertise could benefit from a devolution deal.7 Cumbria County Council, Cumbria Deal: Devolution Proposal, Cumbria County Council, September 2015, www.elibrary.cumbria.gov.uk/elibrary/Content/Internet/538/755/1929/17716/17717/42251145142.PDF  However, the devolution deal collapsed in 2016 when councils failed to agree on a governance model.8 Local Government Chronicle, ‘Deadlock on devo deal for Cumbria’, Local Government Chronicle, 27 May 2016, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.lgcplus.com/politics/devolution-and-economic-growth/deadlock-on-devo-deal-for-cumbria-27-05-2016   Further talks also failed in 2021 when Cumbria’s local authorities failed to reach a consensus on a devolution deal that involved creating two new unitary authorities with an elected mayor for the region.9 Connell, John, ‘Minister’s ambition for Cumbria devolution by May 2021’, In Cumbria, 3 February 2020, retrieved 14 October 2026, www.in-cumbria.com/news/18207887.ministers-ambition-cumbria-devolution-may-2021/ 

Following the failed devolution deal, the Government implemented local government reorganisation in Cumbria. Through the Cumbria (Structural Changes) Order 2022, Cumbria County Council and the six district councils were replaced by two unitary authorities on 1 April 2023. These were Cumberland Council and Westmoreland and Furness Council. 

In 2025,10 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Cumbria devolution consultation’, GOV.UK, updated 17 July 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/consultations/cumbria-devolution/cumbria-devolution-consultation   Cumbria joined the Government’s Devolution Priority Programme (DPP) which put six areas on a fast track to mayoral devolution.11 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Devolution White Paper, 16 December 2024.  Following public consultation between February and April, the government announced in July 2025 that the necessary statutory tests had been met and that mayoral devolution could proceed in the area.12 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Cumbria devolution consultation response’, GOV.UK, 17 July 2025, retrieved 15 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/consultations/cumbria-devolution/outcome/cumbria-devolution-consultation-response  

In October 2025, both councils gave their formal consent to the establishment of a mayoral combined authority (also now known as a mayoral strategic authority) for Cumbria13 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Councils say yes to new Mayor-led authority’, Cumbria Combined Authority, 5 February 2025, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/newsroom/2025/councils-say-yes-new-mayor-led-authority   and a statutory instrument creating Cumbria Combined Authority (CCA) was laid before parliament in December 2026,14 UK Parliament, ‘SI 2026 - Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026’, Statutory Instruments, 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.statutoryinstruments.parliament.uk/instrument/qfWl1lVI    coming into force on 24 February 2026.15 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Cumbria Combined Authority is officially created’, Cumbria Combined Authority, 24 February 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/newsroom/2026/cumbria-combined-authority-officially-created 

The DPP areas were originally due to elect mayors in May 2026. In Cumbria (as in Cheshire and Warrington), the mayoral election was postponed to May 2027 following requests by local leaders to align the mayoral elections with local elections.16 McMahon J, ‘Devolution Priority Programme’, Written Ministerial Statement, 17 July 2025, retrieved 6 October 2026, www.questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2025-07-17/hcws848 

What is Cumbria Combined Authority? 

Cumbria Combined Authority (CCA) is a legal body bringing together Cumbria’s two unitary authorities: Cumberland Council and Westmorland and Furness Council. Each council is a constituent of CCA and each appoints two councillors to be Constituent Council Members on the board.17 Cumbria Combined Authority, Cumbria Combined Authority Constitution, Cumbria Combined Authority, March 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-03/Cumbria%20Combined%20Authority%20Constitution.pdf    

The board sets the long-term vision and strategic direction of the combined authority, such as the allocation of funding. The Cumbria Combined Authority board will be chaired by the mayor once elected.1 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Cumbria Combined Authority Board’, Cumbria Combined Authority, (no date), retrieved 13 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/committees/cumbria-combined-authority-board   In May 2026, the board agreed that Labour councillor and leader or Cumberland Council Mark Fryer would serve as chair until the election of the mayor in May 2027. When in position, the mayor will appoint one of the constituent council members to be their deputy.2 Cumbria Combined Authority, Cumbria Combined Authority Constitution, Cumbria Combined Authority, March 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-03/Cumbria%20Combined%20Authority%20Constitution.pdf  

Cumbria is a part of the Borderlands partnership, a coalition of five councils across the South of Scotland and the North of England, which exists to encourage sustainable and inclusive economic growth and to attract investment into the region.3 Borderlands Partnership, ‘The Partnership’, Borderlands Partnership, (no date), retrieved 14 October 2026, www.borderlandsgrowth.com/the-partnership   The leaders of both of Cumbria’s councils sit on the Borderlands partnership board.

What powers will the mayor and combined authority hold? 

The mayor and combined authority will hold devolved powers over economic development, skills and employment, transport, and housing and planning.

CCA will receive an investment fund of £11.1m per year for 30 years, after the Mayor has been elected.4 Cumberland Council, ‘Devolution’, Cumberland Council, (no date), retrieved 6 October 2026, www.cumberland.gov.uk/your-council/devolution    An allocation of £5.5m has been confirmed for the year 2026/27 ahead of the mayoral election.5 Westmorland and Furness Council, ‘Welcome for confirmation of funding for Cumbria Combined Authority’, Westmorland and Furness Council, 20 February 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.westmorlandandfurness.gov.uk/news/2025/welcome-confirmation-funding-cumbria-combined-authority-0 

CCA took responsibility for local transport planning and become the Local Transport Authority in March 2026.6  Cumbria Combined Authority, Cumbria Combined Authority Board Draft Minutes: 1 September 2026, Cumbria Combined Authority, September 2026, p. 5, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-09/Cumbria%20Combined%20Authority%20Board%20draft%20minutes%20-%201%20September%202026_0.pdf   One important function being afforded to the CCA is the responsibility to develop a Local Transport Plan (LTP) that will identify the regions strategic transport and connectivity priorities.7 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Explanatory Memorandum to the Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, 2026, www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf  , 8  UK Government, ‘Explanatory Memorandum to The Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026’, 2026, available at: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf   Until 31 March 2027, transport functions will be held concurrently between the CCA and the constituent councils as part of a transitional agreement, before fully transferring to the CCA.9 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Explanatory Memorandum to the Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, 2026, www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf   , 10  UK Government, ‘Explanatory Memorandum to The Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026’, 2026, available at: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf  Cumbria has been allocated a total of £2.68m for the next three years to develop its LTP and deliver local transport infrastructure priorities.11 Department for Transport, ‘Resource allocations: 2026 to 2027 and 2028 to 2029’, GOV.UK, 16 July 2026, retrieved 14 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-transport-grant-allocations/resource-allocations-2026-to-2027-and-2028-to-2029  

CCA will receive an allocation of devolved funding from the Adult Skills Funding (ASF), which is used to support adults gain basic qualifications such as level 2 and 3 qualifications to enhance the skills base of the local work force.12 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Skills and employment’, Cumbria Combined Authority, (no date), retrieved 19 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/our-focus-areas/skills-and-employment  , 13  Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, Cumbria Local Skills Improvement Plan 2026–2029, Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, July 2026, www.cumbriachamber.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Cumbria-LSIP-2026-2029-FINAL-POST-SUBMISSION.pdf  The CCA will take an oversight role in Cumbria’s Local Skills Improvement Plan for 2026 to 2029– which translates wider strategies that have identified priority sectors and growth drivers, into a skills delivery framework.14 Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, Cumbria Local Skills Improvement Plan 2026–2029, Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, July 2026, www.cumbriachamber.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Cumbria-LSIP-2026-2029-FINAL-POST-SUBMISSION.pdf  The plan includes aligning ASF to identified priority sectors, such as construction and health and social care, to increase skills supply in these key areas.15 Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, Cumbria Local Skills Improvement Plan 2026–2029, Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, July 2026, www.cumbriachamber.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Cumbria-LSIP-2026-2029-FINAL-POST-SUBMISSION.pdf

CCA also has a statutory responsibility to develop a Local Growth Plan, a 10-year framework for growth designed to set out priorities the authority will focus its devolved powers on to guide investment and contribute to the national mission of increased growth.16 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Guidance for Mayoral Strategic Authorities on developing Local Growth Plans’, GOV.UK, 6 May 2026, retrieved 19 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-growth-plans-england/guidance-for-mayoral-strategic-authorities-on-developing-local-growth-plans   Further, CCA will gain powers under the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 to prepare a Spatial Development Strategy (SDS) to provide a 20+ years planning framework for housing, infrastructure and economic growth that local plans will need to conform to.17 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Explanatory Memorandum to the Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, 2026, www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf 

The functions of Cumbria’s Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner (PFCC) will transfer to the mayor and MSA from after the 2027 election.18 Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, PF009-26: Cumbria PFCC Functions to be Exercised As Is up to Transfer to Mayor, Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, 2026, www.cumbriacms.formationcraft.co.uk/uploads/PF009-26-Cumbria-PFCC-Functions-to-be-Exercised-As-Is-up-to-Transfer-to-Mayor-for-website.pdf   Powers include budgetary, policy, and regulatory duties, accountability oversight, and strategic planning and coordination with community and elected officials. 

The mayor and combined authority’s powers are likely to increase over time. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 introduces new powers for mayors, including the power to charge a levy on developers to fund infrastructure delivery in the area, the power to intervene in local planning authority decisions on applications of potential strategic importance, and the power to make mayoral development orders that grant upfront planning permission to strategic developments.19 UK Government, English Devolution And Community Empowerment Act 2026, 29 April 2026, retrieved 2 October 2026, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2026/23/notes/division/1/index.htm   The government is currently holding a consultation on the implementation of these powers.20 UK Government, Planning powers for mayors in England, 24 August 2026, retrieved 2 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/planning-powers-for-mayors-in-england/planning-powers-for-mayors-in-england

The Act also gives CCA the power to request to become an ‘Established Mayoral Strategic Authority’. Subject to meeting certain criteria and the approval of the Secretary of State, this enhanced status would bring additional powers and a single-pot, ‘integrated’ funding settlement.21 UK Government, English Devolution White Paper, 16 December 2024, retrieved 2 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-devolution-white-paper-power-and-partnership-foundations-for-growth/english-devolution-white-paper

How does CCA compare to the rest of the UK in terms of social and economic outcomes? 

Cumbria has a population of 513,65022 Office for National Statistics, ‘Population estimates for England and Wales: mid-2025’, Office for National Statistics, 8 October 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationestimatesforenglandandwales/mid2025   and generates a gross value added (GVA) of £11,864m per year.23 Office for National Statistics, ‘Regional gross value added (income approach)’, Office for National Statistics, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossvalueaddedgva/datasets/regionalgrossvalueaddedincomeapproach 

The region’s productivity, home standards, digital availability, skills and education are all below the UK or English average at the regional level. One of the region’s more significant underperformance within our analysis is its home standards rate, with 67.1% of private rented accommodation meeting the decent home standard in 2021, compared to an English average of 77.1%. There are further variations between the two local authorities, with Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness at 70.1% and 63.3% respectively.  

A relatively significant variation between the two authorities is seen in productivity, with Cumberland’s gross value added per hour worked at £32.10, and Westmorland and Furness’s at £41.40. Cumberland’s productivity level is also noticeably less than the national average of £41.87.  

Employment rates for 16 to 64 year olds are high across both local authorities, with Cumbria and Westmorland and Furness attaining 82.3% and 82% respectively. This surpasses the UK average of 75.7%. Cumbria also outperforms the UK on weekly income.  

How does CCA overlap with other administrative boundaries? 

The CCA area is coterminous with the police force and fire and rescue service areas. After Cumbria was divided into the two unitary authorities in 2023, the Police and Crime Commissioner took on responsibility for Cumbria Fire and Rescue Service’s governance becoming Cumbria’s Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner (PFCC) on 1 April 2023.1 Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, ‘Fire Governance’, Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, (no date), retrieved 6 October 2026, www.cumbria-pfcc.gov.uk/what-we-do/fire-governance  

The area is covered by two Integrated Care Boards (ICB) – Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB, and North East and North Cumbria ICB. North East and North Cumbria ICB has said it expects to stop serving those in north Cumbria with its role in the county to be taken over by Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB.2 BBC News, ‘North East and Cumbria NHS care board boundaries likely to change’, 7 August 2026, retrieved 6 October 2026, https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly953w3036o 

For the purposes of oversight of children’s social care, SEND and schools, Cumbria is part of a wider area covered by the Department of Education’s north west regional director.3 Cabinet Office, ‘Mark Taylor’, GOV.UK, (no date), retrieved 15 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/people/mark-taylor--2 

Off Devolution
paragraphs: The first mayor of Cumbria will be elected in May 2027, leading a new combined authority for the region. The mayor and combined authority will hold powers over skills, transport, planning, housing, health, public safety and economic development1 Cumberland Council, ‘Devolution’, Cumberland Council, (no date), retrieved 6 October 2026, www.cumberland.gov.uk/your-council/devolution  across the two local areas of Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness.

David Allen, Cumbria’s current Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, is Labour’s candidate for the election.2 Labour Lakes and Dales, ‘Dave Allen selected as Labour's candidate for Cumbria Mayor’, Labour Lakes and Dales, 27 February 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.labourlakesanddales.org.uk/campaigns/2027-mayoral-election/2026/02/27/dave-allen-selected-as-labours-candidate-for-cumbria-mayor

Mike Starkie, previously the independent mayor of Copeland from 2015 to 2020 and Conservative mayor from 2020 to 2023, is the Conservative candidate.3 Kieran Molloy, ‘Former mayor of Copeland running in mayoral elections 2027’, The Westmorland Gazette, 23 August 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.thewestmorlandgazette.co.uk/news/25520126.former-mayor-copeland-running-mayoral-elections-2027

Libby Bateman, a former Cumbria county councillor, is the Liberal Democrat candidate.4 Libby for Cumbria, ‘About me’, Libby for Cumbria, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.libbyforcumbria.uk/meet-libby

Mark Borthwick, an environment policy researcher, is the Green candidate.5 Penrith Town Council, ‘Green Party Announce Candidate for Cumbria Mayor Elections in May 2027’, Penrith Town Council, 18 September 2026, retrieved 19 October 2026, www.penrith.town/news/green-party-announce-candidate-for-cumbria-mayor-elections-in-may-2027

A coalition of Cumbrian local authority leaders previously called for a devolution deal in 2015. Local authority leaders, including the then leader of Cumbria County Council and all of the county’s major council leaders, collectively called for a devolution deal through the Cumbria Deal proposal.6 hitehaven News, ‘Cumbria Deal: An ambitious bid to win “devolution” for county’, Whitehaven News, 10 October 2018, retrieved 15 October 2026, www.whitehavennews.co.uk/news/17119836.cumbria-deal-an-ambitious-bid-to-win-devolution-for-county

This proposal argued that Cumbria’s assets such as nuclear expertise could benefit from a devolution deal.7 Cumbria County Council, Cumbria Deal: Devolution Proposal, Cumbria County Council, September 2015, www.elibrary.cumbria.gov.uk/elibrary/Content/Internet/538/755/1929/17716/17717/42251145142.PDF However, the devolution deal collapsed in 2016 when councils failed to agree on a governance model.8 Local Government Chronicle, ‘Deadlock on devo deal for Cumbria’, Local Government Chronicle, 27 May 2016, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.lgcplus.com/politics/devolution-and-economic-growth/deadlock-on-devo-deal-for-cumbria-27-05-2016  Further talks also failed in 2021 when Cumbria’s local authorities failed to reach a consensus on a devolution deal that involved creating two new unitary authorities with an elected mayor for the region.9 Connell, John, ‘Minister’s ambition for Cumbria devolution by May 2021’, In Cumbria, 3 February 2020, retrieved 14 October 2026, www.in-cumbria.com/news/18207887.ministers-ambition-cumbria-devolution-may-2021/

Following the failed devolution deal, the Government implemented local government reorganisation in Cumbria. Through the Cumbria (Structural Changes) Order 2022, Cumbria County Council and the six district councils were replaced by two unitary authorities on 1 April 2023. These were Cumberland Council and Westmoreland and Furness Council.

In 2025,10 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Cumbria devolution consultation’, GOV.UK, updated 17 July 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/consultations/cumbria-devolution/cumbria-devolution-consultation  Cumbria joined the Government’s Devolution Priority Programme (DPP) which put six areas on a fast track to mayoral devolution.11 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Devolution White Paper, 16 December 2024. Following public consultation between February and April, the government announced in July 2025 that the necessary statutory tests had been met and that mayoral devolution could proceed in the area.12 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Cumbria devolution consultation response’, GOV.UK, 17 July 2025, retrieved 15 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/consultations/cumbria-devolution/outcome/cumbria-devolution-consultation-response

In October 2025, both councils gave their formal consent to the establishment of a mayoral combined authority (also now known as a mayoral strategic authority) for Cumbria13 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Councils say yes to new Mayor-led authority’, Cumbria Combined Authority, 5 February 2025, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/newsroom/2025/councils-say-yes-new-mayor-led-authority  and a statutory instrument creating Cumbria Combined Authority (CCA) was laid before parliament in December 2026,14 UK Parliament, ‘SI 2026 - Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026’, Statutory Instruments, 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.statutoryinstruments.parliament.uk/instrument/qfWl1lVI   coming into force on 24 February 2026.15 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Cumbria Combined Authority is officially created’, Cumbria Combined Authority, 24 February 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/newsroom/2026/cumbria-combined-authority-officially-created

The DPP areas were originally due to elect mayors in May 2026. In Cumbria (as in Cheshire and Warrington), the mayoral election was postponed to May 2027 following requests by local leaders to align the mayoral elections with local elections.16 McMahon J, ‘Devolution Priority Programme’, Written Ministerial Statement, 17 July 2025, retrieved 6 October 2026, www.questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2025-07-17/hcws848

Cumbria Combined Authority (CCA) is a legal body bringing together Cumbria’s two unitary authorities: Cumberland Council and Westmorland and Furness Council. Each council is a constituent of CCA and each appoints two councillors to be Constituent Council Members on the board.17 Cumbria Combined Authority, Cumbria Combined Authority Constitution, Cumbria Combined Authority, March 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-03/Cumbria%20Combined%20Authority%20Constitution.pdf

The board sets the long-term vision and strategic direction of the combined authority, such as the allocation of funding. The Cumbria Combined Authority board will be chaired by the mayor once elected.1 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Cumbria Combined Authority Board’, Cumbria Combined Authority, (no date), retrieved 13 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/committees/cumbria-combined-authority-board  In May 2026, the board agreed that Labour councillor and leader or Cumberland Council Mark Fryer would serve as chair until the election of the mayor in May 2027. When in position, the mayor will appoint one of the constituent council members to be their deputy.2 Cumbria Combined Authority, Cumbria Combined Authority Constitution, Cumbria Combined Authority, March 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-03/Cumbria%20Combined%20Authority%20Constitution.pdf

Cumbria is a part of the Borderlands partnership, a coalition of five councils across the South of Scotland and the North of England, which exists to encourage sustainable and inclusive economic growth and to attract investment into the region.3 Borderlands Partnership, ‘The Partnership’, Borderlands Partnership, (no date), retrieved 14 October 2026, www.borderlandsgrowth.com/the-partnership  The leaders of both of Cumbria’s councils sit on the Borderlands partnership board.
The mayor and combined authority will hold devolved powers over economic development, skills and employment, transport, and housing and planning.

CCA will receive an investment fund of £11.1m per year for 30 years, after the Mayor has been elected.4 Cumberland Council, ‘Devolution’, Cumberland Council, (no date), retrieved 6 October 2026, www.cumberland.gov.uk/your-council/devolution   An allocation of £5.5m has been confirmed for the year 2026/27 ahead of the mayoral election.5 Westmorland and Furness Council, ‘Welcome for confirmation of funding for Cumbria Combined Authority’, Westmorland and Furness Council, 20 February 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.westmorlandandfurness.gov.uk/news/2025/welcome-confirmation-funding-cumbria-combined-authority-0

CCA took responsibility for local transport planning and become the Local Transport Authority in March 2026.6 Cumbria Combined Authority, Cumbria Combined Authority Board Draft Minutes: 1 September 2026, Cumbria Combined Authority, September 2026, p. 5, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-09/Cumbria%20Combined%20Authority%20Board%20draft%20minutes%20-%201%20September%202026_0.pdf  One important function being afforded to the CCA is the responsibility to develop a Local Transport Plan (LTP) that will identify the regions strategic transport and connectivity priorities.7 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Explanatory Memorandum to the Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, 2026, www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf  , 8 UK Government, ‘Explanatory Memorandum to The Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026’, 2026, available at: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf  Until 31 March 2027, transport functions will be held concurrently between the CCA and the constituent councils as part of a transitional agreement, before fully transferring to the CCA.9 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Explanatory Memorandum to the Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, 2026, www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf   , 10 UK Government, ‘Explanatory Memorandum to The Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026’, 2026, available at: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf Cumbria has been allocated a total of £2.68m for the next three years to develop its LTP and deliver local transport infrastructure priorities.11 Department for Transport, ‘Resource allocations: 2026 to 2027 and 2028 to 2029’, GOV.UK, 16 July 2026, retrieved 14 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-transport-grant-allocations/resource-allocations-2026-to-2027-and-2028-to-2029

CCA will receive an allocation of devolved funding from the Adult Skills Funding (ASF), which is used to support adults gain basic qualifications such as level 2 and 3 qualifications to enhance the skills base of the local work force.12 Cumbria Combined Authority, ‘Skills and employment’, Cumbria Combined Authority, (no date), retrieved 19 October 2026, www.cumbria-ca.gov.uk/our-focus-areas/skills-and-employment  , 13 Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, Cumbria Local Skills Improvement Plan 2026–2029, Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, July 2026, www.cumbriachamber.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Cumbria-LSIP-2026-2029-FINAL-POST-SUBMISSION.pdf The CCA will take an oversight role in Cumbria’s Local Skills Improvement Plan for 2026 to 2029– which translates wider strategies that have identified priority sectors and growth drivers, into a skills delivery framework.14 Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, Cumbria Local Skills Improvement Plan 2026–2029, Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, July 2026, www.cumbriachamber.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Cumbria-LSIP-2026-2029-FINAL-POST-SUBMISSION.pdf The plan includes aligning ASF to identified priority sectors, such as construction and health and social care, to increase skills supply in these key areas.15 Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, Cumbria Local Skills Improvement Plan 2026–2029, Cumbria Chamber of Commerce, July 2026, www.cumbriachamber.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Cumbria-LSIP-2026-2029-FINAL-POST-SUBMISSION.pdf

CCA also has a statutory responsibility to develop a Local Growth Plan, a 10-year framework for growth designed to set out priorities the authority will focus its devolved powers on to guide investment and contribute to the national mission of increased growth.16 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, ‘Guidance for Mayoral Strategic Authorities on developing Local Growth Plans’, GOV.UK, 6 May 2026, retrieved 19 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/local-growth-plans-england/guidance-for-mayoral-strategic-authorities-on-developing-local-growth-plans  Further, CCA will gain powers under the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 to prepare a Spatial Development Strategy (SDS) to provide a 20+ years planning framework for housing, infrastructure and economic growth that local plans will need to conform to.17 Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, Explanatory Memorandum to the Cumbria Combined Authority Order 2026, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, 2026, www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/158/pdfs/uksiem_20260158_en_001.pdf

The functions of Cumbria’s Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner (PFCC) will transfer to the mayor and MSA from after the 2027 election.18 Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, PF009-26: Cumbria PFCC Functions to be Exercised As Is up to Transfer to Mayor, Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, 2026, www.cumbriacms.formationcraft.co.uk/uploads/PF009-26-Cumbria-PFCC-Functions-to-be-Exercised-As-Is-up-to-Transfer-to-Mayor-for-website.pdf  Powers include budgetary, policy, and regulatory duties, accountability oversight, and strategic planning and coordination with community and elected officials.

The mayor and combined authority’s powers are likely to increase over time. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 introduces new powers for mayors, including the power to charge a levy on developers to fund infrastructure delivery in the area, the power to intervene in local planning authority decisions on applications of potential strategic importance, and the power to make mayoral development orders that grant upfront planning permission to strategic developments.19 UK Government, English Devolution And Community Empowerment Act 2026, 29 April 2026, retrieved 2 October 2026, https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2026/23/notes/division/1/index.htm  The government is currently holding a consultation on the implementation of these powers.20 UK Government, Planning powers for mayors in England, 24 August 2026, retrieved 2 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/planning-powers-for-mayors-in-england/planning-powers-for-mayors-in-england

The Act also gives CCA the power to request to become an ‘Established Mayoral Strategic Authority’. Subject to meeting certain criteria and the approval of the Secretary of State, this enhanced status would bring additional powers and a single-pot, ‘integrated’ funding settlement.21 UK Government, English Devolution White Paper, 16 December 2024, retrieved 2 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-devolution-white-paper-power-and-partnership-foundations-for-growth/english-devolution-white-paper

Cumbria has a population of 513,65022 Office for National Statistics, ‘Population estimates for England and Wales: mid-2025’, Office for National Statistics, 8 October 2026, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationestimatesforenglandandwales/mid2025  and generates a gross value added (GVA) of £11,864m per year.23 Office for National Statistics, ‘Regional gross value added (income approach)’, Office for National Statistics, retrieved 13 October 2026, www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossvalueaddedgva/datasets/regionalgrossvalueaddedincomeapproach

The region’s productivity, home standards, digital availability, skills and education are all below the UK or English average at the regional level. One of the region’s more significant underperformance within our analysis is its home standards rate, with 67.1% of private rented accommodation meeting the decent home standard in 2021, compared to an English average of 77.1%. There are further variations between the two local authorities, with Cumberland and Westmorland and Furness at 70.1% and 63.3% respectively.

A relatively significant variation between the two authorities is seen in productivity, with Cumberland’s gross value added per hour worked at £32.10, and Westmorland and Furness’s at £41.40. Cumberland’s productivity level is also noticeably less than the national average of £41.87.

Employment rates for 16 to 64 year olds are high across both local authorities, with Cumbria and Westmorland and Furness attaining 82.3% and 82% respectively. This surpasses the UK average of 75.7%. Cumbria also outperforms the UK on weekly income.

The CCA area is coterminous with the police force and fire and rescue service areas. After Cumbria was divided into the two unitary authorities in 2023, the Police and Crime Commissioner took on responsibility for Cumbria Fire and Rescue Service’s governance becoming Cumbria’s Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner (PFCC) on 1 April 2023.1 Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, ‘Fire Governance’, Cumbria Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner, (no date), retrieved 6 October 2026, www.cumbria-pfcc.gov.uk/what-we-do/fire-governance

The area is covered by two Integrated Care Boards (ICB) – Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB, and North East and North Cumbria ICB. North East and North Cumbria ICB has said it expects to stop serving those in north Cumbria with its role in the county to be taken over by Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB.2 BBC News, ‘North East and Cumbria NHS care board boundaries likely to change’, 7 August 2026, retrieved 6 October 2026, https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly953w3036o

For the purposes of oversight of children’s social care, SEND and schools, Cumbria is part of a wider area covered by the Department of Education’s north west regional director.3 Cabinet Office, ‘Mark Taylor’, GOV.UK, (no date), retrieved 15 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/people/mark-taylor--2
On 6 May 2027, voters will elect the first mayor of Cheshire and Warrington.

articles.title: 2027 Tax Brackets
articles.standfirst: Explore the IRS inflation-adjusted 2027 tax brackets, for which taxpayers will file tax returns in early 2028.
paragraphs: On a yearly basis, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) adjusts more than 60 tax provisions for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin to prevent what is called “bracket creepBracket creep occurs when inflation, or real income growth, pushes taxpayers into higher income tax brackets. Bracket creep results in an increase in income taxes without an increase in real income. Many tax provisions—both at the federal and state levels—are adjusted for inflation. Over time, bracket creep can increase how much income tax people owe as their income grows, either due to inflat.” Bracket creep occurs when inflation, rather than real increases in income, pushes people into higher income tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. or reduces the value they receive from credits and deductions.

The IRS previously used the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as a measure of inflation prior to 2018. However, with the TaxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA), the IRS now uses the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U) to adjust income thresholds, deduction amounts, and credit values accordingly.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), passed in July 2025, made permanent most of the TCJA individual tax provisions scheduled for expiration at the end of 2025 and made other changes to individual taxes that will impact tax parameters for the 2027 tax year.
The new inflation adjustments are for tax year 2027, for which taxpayers will file tax returns in early 2028.
On average, tax parameters that are adjusted for inflation will increase by about 3.2 percent.

In 2027, the income limits for all tax brackets and all filers will be adjusted for inflation and can be found in Table 1. The federal income tax has seven tax rates in 2027: 10 percent, 12 percent, 22 percent, 24 percent, 32 percent, 35 percent, and 37 percent. The top marginal income tax rate of 37 percent will hit taxpayers with taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. above $661,375 for single filers and above $793,650 for married couples filing jointly.
The standard deduction will increase by $500 for single filers and by $1,000 for joint filers compared to the 2026 tax year (Table 2).

Seniors at or over age 65 may claim an additional standard deduction of $2,100 for single filers and $1,700 for joint filers. On top of this, taxpayers aged 65 and older who either itemize or claim the standard deduction may claim a new $6,000 deduction per qualifying taxpayer, phasing out at a six percent rate for those earning over $75,000 (single) and $150,000 (joint) as part of the separate senior deduction under the OBBBA. This new deduction is not indexed for inflation and is scheduled to expire at the end of 2028.
The personal exemption for 2027 remains at $0 (eliminating the personal exemption was part of the TCJA, and the $0 amount was made permanent as part of the OBBBA).

The alternative minimum tax (AMT) was created in the 1960s to prevent high-income taxpayers from avoiding the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source. This parallel income tax system requires high-income taxpayers to calculate their tax bill twice: once under the ordinary income tax system and again under the AMT. The taxpayer then needs to pay the higher of the two.

The AMT uses an alternative definition of taxable income called alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI). To prevent low- and middle-income taxpayers from being subject to the AMT, taxpayers are allowed to exempt a significant amount of their income from AMTI. However, the exemption phases out for high-income taxpayers. The AMT is levied at two rates: 26 percent and 28 percent.

The AMT exemption amount for 2027 is $93,000 for singles and $144,700 for married couples filing jointly (Table 3), a continuation of the TCJA design adjusted for inflation after the structure was made permanent in the OBBBA.
In 2027, the 28 percent AMT rate applies to AMT excess taxable income above $252,500 for all taxpayers ($126,250 for married couples filing separate returns).

AMT exemptions phase out at 50 cents for every dollar of AMTI exceeding $515,950 for single filers and $1,031,900 for married taxpayers filing jointly (Table 4). The OBBBA’s changes to the AMT returned the phaseout thresholds to 2018 levels and accelerated the phaseout rate from 25 percent previously.

The maximum earned income tax credit (EITC) in 2027 for single and joint filers is $685 if the filer has no children (Table 5). The maximum credit is $4,573 for one child, $7,552 for two children, and $8,496 for three or more children.
The maximum child tax credit (CTC) in 2027 is $2,300 per qualifying child, an increase of $100 compared to the previous year. The OBBBA indexed the CTC to inflation.
The refundable portion of the child tax credit is adjusted for inflation and will be $1,800 for 2027.
Long-term capital gains face different brackets and rates than ordinary income (Table 6).
The TCJA included a 20 percent deduction for pass-through businesses, and the OBBBA made this deduction permanent.

Limits on the deduction begin phasing in for taxpayers with income above $208,300 (or $416,600 for joint filers) in 2027 (Table 7). The OBBBA expanded the income range over which the deduction limitations phase in from $50,000 to $75,000 for single filers and from $100,000 to $150,000 for taxpayers married filing jointly.
In 2027, the gift tax exclusion will increase to $20,000 per recipient, up from $19,000 in both 2025 and 2026.
The exclusion is increased to $201,000 from $194,000 for gifts to spouses who are not citizens of the United States.

The estate taxAn estate tax is imposed on the net value of an individual’s taxable estate, after any exclusions or credits, at the time of death. The tax is paid by the estate itself before assets are distributed to heirs. exemption is adjusted for inflation and will be $15,480,000 in 2027.

Alex Durante is a Senior Economist at the Tax Foundation, working on federal tax policy and model development. Alex worked as a research assistant at the Federal Reserve Board and served as a staff economist on the Council of Economic Advisers.

articles.title: EU Tax Omnibus Proposal: Suggestions for Improving Its Legal Design and Increasing Its Political Viability
articles.standfirst: Tax Foundation Europe's input to the European Commission’s public consultations on the Tax Omnibus proposal reviews selected issues that have an impact on growth and competitiveness.
paragraphs: Tax Foundation Europe’s mission is to develop research and educate policymakers on tax matters that impact the growth and competitiveness of the European Union’s economy. Accordingly, our input to the European Commission’s public consultations on the Tax Omnibus proposal (the “Proposal”) is not comprehensive but a review of selected issues that have an impact on growth and competitiveness. We hope to contribute meaningfully to the discussions currently happening at the Council.

The first issue we address is the elimination of the holding requirement from the Parent-Subsidiary (PSD) and Interest and Royalty (IRD) directives to benefit from the exemption from withholdingWithholding is the income an employer takes out of an employee’s paycheck and remits to the federal, state, and/or local government. It is calculated based on the amount of income earned, the taxpayer’s filing status, the number of allowances claimed, and any additional amount the employee requests. taxes on dividend, interest, and royalty payments. The second is the nature of the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) as a minimum standard of protection of Member States’ tax bases or minimum harmonization.

The PSD and IRD have slightly different requirements for the equity, debt, and intellectual property (IP) rights holder to benefit from the exemption from withholding tax on the dividend, interest, and royalty payment. Among other requirements, the PSD requires the parent company to hold at least 10 percent of the shares of the subsidiary (directly or indirectly), whereas the IRD requires that associated companies be connected by at least 25 percent of shareholding directly or via a common parent. Below these thresholds and subject to the EU Treaties, Member States remain free to levy a withholding tax on the relevant cross-border payment. The Proposal would abolish those thresholds, meaning that Member States would no longer be free to levy withholding taxes on cross-border payments to so-called portfolio investments (i.e., below 10 percent and 25 percent).

Member States have argued that the amendment would shift the PSD and IRD from facilitating the grouping of companies within the EU toward reallocating taxing rights among Member States. Because that reallocation would affect national tax revenues differently, the Proposal could have asymmetrical fiscal effects across Member States.

We first examine the changing nature of the PSD and IRD and whether the avoidance of double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. is equally justified for controlling and portfolio investments. We then assess the Proposal’s potential impact on Member States’ tax revenues and suggest alternatives that could address budgetary concerns while preserving the Proposal’s competitiveness objective.

As mentioned in the previous section, for the shareholdings not covered by the directives, Member States remain free to levy a withholding tax on outbound payments of dividends, interest, and royalties.

For dividend income, this might cause triple taxation. First, the distributing company’s profits are taxed with a corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. in its state of residence. Second, the receiving company is taxed by the state of the distributing company on the amount of dividends distributed. Third, the receiving company is again taxed in its state of residence, as the dividends received enter its tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. for corporate income tax purposes.

For interest and royalty income, there might be double taxation. First, the interest and royalties received by the receiving company are taxed via withholding tax by the paying company’s state. Second, the interest and royalties received by the receiving company are taxed in its state of residence as the interest and royalties enter its tax base for corporate income purposes.
EU law sets a limit to this power, as it requires Member States to treat resident and non-resident taxpayers in the same way when they are in a comparable situation.

Broadly, for dividends, this means that Member States cannot levy a withholding tax on all dividend payments (within and outside their territory) and grant an exemption or credit to their recipient only when a resident.[1] In the simplest scenario possible, a Member State that exempts all dividends received by domestic companies from their domestic subsidiaries from corporate income tax cannot simultaneously levy a withholding tax on dividends paid abroad.[2]

For interest and royalties, granting national treatment to non-residents mostly means that source Member States levying a withholding tax may have to take into account the expenses connected to that income in the source state—as it would do for its own residents[3]—and tax that item of income on a net basis.[4] On the other end of the payment, a Member State would typically subject any received interest and royalty payment to tax, regardless of their source being domestic or not, meaning that equal treatment would not help solve the juridical double taxation outcome.[5]

This summary shows that EU fundamental freedoms constrain outbound withholding taxes more strictly for dividends than for interest and royalties. For dividends, Member States’ room for manoeuvre is narrower; for interest and royalties, it is broader. The distinction arises because dividends are distributions of after-tax profits, usually exempted upon receipt, whereas interest and royalty payments are generally deductible expenses for the paying company and income for the recipient.[6]

The double tax conventions (DTCs) entered into by the Member States among each other also limit the Member States’ power to levy withholding taxes on outbound payments. Typically, these DTCs (i) limit the rate of withholding tax that the state of the paying company can levy,[7] and (ii) oblige the state of residence of the receiving company to grant credit for the withholding tax paid abroad.[8]

However, despite the constraints imposed by EU law and DTCs on Member States, there can be instances of definitive double taxation within the internal market. To the extent that source states treat resident and non-resident taxpayers the same, Member States can levy EU law-compliant withholding taxes on dividend, interest, and royalty payments. Double tax treaties may not come to the rescue.[9] In fact, there are instances that DTCs cannot solve, such as triangular or multi-country cases,[10] as well as divergent interpretations of treaty terms by treaty partners. This may lead to instances of definitive double taxation within the Union.

For portfolio investments, there is no clear empirical evidence that the existence of (definitive) withholding taxes per se influences the investment location decision. However, as domestic, EU law or DTC-based exemptions from withholding taxes come with administrative requirements, often Member States levy their (higher) statutory withholding tax instead of the lower (treaty) rate, pending the verification of these requirements. Refunds of the difference come with a time lag. Administrative costs and time lags have been proven to be negatively correlated with investment decisions.[11] In other words, the higher the recovery costs of (over)withheld taxes,[12] the lower the investments in a given jurisdiction, potentially affecting the functioning of the internal market.

The exemption from the application of withholding taxes on outbound payments is currently limited to so-called “direct shareholdings,” i.e., above 10 percent in the PSD and 25 percent in the IRD. Originally, before dropping to 10 percent, the PSD also had a 25 percent shareholding requirement.[13] Scholars have explained that if 25 percent could loosely mimic substantial minority rights under the corporate laws of several Member States, 10 percent looks like an arbitrary threshold to benefit from the avoidance of double taxation.[14]

Besides, the more beneficial treatment of direct holdings compared to portfolio holdings does not seem convincing enough. The OECD Commentary to Article 10 of the OECD Model Convention, which also grants more beneficial treatment to direct holdings (above 25 percent), explains that the reason behind such different treatment is to avoid recurrent taxation and facilitate international investment. However, this may well apply to both direct and portfolio investments.[15] A dividend or an interest payment is taxed twice, once by the paying company’s state via withholding tax and once by the receiving company’s state via corporate income tax, regardless of the percentage of investment.[16]

A more convincing argument concerns neutrality between establishing a subsidiary and operating through a permanent establishment (PE) abroad. Because a permanent establishment is part of the same legal entity as its head office, transfers between them do not constitute dividend distributions and are therefore not subject to dividend withholding tax. If dividends distributed by a subsidiary were subject to withholding tax, businesses could have a tax incentive to choose a permanent establishment instead. Exempting direct holdings from withholding tax therefore helps preserve neutrality between the two legal forms.[17]

However, granting exemption to portfolio investments as well would not defeat that goal.[18] By exempting all dividend payments from withholding taxes, PEs and subsidiaries would still be treated equally, and portfolio investors would not be subject to a double layer of taxation.

The Proposal’s fiscal impact would differ across Member States according to whether, and on which categories of income, they impose statutory withholding taxes on dividends, interest, and royalties. Those statutory rules, however, provide only a partial picture of the Proposal’s effect on Member States’ tax revenues.

As seen in section 1.1. above, EU law and DTCs constrain the source Member States’ ability to levy withholding taxes, in toto or in terms of rate. Furthermore, EU law or DTCs can require residence Member States to credit the withholding taxes levied at source. This means that capital-exporting countries generally provide credit for the taxes withheld at source. Capital-importing countries instead keep the revenues from the taxes withheld at source. The elimination of withholding taxes on outbound payments has positive revenue impacts for the former and negative revenue impacts for the latter.

Eurostat’s balance of payments statistics show that net exporters of portfolio investments are Germany, Italy, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, Greece, Portugal, Cyprus, Malta, Croatia, Bulgaria, Estonia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Latvia; while net importers of portfolio investments are Luxembourg, France, the Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Poland, Romania, Hungary, Austria, Finland, and Czechia.[19]

Bearing in mind the important caveat that these figures combine assets and liabilities held within and outside of the EU, this picture shows that the Proposal might have a negative revenue impact only on those capital-importing countries that currently levy withholding taxes on dividends, interest, and royalties of portfolio investors. To the contrary, it might have positive revenue impacts on portfolio capital-exporting countries, such as Italy or Germany, currently providing credit for those withholding taxes levied abroad.

The asymmetrical revenue impact has been brought forward as a concern by multiple Member States. The claim is that by allowing all flows to go untaxed in the country of source, the directives (especially the IRD) would become instruments that re-allocate taxing powers on these income categories exclusively to the residence Member States.[20]

While (re)allocating taxing powers does not have any impact on economic growth per se, complying with an ineffective allocation does. It has been shown in the sections above that EU law and DTCs leave situations of definitive double taxation to persist within the Union, and that lengthy refunds for over-withheld taxes discourage cross-border investment. As a result, (re)allocating taxing rights in a simpler way by establishing that source countries need not burden outbound payments with taxes does advance the internal market.

However, making cross-border payments flow untaxed does not need to entail an asymmetrical revenue cost. The now-repealed Savings Directive, which transitionally required certain source Member States to tax savings income through a withholding tax, foresaw a revenue sharing mechanism according to which source Member States would retain 25 percent of the withholding tax revenues and residence Member States the remaining 75 percent. Inspired by this solution, it is proposed here that the Council insert a revenue-sharing clause in the directives under which capital-exporting countries that would gain from the Proposal transfer all or part of that gain to capital-importing countries that would lose revenue from its adoption.

In practical terms, the objective would be to preserve the Proposal’s removal of withholding taxes while compensating for its uneven fiscal effects. Member States that gain because they no longer need to credit foreign withholding taxes would contribute toward offsetting the revenue lost by Member States that can no longer collect those taxes at source.

Because tracing individual dividend, interest, and royalty flows would be complex, the revenue-sharing clause could instead use a statistical formula. The formula would first approximate the annual returns on aggregate equity and debt assets held in other Member States. It would then apply separate rates to the (assumed) dividend, interest, and IP rights returns to calculate the amount that capital-exporting countries would transfer to capital-importing countries.[21]

For dividends, it is suggested that a rate of 2.34 percent be applied to the assumed return on equity. The rate is intended to approximate the average maximum withholding tax that a Member State could impose on an outbound dividend consistently with CJEU case-law.

As explained in section 1.1.1, when resident and non-resident corporate shareholders are in comparable situations, the source Member State may not tax an outbound dividend more heavily than an equivalent domestic dividend. The relevant benchmark is therefore the domestic tax burden borne by a resident company receiving a dividend, rather than the statutory withholding tax rate virtually applicable to the outbound payment.[22]

The calculation translates that benchmark into an EU average in two steps. First, it determines the average share of domestic dividends that remains taxable in the hands of resident corporate recipients after applying domestic exemptions or partial inclusions across all EU Member States.[23] Second, it multiplies that average taxable share by the average EU corporate income tax rate, including applicable surcharges and regional taxes.[24] Expressed schematically: average EU CIT rate × average taxable share of domestic dividends = 2.34 percent.

For interest and royalties instead, it is suggested to apply a rate of 6 percent on (assumed) interest and IP rights yields.[25] This common rate is based on average DTC-based withholding tax rates on interest and royalty income in DTCs among EU Member States.

The formula could be updated annually in two respects: each Member State’s classification as a capital importer or exporter and the applicable rates, to reflect changes in domestic CIT rates and DTC withholding tax rates.

An alternative with a clearer EU-wide distributional rationale would be to treat these amounts as EU own resources. Rather than benefiting a single Member State, the revenue forgone would finance common EU expenditures. Only capital-exporting countries would transfer amounts to the EU budget because, absent such a transfer, they would benefit from the Proposal by no longer having to credit foreign withholding taxes. The amounts transferred would roughly correspond to the foreign tax credits they currently grant, making the operation broadly revenue-neutral for those countries compared with the status quo.

The position of capital-importing countries is different. Compared with the status quo, they would lose the revenue they currently collect from outbound withholding taxes and would not receive a direct fiscal transfer in return. They would nevertheless benefit collectively from the fact that capital-exporting countries would continue to forgo an equivalent amount of revenue, now to finance common EU expenditures rather than foreign tax credits.[26] As a result, there is equity in the distributional key of the own resource.

Article 3 of the ATAD provides that the Directive is only a minimum standard of protection of Member States’ tax bases. This means that, subject to compliance with the EU Treaties, Member States can go beyond the measures contained in the ATAD. The Proposal puts this in question in several of the proposed provisions.

As noted already in our June 2026 blog post,[27] the controlled foreign company (CFC) provision and the interest limitation rule in the Proposal contain wording that might limit Member States’ ability to go beyond the “minimum standard” set by the Directive. However, it does so in a manner that remains unclear.

Whereas the new exclusions from the CFC seem to be mandatory, it is not clear whether the same holds true for Model A or the one-third of passive income exclusion, as there is no explicit prohibition on the Member States adopting rules that differ from them, and yet the Proposal uses the wording “the Member States shall.”

Member States and taxpayers therefore face three potentially conflicting signals: (i) Article 3 states the general rule that Member States may adopt measures that go beyond ATAD’s minimum standard; (ii) the proposed CFC rule expressly prohibits divergence from only certain provisions; and (iii) other provisions outside that express prohibition use the mandatory formulation “Member States shall.” It is therefore unclear whether those other provisions establish exhaustive requirements or remain subject to Article 3’s minimum-standard approach.

This lack of clarity gravely undermines the harmonization effort that justifies the adoption of a directive under Article 115 TFEU, as Member States might interpret those provisions in a constellation of different ways. This has repercussions for the competitiveness of the EU’s tax system at large, and legal certainty for businesses operating within it.

Directives may combine different forms of harmonization,[28] and the Proposal appears to move ATAD in that direction. ATAD Article 3 should therefore be amended to state that the Directive establishes a minimum standard of protection “unless otherwise provided.” Under this approach, the minimum-standard rule would continue to apply by default, while provisions using “Member States shall” or other explicit language of exhaustiveness would operate as maximum harmonization.

In parallel, the CFC provision should follow one of two approaches. The first would delete the new paragraph eight—the express prohibition—and use “shall” for mandatory provisions and “may” for optional provisions. The second would retain paragraph eight but extend its express prohibition to paragraphs two and three, making clear that all of those provisions are mandatory.

In a similar fashion, the Proposal clarifies that the newly introduced R&D full expensing provision is a minimum harmonization provision, meaning that Member States can maintain or introduce alternative domestic measures if they consider those domestic measures to provide a more favorable treatment than the one granted by the Proposal. Member States are rightfully concerned about how to assess that equivalence.[29]
The R&D full expensing provision requires Member States to allow the taxpayer to deduct qualifying R&D capital expenditure from their taxable base in the year of acquisition, or within four years.

Subject to compatibility with the state aid prohibition, Member States could grant full expensing to a broader set of asset classes, or extend the period in which the application could be made. However, as there is a variety of R&D incentives in place, Member States are doubtful as to whether their own existing incentive is more favorable than the Proposal’s.

DepreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco schedules require businesses to deduct investment costs from their taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. over multiple years, typically reflecting an asset’s expected lifespan. However, since deductions arrive only gradually, inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin and the time value of money erode their value in real terms, raising the cost of capital. The longer the depreciation schedule, the smaller the share of investment costs businesses can recover. Full expensing fixes this by allowing deduction of the entire amount of capital expenditure in the year of acquisition, making the amount of nominal deduction coincide with the real value of the expense.[30]

As a result, one criterion to determine equivalence between a domestic R&D incentive and the Proposal’s full expensing might be the net present value of deductions allowed. In other words, if the domestic rule allows the taxpayer to recover at least the real value of its capital investment, the rule is equivalent. Neutral cost recoveryCost recovery refers to how the tax system permits businesses to recover the cost of investments through depreciation or amortization. Depreciation and amortization deductions affect taxable income, effective tax rates, and investment decisions. rules would be an example, as they adjust depreciation allowances for inflation and a notional return on capital.[31] In certain cases, a super deduction might also give the same economic result.

However, the variety of options potentially emerging from the Proposal only establishing a minimum floor puts into question whether the provision would realize its harmonization goal. This might be problematic from the perspective of the legal basis used for the directive’s adoption—Article 115 TFEU—as the Court of Justice requires that a directive genuinely aims at removing obstacles to the internal market. If the obstacle that the Proposal is aiming at removing is different R&D incentive rules across Member States, having a variety of (economically equivalent) incentives might not deliver on the objective. If the obstacle is facing different tax liabilities for businesses engaged in R&D activities across EU Member States, the provision does not fix that, as it does not establish a common corporate tax base and rate. Hence, it is suggested to clarify the scope of the R&D full expensing provision and the alternative regimes that would be equivalent to it.

Tax Foundation Europe considers the Proposal broadly favorable to the functioning of the internal market and focuses on two legal issues with implications for EU economic growth. First, eliminating the holding thresholds for withholding tax exemptions could strengthen the internal market, particularly if accompanied by simpler requirements for obtaining relief. Although the IRD amendments would shift taxing rights toward residence Member States, their uneven fiscal effects could be addressed through a statistical revenue sharing mechanism or by treating the corresponding amounts as an EU own resource. Second, the ATAD amendments blur the directive’s character as a minimum standard. Article 3 and the CFC provision should therefore distinguish expressly between mandatory and optional rules. The Proposal should also define which domestic R&D regimes are equivalent to full expensing by reference to a clear criterion, such as the real value of the deductions they provide.

However, this requires the creditable amount to coincide with the tax levied in the source state, and the taxpayer not to be in a loss position. See Ivan Lazarov, “Case Law Trend: Withholding Taxation Under the Fundamental Freedom,” Intertax 51:6 (2023).

Case C-319/02, Manninen. For an overview of the case-law, see, for instance, European Parliament, Directorate-General for Internal Policies, “The impact of the rulings of the European Court of Justice in the area of direct taxation 2010,” (2011), https://www.europarl.europa.eu/document/activities/cont/201203/20120313ATT40640/20120313ATT40640EN.pdf.
[3] This also applies to outbound dividend withholding taxes. See Joined Cases C-10/14, C-14/14 and C-17/14, Miljoen.

[5] Case C-513/04, Kerckhaert and Morres. In the literature, Georg Kofler and Ruth Mason, “Double Taxation: A European ‘Switch In Time?’” Columbia Journal of European Law (2007), https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=979750.

However, real-world cases are much more complex, as there are dividends with interest-like features and interest with dividend-like features. See Wolfgang Schön, “International Tax Coordination for a Second-Best World (Part II),” World Tax Journal, IBFD (2010).

[7] As per the OECD Model Convention, source states can levy a withholding tax on dividend income from portfolio investment at the rate of 15 percent and interest at 10 percent, while they would have to exempt royalties altogether. However, Member States can and do deviate from such model rules in their concrete treaty practice.

[8] Double tax conventions do not oblige the state of residence of the receiving company to grant a credit or an exemption for the corporate income tax paid by the distributing company on its profits, before distribution.

[9] As explained above, for dividend payments, the extent to which double taxation can remain within the EU is much smaller, as the Member State of the receiving company would have to relieve the recipient company in the same way that a company receiving domestic dividends is (Manninen).

[10] Triangular situations occur, for instance, if a company is a dual resident and receives income from sources in a third state, or if a company resident in one state receives income from another state that is attributable to a permanent establishment (PE) in a third state. The key issue arising from these situations is that the PE state is not required to apply the conditions of the treaty it has in force with the source state, as the PE is not entitled to treaty benefits in the PE state. See Emily Fett, Triangular Cases: The Application of Bilateral Income Tax Treaties in Multilateral Situations, IBFD, Doctoral Series (2014).
