articles.title: The 2020s: a horror film in four charts
articles.standfirst:
Last week’s Budget contained one truly terrifying statistic – the 2020s are set to be the worst decade for living standards on record, enjoying a tenth of the growth of the disappointing 2010s. Some things are important enough to dig deep. This blog is for those who don’t just want to watch the horror movie … Continued
The post The 2020s: a horror film in four charts appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: Last week’s Budget contained one truly terrifying statistic – the 2020s are set to be the worst decade for living standards on record, enjoying a tenth of the growth of the disappointing 2010s. Some things are important enough to dig deep. This blog is for those who don’t just want to watch the horror movie but who, like me, enjoy figuring out what’s really going on.

TL;DR it’s bad however you cut it. The typical family looks set to do even worse than the headline, as housing costs and taxes rise. But! There’s a twist in the final act that offers a glimmer of hope…

You first need to know two main characters: RHDI and HBAI. These are the two main measures of living standards, or the incomes of households over time. RHDI (Real Household Disposable Income) is derived from the national accounts – the macro data on the size of the economy and how much of that is going to households, divided by the number of people – and is forecast by the OBR. HBAI (Households Below Average Income) is a survey-based measure of what households’ incomes actually are; we produce our own projections of it and, throughout this blog, use the after-housing-costs version and focus on non-pensioner households. Crucially, HBAI lets us look at what is happening to households of different incomes and characteristics.

These characters are frenemies. RHDI is the big-budget blockbuster shown on Budget day – complete with special effects, like counting the rent homeowners notionally pay themselves as “income”. HBAI is the indie film about real people, released two years late. Both with their strengths and their drawbacks. We tend to avoid putting them on screen together because it gets a bit complicated when they get together – but it can be instructive to compare and contrast.

First, let’s check how these two measures (mean per-person RHDI, and median non-pensioner household income measured after housing costs) compare over different decades. They measure different things but the conclusion is the same: the 2020s are set to be the worst on record for living standards.

The gruesome detail is that typical non-pensioner household incomes are set to fall over the 2020s. I was particularly keen to dig into why we expect typical incomes to fall 3 per cent (a drop of over £1,000) over the next two years while the OBR is forecasting slowly growing RHDI. The chart below breaks down some of the differences between RHDI and HBAI in steps to try and get to the bottom of this.

Two differences stand out. First, housing costs (the difference between the red and green lines), which are deducted from HBAI, rise significantly over the next two years as mortgagors keep refixing at higher rates. The OBR expects the average effective mortgage rate to climb from around 4 per cent in 2026 to 4½ per cent in 2028. Second, a big chunk of the remaining difference (the gap between red and purple) is not explained by the obvious definitional differences. The most likely culprit is that on our reading of the OBR figures almost all of the RHDI growth over the next two years (around 0.9 of 1.1 percentage points) comes from non-labour income. Some of this isn’t cash in anyone’s pocket (homeowners’ imputed rent and pension fund returns), while the part that is – interest and dividends – is poorly captured in survey data and goes disproportionately to richer and older households.
2. The victims are spread across the landscape (of the income distribution…)

It’s all very well talking in averages, or about Mr and Mrs Median, but these can hide families with vastly different experiences. And this time what’s striking is how widely the pain is shared: as the chart below shows, living standards fall right across the income distribution, with no simple rich-versus-poor gradient.

The biggest falls are at the top, but the bottom is hit hard too – and a fall of this size bites far harder for a family with no savings to fall back on. Data can be less reliable for the very poorest households, but the data we do have suggests an extraordinarily difficult 8 per cent fall in living standards for the second-poorest twentieth of the population (we exclude the even-less-reliable bottom 5 per cent). The richest twentieth see the biggest drop. That owes something to tax changes falling especially at the top (and may be overstated if there is non-labour income growth that we are not capturing in our projections).

We showed in our TOTC Budget special that the gap in living standards (RHDI) between the 2020s and the rest of the post financial crisis period was not explained by disappointing growth – GDP per person grows at a similarly sluggish pace, between 0.6 and 0.7 per cent a year, in both periods. The main culprit is net taxes and benefits, which boosted household incomes after the financial crisis but drags on them through the 2020s. We’ve now learnt that the rise in housing costs is also crucial for typical non-pensioner households .

But there’s one more mystery. On the OBR’s forecast (combined with outturns), real average earnings are set to grow by just 1 per cent over the decade, while GDP per worker grows by around 6 per cent. But why? Did I miss a decoupling of earnings and growth?

Well, no – or rather, this decoupling is a feature of the OBR forecast, but not (yet) of the UK as it stands (see our final chart). Up to 2025-26, pay, GDP per worker and GDP per person moved roughly together (even if not by much!). But the OBR judges that, going forward, the labour share will fall back as firms rebuild their margins, and this, alongside consumer prices continuing to rise faster than the prices of what the UK produces, leads to the growing gap.

So, as we look away from Halloween and towards Christmas, here’s a glimmer of hope: if the OBR is wrong about this, then the 2020s could at least get better from here. If incomes grew over the last three years of the decade at the (hardly stellar) pace of the 2010s, RHDI growth this decade would be nearly three times what is now forecast. Still the worst decade on record – but more B-movie than horror show.

articles.title: Is Burnham right about joining the EU single market without a referendum?
articles.standfirst:
Andy Burnham’s Labour could make a case for offering a single market agreement without a referendum, but the Tories and Reform could pledge to reverse it on the same basis, writes Derrick Wyatt. The EU will be looking for stronger signs of UK commitment than this. Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a … Continued
The post Is Burnham right about joining the EU single market without a referendum? first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Andy Burnham’s Labour could make a case for offering a single market agreement without a referendum, but the Tories and Reform could pledge to reverse it on the same basis, writes Derrick Wyatt. The EU will be looking for stronger signs of UK commitment than this.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

Andy Burnham has said recently that options for future UK links with the EU include a return to the free movement of persons, joining the single market or a customs union, or joining the EU. Burnham has said that a new referendum would be needed to join the EU, but not necessarily to join the single market.

Burnham is right that it would be inconceivable for the UK to rejoin the EU without the backing of a referendum. EU membership involves such far-reaching legal and economic consequences, and would be so difficult and time-consuming to reverse, that simply winning a general election would fail to legitimise joining in the eyes of political parties and voters opposed to the move.

But he is wrong on the second point. If the UK made a single market agreement with the EU, along the lines of the EU/EFTA Agreement, under which Norway and Iceland participate in the single market, a referendum would still be necessary. Under such an agreement, whereby the UK signed up to free movement and the rest of the single market package, including agreeing to apply EU law as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the EU, and making financial contributions to EU projects, the effects for the UK would be analogous to those of full EU membership. A general election result alone would no more politically legitimise single market membership than re-joining the EU itself.

A single market agreement along the above lines would require the UK to apply new EU laws without having a say in their content. Single market rules cannot simply be dismissed as technical trade rules nobody cares about. Some regulate subject matter of political as well as economic importance, such as take-overs and mergers, the regulation of banks and insurance companies, and the rights of patients to go to other EU countries to receive health care at the expense of their home country funding bodies.

Under such an agreement, the EU rules on financial services which would apply to the UK could adversely affect London’s worldwide competitiveness as a financial centre, which could in turn affect the significant tax revenues received by the government from financial and related professional services. By virtue of the UK participating in the single market without being a full EU member, the governments of the EU countries which are home to London’s major competitors in finance -Paris and Frankfurt – would have a large say in the making of such rules, but the UK would have none.
That said, more Brits seem willing to accept the trade-off between perceived economic advantage, and the loss of democratic control implicit in rejoining the single market, than are opposed.
Polls in 2023 and 2024 showed absolute majorities for the UK joining the single market, accepting that that involves the free movement of persons.

According to the 2024 poll, even those intending to vote for Reform UK split 44 /45 per cent when asked if they would accept the free movement of persons if the UK could regain special access to the European market.
In a recent Messina poll, support was down from these earlier highs, but 45 per cent supported joining the single market, either strongly or somewhat, with 23 per cent opposed.

The democratic objections to joining the single market might be overcome if all EU rules applied in the UK had been approved by the UK Parliament, and if the UK was guaranteed a speedy exit if the EU insisted on the UK applying new rules the UK found impossible to accept.
Such an agreement could enter into force for the UK under an Act of Parliament, and suspend most of the current UK/EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA).

On this hypothesis, the UK Parliament would periodically consider new single market rules introduced by the EU, and vote on incorporating them into UK law. If Parliament accepted the new EU rules, they would be applied in the UK. If Parliament rejected a new piece of single market legislation, or overturned existing EU rules, the EU would be entitled to give notice to terminate the UK’s single market access in, say, one year, and the provisions of the TCA suspended by the single market agreement would be revived. In practice there could be wiggle room if the UK rejected EU legislation which mattered less to the EU than keeping the UK in the single market.
The UK and the EU could terminate the single market agreement anyway if they gave one year’s notice – which is the position in the EU/EFTA Agreement.

Terms of withdrawal, such as residence rights of migrants, and payment of outstanding financial contributions, could be agreed in advance. This would avoid termination of the single marker agreement leading to lengthy negotiations similar to the UK’s withdrawal from the EU and facilitate a smooth and speedy transition back to the TCA.

If these safeguards were adopted, one could argue that a referendum wouldn’t be necessary, because the UK Parliament’s role would not be undermined by EU law, and a speedy exit from the single market could always be ensured.
If the model discussed above were taken forward, no popular vote beyond that involved in the next general election would be needed to legitimise the initiative in democratic terms

But that approach might not prove attractive to the EU, and would suffer from an obvious political weakness. If Labour could take the UK into a single market agreement in the next Parliament without a referendum, the Tories or Reform could simply pledge to reverse the process in the Parliament after that.

The vulnerability of such an agreement to reversal by a hostile future UK government would be off-putting to the EU. Member States and EU institutions would be reluctant to expend time and energy negotiating the UK’s re-entry into the single market with the Labour government only to find that the Conservatives and Reform UK promised to overturn the agreement were they to come to power.

A YouGov poll in June this year showed 55 per cent supporting a return to the EU, with this support falling to 35 per cent if the UK had to re-join without its prior opt-outs. Burnham’s comments indicate he would want opt-outs from the euro and the border-check-free Schengen Area before he would back EU membership for the UK. This could receive a mixed reception across the Channel, but the forecast of two anonymous EU officials reported in Politico was that the EU would be flexible about this.

Burnham has ruled out an election in the next 12 months, but his airing of ambitious options for future EU links might only bring political advantage for as long as a European feel-good factor overshadowed too much argument over details such as the scale of UK financial contributions to the EU if the UK joined a single market agreement or the EU, and in the latter case the tricky question of opt-outs.

paragraphs: The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate by 25bps to 4% on Thursday. December’s meeting now looks like a coin flip, with the path of oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor

The committee’s messaging was more hawkish than before. Higher energy futures prices and more evidence of domestic resilience both increase the risk of second-round effects emerging. The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike is likely, in December or February.

The majority gave the impression that once Bank Rate reaches 4.25%, subsequent decisions will be a closer call. We continue to think that second-round effects on pay and margins will prove limited, so we maintain our forecast that Bank Rate will peak at 4.25%, but the risks are skewed to the upside.

articles.title: Japan sees limited AI-driven productivity gains in the near term
articles.standfirst: Generative AI should offer some support to Japan’s potential growth by boosting its total factor productivity, but less than in most other advanced economies in the near term. Slow adoption is likely to limit the gains.
paragraphs: Generative AI should offer some support to Japan’s potential growth by boosting its total factor productivity, but less than in most other advanced economies in the near term. Slow adoption is likely to limit the gains.

We think Japan has significant potential to benefit from generative AI, given its relatively high exposure to and preparedness for AI technology. The recent acceleration in corporates’ software investment in response to Japan’s severe labour shortages appears to have laid some of the groundwork for AI utilisation, while the country’s ICT capital stock still lags far behind that of the US.

However, in practice, adoption of new tech is likely to be slow. Japan has lagged behind on digitalisation for many years. The shortage of IT personnel is a key bottleneck, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises. Its adoption rate is beginning to fall behind those of other advanced economies and China.

There’s high uncertainty around AI’s impact on productivity. Our optimistic ‘AI breakthrough’ scenario features faster adoption and stronger productivity gains than in our baseline, pushing GDP 7ppts above our forecast by 2035. But this still wouldn’t fully offset the drag from the labour supply’s decline on potential growth.

On the downside, there’s considerable risk that the AI boost to workplace efficiency won’t translate into higher productivity at the macro level, given Japan’s rigid corporate structures and labour market practices, particularly among permanent employees. In a scenario of lower pass-through of efficiency gains from workers to the economy, together with slower adoption of the tech, Japan’s potential growth rate would turn negative by the mid-2030s.

articles.title: The State Tax Competitiveness Index Is Your Guide to Economic “Wins Above Replacement”
articles.standfirst: Taxes are an important part of the mix, and modernizing a state’s tax structure helps position it for growth. States that rank better on the Index have better-structured tax codes, and states with better-structured tax codes get Wins Above Replacement.
paragraphs: This week, we published our annual State Tax Competitiveness Index, an extremely valuable diagnostic tool comparing states’ taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. structures across more than 150 variables. Unlike most studies of state taxes, it is focused on the how more than the how much, in recognition of the fact that there are better and worse ways to raise revenue. Inevitably, though, the publication of the Index raises some questions, like: if Wyoming and South Dakota lead in the rankings, why aren’t more companies heading for the Black Hills?

Tax competition is a little like WAR—not conflict, but Wins Above Replacement. The term comes from baseball, where it is intended as a sabermetric statistic to measure how many more wins a team can claim due to a specific player above the amount that would be generated by a replacement-level player. It’s much the same in public finance: a well-structured tax code won’t make the Wyoming Basin a metropolis, nor will poor tax structure make Manhattan a ghost town. But tax structure does play a role in a state’s economic successes or failures, and often a substantial one. Every state can benefit from a simple, neutral, transparent, pro-growth tax structure.

The Index scores states across five sub-indices, each representing a major component of state tax codes: corporate taxes, individual income taxes, sales and excise taxes, property and wealth taxes, and unemployment insurance taxes. Rather than weighting each sub-index equally, their weight is determined according to the variance across states in each category, which has the effect of assigning more weight to areas where states have more room to compete.

Of course, it’s hard to introduce any structural flaws to the design of a tax one does not impose, so some states, by forgoing a tax altogether (the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax., or the sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. ), score perfectly on a sub-index or some portion of one. This is why states like Wyoming and South Dakota, which both forgo income taxes, do so well on the Index. States that can avoid imposing one or more of the major taxes either have to lean very heavily on the other major tax types (which can mean lower rankings on those components), choose to operate on leaner budgets, take advantage of natural resources like oil and gas, or have demographics (like Florida) where other taxes can generate a surprising amount of revenue.
In other words, the Wyoming model may not be possible in some states—but the Missouri, Utah, North Carolina, North Dakota, Idaho, Indiana, and Oklahoma models are.

Those states ranked 9th through 15th in this year’s Index. They also impose each of the major taxes, but at moderate rates and with comparatively well-designed tax structures. Many of these states have substantially modernized their tax codes over the past two decades: Utah beginning in 2006, Indiana starting in 2011, North Carolina with a string of reforms that began in 2013, Idaho beginning in 2022, North Dakota in 2023, and Missouri with a series of rate cuts and reforms in recent years, including capital gains taxA capital gains tax is levied on the profit made from selling an asset and is often in addition to corporate income taxes, frequently resulting in double taxation. These taxes create a bias against saving, leading to a lower level of national income by encouraging present consumption over investment. repeal in 2025. Oklahoma, too, has adopted tax reforms in recent years, including eliminating its marriage penaltyA marriage penalty is when a household’s overall tax bill increases due to a couple marrying and filing taxes jointly. A marriage penalty typically occurs when two individuals with similar incomes marry; this is true for both high- and low-income couples. and capital stock tax in 2024 and reducing its individual income tax rates and consolidating brackets effective in 2026.

For taxpayers, the Index is a good starting point for understanding how their state compares to its peers. But for policymakers and others interested in how to improve the structure of their state’s tax code, it’s more than that: it’s a valuable diagnostic tool, with tables that allow readers to compare their state to its peers on everything from throwback rules and the treatment of net operating losses to whether the individual income tax’s brackets are indexed and the state authorizes split-roll property taxation.

If you saddled South Dakota with New York’s tax code, the state would struggle. People are clearly willing to pay a premium to live in New York—on real estate, on consumer purchases, and yes, on taxes. But there are limits, to say nothing of the fact that a system that is bearable in Manhattan may be considerably more burdensome in Syracuse. And, as the former governor of New York noted repeatedly, even in states like New York, tax burdens and tax structures matter. New York actually dramatically improved in the corporate component of the Index several years ago due to meaningful corporate tax reforms adopted on a bipartisan basis.

So yes, we’ve heard your questions about whether we are really saying that businesses would rather be in Mitchell, South Dakota, than Manhattan, or Sioux Falls than San Francisco, and there’s clearly a lot more that goes into location decisions than just taxes—rates or structure. But taxes are something within policymakers’ control, and even within a given revenue target, there are better and worse ways to raise that revenue.

The Index measures tax structure, not all the other things businesses care about, like an educated workforce, quality of life, proximity to relevant markets, or even the weather—and some of these things involve trade-offs. Taxes, however, are an important part of the mix, and modernizing a state’s tax structure helps position it for growth. States that rank better on the Index have better-structured tax codes, and states with better-structured tax codes get Wins Above Replacement.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Janelle Fritts is a Senior Policy Analyst with the Tax Foundation’s Center for State Tax Policy. She is the lead researcher on the annual State Tax Competitiveness Index and serves as a resource to policymakers in their efforts to modernize and improve the structures of their state tax codes. Her work has been cited in The New York Times, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, and numerous state media outlets across the country.

articles.title: 2027 State Tax Competitiveness Index
articles.standfirst: The State Tax Competitiveness Index enables policymakers, taxpayers, and business leaders to gauge how their states’ tax systems compare. While there are many ways to show how much state governments collect in taxes, the Index evaluates how well states structure their tax systems and provides a road map for improvement.
paragraphs: The study before you, which has been published as the State Business Tax Climate Index since 2003, was rebranded as the State Tax Competitiveness Index for the 2025 edition to better reflect what it assesses: states’ overall tax competitiveness, not just the business tax climate. This wasn’t just an exercise in slapping a new title on the cover and calling it a day. Rather, we reworked the Index from the ground up to make it a better product.

For more than two decades, the Index has helped policymakers evaluate their tax codes, serving as a road map for reform. Each year, the study underwent methodological refinements—which we always outlined—to capture changing elements of the tax code, like the introduction of global intangible low-taxed income, which has since been changed to net CFC tested income, or the design of remote seller taxes following the Supreme Court’s Wayfair decision. But the pace of change has accelerated in recent years, with the adoption of the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the Supreme Court’s Wayfair decision, the rise of remote work and other outgrowths of the global pandemic (including a roiling of unemployment insurance tax regimes), the adoption of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the adoption of the nation’s first digital advertising taxes, and an emerging interest in new or expanded taxes on wealth, unrealized gains, data, digital products, and more.

We saw a need to address these more comprehensively, and to provide additional granularity in our evaluation of tax provisions already encompassed by the Index. The old Index did its job well. Indeed, independent evaluations demonstrated a strong correlation between Index ranks and state economic outcomes. But we wanted to expand and refresh the publication before it got stale, to stay ahead of new developments in tax. A refresh also gave us a chance to better systematize and rebalance the treatment of a few outlier state tax provisions that had to be shoehorned into the methodology of prior editions.

With the 2025 refresh, we did more than update the methodology and adopt a new name. We also rethought the presentation of the Index’s treasure trove of tax policy information. The Index’s 150+ variables are no longer hidden away in appendix tables, and the online publication, formerly just an interactive map accompanied by a lengthy PDF, was reimagined for a digital environment.

Now, each state receives its own summary, highlighting several of the most notable features of its tax code and explaining why it ranks as it does on the Index—along with some state-specific reforms that would improve its tax competitiveness. And users now have access to interactive, sortable, filterable datasets, in addition to some new visuals and historical rate tools. We invite you to explore. See your state’s policy choices on every variable in the Index. Add another state or two and compare them. Or drill down to a single variable or set of variables and see how all states perform on them.

This is the third year under the new methodology, but if you’re comparing our rankings this year to old editions from 2024 or before, you might notice that some ranks have shifted a bit more than we usually see from year to year. Some of that, of course, is simply because states have been incredibly busy recently, adopting significant changes to their tax codes. But some of it is due to our methodological changes.

To ensure an apples-to-apples comparison, and in the interest of transparency, we have backcast states’ rankings under the new methodology going back seven years prior to this current edition. These are the controlling rankings, and are the ones that should be cited to show actual movement by states in recent years. This is nothing new: we’ve always backcast to account for methodological revisions. What’s different in the new edition is the scope of the change, as we’ve added more variables and made more adjustments than in prior years.

Readers interested in the details of what has changed are invited to read on to learn about our revised methodology, and for explanations of our variables. Most readers, however, will likely wish to jump ahead to the overall rankings, their state’s page, or the newly interactive datasets.

For all readers, we hope that the 2027 State Tax Competitiveness Index will serve as a useful guide for navigating state tax policy. It ranks, both overall and across five subindices—corporate taxes, individual income taxes, sales and excise taxes, property and wealth taxes, and unemployment insurance taxes—how states compete, and where each has room to improve. And for would-be reformers, our datasets (now much more accessible!) are an invaluable guide to how states structure their tax codes, and where they diverge—for good and for ill—from their peers.

Even a good road map, however, is not always a sufficient substitute for a guide. That’s why the Tax Foundation has a team of state tax experts whose primary purpose is to help educate policymakers and the public. As always, we invite you to reach out with your questions. That’s why we’re here. Katherine Loughead Vice President of State Policy, Tax Foundation

The Tax Foundation’s State Tax Competitiveness Index enables policymakers, taxpayers, and business leaders to gauge how their states’ tax systems compare. While there are many ways to show how much state governments collect in taxes, the Index evaluates how well states structure their tax systems and provides a road map for improvement.[1]

The absence of a major tax is a common factor among many of the top 10 states. Property taxes and unemployment insurance taxes are levied in every state, but there are several states that do without one or more of the major taxes: the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax., the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, or the sales tax. South Dakota and Wyoming have no corporate or individual income tax; Alaska and New Hampshire have no individual income or state-level sales tax; Florida, Tennessee, and Texas have no individual income tax; and Montana has no sales tax.

This does not mean, however, that a state cannot rank well while still levying all the major taxes. Missouri and Utah, for example, levy all the major tax types, as do all the other states that rank 11th to 16th: North Carolina, North Dakota, Idaho, Indiana, Oklahoma, and Nebraska.

The states in the bottom 10 tend to have a number of issues in common: complex, nonneutral taxes with comparatively high rates. New Jersey, for example, is hampered by some of the highest property tax burdens in the country, has the highest-rate corporate income tax in the country, and has one of the highest-rate individual income taxes. Additionally, the state levies an inheritance taxAn inheritance tax is levied upon the value of inherited assets received by a beneficiary after a decedent’s death. Not to be confused with estate taxes, which are paid by the decedent’s estate based on the size of the total estate before assets are distributed, inheritance taxes are paid by the recipient or heir based on the value of the bequest received. and maintains some of the nation’s worst-structured individual income taxes.

Of course, it is difficult to introduce any structural flaws to the design of a tax one does not impose, so some states, by forgoing a tax altogether (the individual income tax, the corporate income tax, or the sales tax) score perfectly on a subindex or some portion of one. But for policymakers and others interested in how to improve the structure of their state’s tax code, it’s more than that: it’s a valuable diagnostic tool, with tables that allow readers to compare their state to its peers on a wide range of factors—tax rates, yes, but also throwback rules, the treatment of net operating losses, recapture provisions, indexation, spit roll taxation, convenience rules, expensing, and much more.

And even in states like New York tax burdens, and tax structures, matter.
Taxes are not everything, but they do matter, and they are within the control of policymakers. Even within a given revenue target, there are better and worse ways to raise revenue.

States that rank better on the Index have better-structured tax codes, and states with better-structured tax codes get Wins Above Replacement.

Arizona fell three places overall, from 14th to 17th. Arizona passed conformity legislation with several retroactive provisions, but since the legislation contained no emergency clause, the retroactivity was not legally in effect as of the Index’s snapshot date of July 1, 2026. This timing, in addition to not conforming to full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. under Section 168(k), resulted in its corporate income tax ranking falling from 16th to 20th. Arizona’s fiscal year 2027 budget, which took effect on July 1, 2026, included a three-year moratorium on tax incentives on new data center tax projects, with a resulting drop in the state’s sales and use tax ranking from 35th to 40th due to the suspension of sales tax exemptions for the qualifying equipment purchases of new data centers. The state’s tangible personal property (TPP) tax exemptionA tax exemption excludes certain income, revenue, or even taxpayers from tax altogether. For example, nonprofits that fulfill certain requirements are granted tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), preventing them from having to pay income tax. increased from $269,905 to $500,000, slightly improving its property and wealth tax ranking.

Despite reductions to its top individual income tax rate (from 3.9 percent to 3.7 percent), Arkansas fell 3 spots overall to 32nd. This was driven largely by other states’ improvements in combination with Arkansas’s continued nonconformity with the federal full expensing allowance under Section 168(k), causing its corporate income tax ranking to fall nine places to 19th.

Georgia dropped from 18th to 24th in its overall ranking, driven largely by a reduction in its corporate income tax score. Georgia did not conform to the competitive corporate expensing provisions in the OBBBA, including Section 168(n), leading the state to be passed by competitors like Kansas and Oklahoma, which conformed to expensing provisions or reduced their individual income tax rates. Georgia also partially exempted tips and overtime pay from its individual income tax, narrowing the base.

Idaho’s ranking fell four places overall (from 9th to 13th), including falling eight places on the individual income tax component, primarily due to the state’s decision to conform to the OBBBA’s temporary individual deductions for tips and overtime. Conforming to these provisions costs the state a substantial amount of revenue without generating much economic growth.

Indiana fell three spots, to 14th overall. Despite a low, flat state individual income tax rate of 2.95 percent, Indiana authorizes counties to impose local income taxes at rates that nearly double the combined rate in some jurisdictions. Additionally, Indiana narrows its tax base by offering income tax deductions for qualified tips and overtime pay. As a result, Indiana’s individual income tax ranking fell from 21st to 28th. Indiana does not conform to key expensing provisions, including Section 168(k) and Section 174A, while several competing states do. As a result, its corporate income tax ranking fell from 7th to 11th. Indiana maintains a property and wealth tax ranking of 4th, due in part to the increase to its tangible personal property (TPP) tax exemption from $80,000 to $2 million.

Iowa fell just slightly on this year’s Index, from 17th to 18th overall. One major variable change was its individual income tax ranking, falling eight places to 18th. Because Iowa uses federal taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. as the starting point for state income tax liability, newer federal provisions such as no tax on tips, overtime, and auto loans narrow the state’s individual income tax base. Additionally, five states that climbed ahead of Iowa on this component further reduced their flat and top marginal income tax rates (Georgia, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Utah). While Iowa’s individual ranking fell several spots on the Index, this was offset as its corporate income tax ranking rose eight places to 17th due to conforming to full bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. and decoupling from the taxation of net CFC tested income. Prior-year unemployment insurance tax reforms have continued to improve Iowa’s ranking on this portion of the Index, moving it from 35th to 30th.

Kansas’ ranking improved four places overall (from 23rd to 19th), including seven places on the corporate tax component and five places on the individual income tax component. These improvements were primarily attributable to Kansas’ rolling conformity to the OBBBA’s pro-growth business expensing provisions. Kansas did fall seven places, however, on the property tax component, due in part to a substantial increase in the state’s property tax collections per capita.

As part of the final phase-in of the 2024 tax reform package, Louisiana saw a 17-place improvement in its property tax rank due to the elimination of the state’s capital stock tax, a damaging tax that taxes businesses regardless of profit. This, along with newly allowing S corporations to file through the individual income tax, helped boost Louisiana from 32nd to 23rd overall.

Maine slid seven places, from 33rd to 40th, with the adoption of a 2 percent “high-income surcharge” that brings the state’s top individual income tax rate to 9.15 percent on incomes over $1 million. The new rate also includes a large marriage penaltyA marriage penalty is when a household’s overall tax bill increases due to a couple marrying and filing taxes jointly. A marriage penalty typically occurs when two individuals with similar incomes marry; this is true for both high- and low-income couples. and gives Maine the eighth-highest top rate in the country.

Michigan’s score was very close to several other states in 2026 but fell behind them in 2027 when it did not conform to the improved expensing provisions in the OBBBA. Combined with a new exemption for tipped and overtime income and a comparatively low Section 179 limit, the Great Lake State dropped 9 places overall, from 16th to 25th, and from 18th all the way to 30th on the individual income tax component.

Mississippi saw its individual income tax score improve from 34th to 29th, due to an income tax rate reduction from 4.4 to 4 percent. Mississippi also decreased its capital stock tax rate from 0.075 percent to 0.05 percent. However, due to other states also improving, Mississippi’s overall rank fell one place, from 26th to 27th.

Missouri saw its overall rank improve from 12th to 9th this year, breaking into the Index’s top 10. Part of this score increase came from conforming to the new and increased expensing provisions included in the OBBBA. Unlike Idaho, Indiana, and North Dakota, which fell behind, the Show-Me State resisted conforming to the exemptions for tipped and overtime pay, which would have narrowed its income tax base.

Montana’s overall ranking fell two spots, from 5th to 7th. Although a lower top income tax rate of 5.65 percent and the elimination of the state’s marriage penalty took effect this year, Montana’s individual income tax ranking fell from 13th to 21st. Because Montana uses federal taxable income as the starting point for state income tax liability, newer federal provisions such as no tax on tips, overtime, and auto loans narrow the state’s individual income tax base. Additionally, five states that climbed ahead of Montana on this component further reduced their flat and top marginal income tax rates (Georgia, Kentucky, Nebraska, North Carolina, and Oklahoma). Montana’s conformity to full bonus depreciation under Section 168(k) and Section 174A contributed to its corporate income tax ranking improving from 26th to 18th. The continued phase-in of Montana’s tiered-structure property tax reforms contributed to it falling from 16th to 20th on the property and wealth tax variable.

Nebraska improved eight places overall, from 24th to 16th, due to the continued phase-down of its income tax rates. The state’s top individual income tax rate decreased from 5.2 percent to 4.55 percent, with a resulting elimination of its fourth bracket, moving Nebraska from 22nd to 13th on the individual income tax component. The state’s flat corporate rate also decreased to 4.55 percent, and its conformity to full bonus depreciation has allowed the Cornhusker State’s corporate tax rank to climb four spots to 9th.

New Mexico improved three places, from 31st to 28th overall, because the state automatically conformed to the restoration of first-year expensing for research and experimentation expenses, and to the higher cap for small business expensing under Section 179, while some of its peer states did not.

North Carolina rose two spots overall from 13th to 11th. An individual income tax rate reduction from 4.25 percent to 3.99 percent improved its individual income tax ranking, with the state moving up four spots to 19th. The state’s corporate ranking remained relatively stable. Although North Carolina does not conform to federal bonus depreciation provisions, it continues to levy the nation’s lowest corporate income tax rate among states that impose one. That rate declined further this year from 2.25 to 2.0 percent.

Ohio moved from a graduated-rate individual income tax to a flat individual income tax at a lower rate of 2.75 percent, improving its individual income tax ranking five places, from 38th to 33rd, while helping improve the state’s overall ranking from 38th to 36th.

As a result of tax bills passed in 2025, Oklahoma moved from six individual income tax brackets to three, and from a top rate of 4.75 to 4.5 percent, improving the state’s individual income tax rank by 13 places. The state also conformed to the improved expensing treatment enacted by the OBBBA, while resisting the option to exempt tips and overtime pay from the income tax. All these improvements brought Oklahoma’s rank from 19th to 15th overall.

South Carolina passed rate reductions this year, bringing its top individual income tax rate from 6 percent to 5.21 percent. However, the scoring benefit of the rate reduction was outweighed by its lagged general conformity, low Section 179 limitation, and lack of Section 168(n) expensing. In the end, South Carolina’s overall ranking dropped six spots, from 28th to 34th.

Utah improved five places, to 10th overall, as the state conformed to pro-growth provisions of the OBBBA from which some of its peers decoupled. Utah trimmed its individual and corporate income tax rates to 4.45 percent, building on years of modest rate reductions. More substantially, however, it conformed to the restoration of first-year expensing for both manufacturing machinery and equipment and for research and experimentation expenses. Utah also conformed to the new higher small business expensing cap under Section 179, and its inflation-adjusted tangible personal property (TPP) tax de minimis exemption improved relative to states with unindexed exemptions. Utah’s greatest improvement was in its corporate tax component, where its rank improved 7 places, from 15th to 8th.

Virginia fell four places overall to 31st, a decline mostly attributable to other states adopting competitive reforms while the Commonwealth stood still. Virginia’s corporate tax ranking dropped the most compared with its other Index rankings, sliding from 17th to 24th. While many states conform to full bonus depreciation under Section 168(k) and Section 174A, Virginia remains decoupled from these provisions. Additionally, the Commonwealth allows municipalities to establish local gross receipts taxes, further reducing its competitiveness.

Although Washington’s overall rank fell one place, from 46th to 47th, the state improved five places on the property and wealth tax component after reverting the top estate tax rate from 35 percent to 20 percent. The inclusion of digital advertising in the sales tax base, part of a broader expansion of business-to-business taxation of digital products, dropped Washington’s sales and excise tax component rank from 49th to 50th. A recently adopted 9.9 percent tax on income above $1 million goes into effect in 2028 and does not affect current rankings.

West Virginia’s ranking improved six places overall (from 35th to 29th), including seven places on the corporate component and five places on the individual component, due to the state’s conformity to the OBBBA’s business expensing provisions. However, West Virginia fell five places on the property tax component due to changes that exacerbated the state’s property tax split roll ratio, shifting more of the property tax burden onto commercial properties, and due to an increase in the state’s property tax collections per capita.

Arkansas already saw an individual income tax rate reduction in 2026, but in 2027, the state’s corporate income tax rate is scheduled to fall to 4.1 percent. As such, that change falls outside of the snapshot date for this edition but will affect future years’ scores.

As part of a tax reform package passed this year, Georgia’s top individual income tax rate will fall by 0.125 percentage points annually if revenue thresholds are met, with the standard deductionThe standard deduction reduces a taxpayer’s taxable income by a set amount determined by the government. If those tax changes are triggered, Georgia will see Index score improvements in coming years.

In May 2026, Hawaii lawmakers adopted a new, additional tax bracket with a rate of 13 percent on residents with incomes over $500,000 ($1 million for married filers). While this change does not take effect until 2027, Hawaii can expect to see a drop in both its individual income tax rank and overall rank in coming years, much like Maine has seen in the current Index.

In June 2026, Illinois adopted a budget that included several new and increased taxes. Several of these new taxes, including a targeted advertising services tax, a digital asset tax, and a social media platform fee, are scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027, affecting Illinois’ performance on the 2028 Index.

In May 2026, Iowa lawmakers enacted legislation establishing a property tax levy limit for counties and municipalities. Because the new levy limit does not take effect until 2027, the change falls outside of this year’s snapshot of the Index.

In early 2026, New Mexico lawmakers enacted a law decoupling the state from the expensing provisions in Sections 168(k) and 168(n) of the IRC. The same act newly expands the corporate tax base to include NCTI, an aggressive change that can create double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. of foreign income. As these changes do not take effect until January 1, 2027, they will negatively impact New Mexico’s score in future Index editions.

Since the state adopted a tax reform package in 2021, North Carolina’s individual and corporate income tax rates have seen repeated reductions. If revenues follow projections, the individual income tax rate will drop to 3.49 percent in 2027 and 2.99 percent in 2028. Also in 2028, the corporate rate is scheduled to drop to 1 percent, with total elimination of the corporate income tax planned for 2030.

H 7127 was adopted, creating a new three percentage-point surtax on individual income over $1 million. This policy change will phase in over three years, raising the state’s top marginal individual income tax rate from 5.99 in 2026 to 6.99 percent in 2027, 7.99 percent in 2028, and 8.99 percent in 2029. This change will hurt Rhode Island’s performance on future editions of the Index.

Utah enacted a tax on “targeted advertising” in 2026, which, while ostensibly broad, practically includes digital advertising alone. This change takes effect in January 2027, so it does not affect Utah’s score for this edition but will be reflected in next year’s Index.

Despite the state’s judicial history of ruling against income taxes, Washington lawmakers adopted a new 9.9 percent tax in 2026 on income above $1 million. This tax will go into effect in 2028, likely facing legal questions before then, and significantly affecting the state’s future Index scores.

Taxation is inevitable, but the specifics of a state’s tax structure matter greatly. The measure of total taxes paid is relevant, but other elements of a state tax system can also enhance or harm the competitiveness of a state’s business environment. The State Tax Competitiveness Index distills many complex considerations to an easy-to-understand ranking.

The modern market is characterized by mobile capital and labor, with all types of businesses, small and large, tending to locate where they have the greatest competitive advantage. The evidence shows that states with the best tax systems will be the most competitive at attracting new businesses and most effective at generating economic and employment growth. It is true that taxes are but one factor in business decision-making. Other concerns also matter–such as access to raw materials or infrastructure or a skilled labor pool–but a simple, sensible tax system can positively impact business operations with regard to these resources. Furthermore, unlike changes to a state’s health-care, transportation, or education systems, which can take decades to implement, changes to the tax code can quickly improve a state’s competitiveness.

It is important to remember that even in our global economy, states’ stiffest competition often comes from other states. The Department of Labor reports that most mass job relocations are from one US state to another rather than to a foreign location.[2] Certainly, job creation is rapid overseas, as previously underdeveloped nations enter the world economy, though in the aftermath of federal tax reform, US businesses no longer face the third-highest corporate tax rate in the world, but rather one in line with averages for industrialized nations.[3] State lawmakers are right to be concerned about how their states rank in the global competition for jobs and capital, but they need to be more concerned with companies moving from Detroit, Michigan, to Dayton, Ohio, than from Detroit to New Delhi, India. This means that state lawmakers must be aware of how their states’ business climates match up against their immediate neighbors and to other regional competitor states.

Anecdotes about the impact of state tax systems on business investment are plentiful. In Illinois in the early 2000s, hundreds of millions of dollars of capital investments were delayed when then-Governor Rod Blagojevich (D) proposed a hefty gross receipts taxGross receipts taxes are applied to a company’s gross sales, without deductions for a firm’s business expenses, like compensation, costs of goods sold, and overhead costs. Unlike a sales tax, a gross receipts tax is assessed on businesses and applies to transactions at every stage of the production process, leading to tax pyramiding..[4] Only when the legislature resoundingly defeated the bill did the investment resume. In 2005, California-based Intel decided to build a multibillion-dollar chip-making facility in Arizona due to its favorable corporate income tax system.[5] In 2010, Northrup Grumman chose to move its headquarters to Virginia over Maryland, citing the better business tax climate.[6] In 2015, General Electric and Aetna threatened to decamp from Connecticut if the governor signed a budget that would increase corporate tax burdens, and General Electric actually did so.[7] Anecdotes such as these reinforce what we know from economic theory: taxes matter to businesses, and those places with the most competitive tax systems will reap the benefits of business-friendly tax climates.

Tax competition is an unpleasant reality for state revenue and budget officials, but it is an effective restraint on state and local taxes. When a state imposes higher taxes than a neighboring state, businesses will cross the border to some extent. Therefore, states with more competitive tax systems score well in the Index because they are best suited to generate economic growth.

State lawmakers are mindful of their states’ tax competitiveness, but they are sometimes tempted to lure businesses with lucrative tax incentives and subsidies instead of broad-based tax reform. This can be a dangerous proposition, as the example of Dell Computers and North Carolina illustrates. North Carolina agreed to $240 million worth of incentives to lure Dell to the state. Many of the incentives came in the form of tax credits from the state and local governments. Unfortunately, Dell announced in 2009 that it would be closing the plant after only four years of operations.[8] A 2007 USA TODAY article chronicled similar problems other states have had with companies that receive generous tax incentives.[9]

Lawmakers make these deals under the banner of job creation and economic development, but the truth is that if a state needs to offer such packages, it is most likely covering for an undesirable business tax climate. A far more effective approach is the systematic improvement of the state’s business tax climate for the long term to improve the state’s competitiveness. When assessing which changes to make, lawmakers need to remember two rules:

To some extent, tax-induced economic distortions are a fact of life, but policymakers should strive to maximize the occasions when businesses and individuals are guided by business principles and minimize those cases where economic decisions are influenced, micromanaged, or even dictated by a tax system. The more riddled a tax system is with politically motivated preferences, the less likely it is that business decisions will be made in response to market forces. The Index rewards those states that minimize tax-induced economic distortions.

Ranking the competitiveness of 50 very different tax systems presents many challenges, especially when a state dispenses with a major tax entirely. Should Utah’s tax system, which includes three relatively neutral taxes on sales, individual income, and corporate income, be considered more or less competitive than Alaska’s tax system, which includes a particularly burdensome corporate income tax but no statewide tax on individual income or sales?

The Index deals with such questions by comparing the states on more than 150 variables in the five major areas of taxation (corporate taxes, individual income taxes, sales and excise taxes, unemployment insurance taxes, and property and wealth taxes) and then adding the results to yield a final, overall ranking. This approach rewards states on particularly strong aspects of their tax systems (or penalizes them on particularly weak aspects), while measuring the general competitiveness of their overall tax systems. The result is a score that can be compared to other states’ scores. Ultimately, both Alaska and Utah score well.

Economists have not always agreed on how individuals and businesses react to taxes. As early as 1956, Charles Tiebout postulated that if citizens were faced with an array of communities that offered different types or levels of public goods and services at different costs or tax levels, then all citizens would choose the community that best satisfied their particular demands, revealing their preferences by “voting with their feet.” Tiebout’s article is the seminal work on the topic of how taxes affect the location decisions of taxpayers.

Tiebout suggested that citizens with high demands for public goods would concentrate in communities with high levels of public services and high taxes, while those with low demands would choose communities with low levels of public services and low taxes. Competition among jurisdictions results in a variety of communities, each with residents who all value public services similarly.

However, businesses sort out the costs and benefits of taxes differently from individuals. For businesses, which can be more mobile and must earn profits to justify their existence, taxes reduce profitability. Theoretically, businesses could be expected to be more responsive than individuals to the lure of low-tax jurisdictions. Research suggests that corporations engage in “yardstick competition,” comparing the costs of government services across jurisdictions. Shleifer (1985) first proposed comparing regulated franchises in order to determine efficiency. Salmon (1987) extended Shleifer’s work to look at subnational governments. Besley and Case (1995) showed that “yardstick competition” affects voting behavior, and Bosch and Sole-Olle (2006) further confirmed the results found by Besley and Case. Tax changes that are out of sync with neighboring jurisdictions will impact voting behavior. In a recent study, De Paula et al. (2025) found that the nature of tax competition among US states changes over time and that “economic” neighbors may play an even more important role in tax-setting behavior than geographic neighbors.

The economic literature over the past 60 years has slowly cohered around this hypothesis. Ladd (1998) summarizes the post-World War II empirical tax research literature in an excellent survey article, breaking it down into three distinct periods of differing ideas about taxation: (1) taxes do not change behavior; (2) taxes may or may not change business behavior depending on the circumstances; and (3) taxes definitely change behavior.

Period one, with the exception of Tiebout, included the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s and is summarized succinctly in three survey articles: Due (1961), Oakland (1978), and Wasylenko (1981). Due’s was a polemic against tax giveaways to businesses, and his analytical techniques consisted of basic correlations, interview studies, and the examination of taxes relative to other costs. He found no evidence to support the notion that taxes influence business location. Oakland was skeptical of the assertion that tax differentials at the local level had no influence at all. However, because econometric analysis was relatively unsophisticated at the time, he found no significant results to support his intuition. Wasylenko’s survey of the literature found some of the first evidence indicating that taxes do influence business location decisions. However, the statistical significance was lower than that of other factors, such as labor supply and agglomeration economies. Therefore, he dismissed taxes as a secondary factor at most.

Period two was a brief transition during the early to mid-1980s. This was a time of great ferment in tax policy as Congress passed major tax bills, including the so-called Reagan tax cut in 1981 and a dramatic reform of the federal tax code in 1986. Articles revealing the economic significance of tax policy proliferated and became more sophisticated. For example, Wasylenko and McGuire (1985) extended the traditional business location literature to nonmanufacturing sectors and found, “Higher wages, utility prices, personal income tax rates, and an increase in the overall level of taxation discourage employment growth in several industries.” However, Newman and Sullivan (1988) still found a mixed bag in “their observation that significant tax effects [only] emerged when models were carefully specified.”

Ladd was writing in 1998, so her “period three” started in the late 1980s and continued up to 1998, when the quantity and quality of articles increased significantly. Articles that fit into period three begin to surface as early as 1985, as Helms (1985) and Bartik (1985) put forth forceful arguments based on empirical research that taxes guide business decisions. Helms concluded that a state’s ability to attract, retain, and encourage business activity is significantly affected by its pattern of taxation. Furthermore, tax increases significantly retard economic growth when the revenue is used to fund transfer payments. Bartik concluded that the conventional view that state and local taxes have little effect on business is false.

Papke and Papke (1986) found that tax differentials among locations may be an important business location factor, concluding that consistently high business taxes can represent a hindrance to the location of industry. Interestingly, they use the same type of after-tax model used by Tannenwald (1996), who reaches a different conclusion.

Bartik (1989) provides strong evidence that taxes have a negative impact on business start-ups. He finds specifically that property taxes, because they are paid regardless of profit, have the strongest negative effect on business. Bartik’s econometric model also predicts tax elasticities of -0.1 to -0.5 that imply a 10 percent cut in tax rates will increase business activity by 1 to 5 percent. Bartik’s findings, as well as those of Mark, McGuire, and Papke (2000), and ample anecdotal evidence of the importance of property taxes, buttress the argument for inclusion of a property index devoted to property-type taxes in the Index.
By the early 1990s, the literature had expanded sufficiently for Bartik (1991) to identify 57 studies on which to base his literature survey. Ladd succinctly summarizes Bartik’s findings:

The large number of studies permitted Bartik to take a different approach from the other authors. Instead of dwelling on the results and limitations of each individual study, he looked at them in the aggregate and in groups. Although he acknowledged potential criticisms of individual studies, he convincingly argued that some systematic flaw would have to cut across all studies for the consensus results to be invalid. In striking contrast to previous reviewers, he concluded that taxes have quite large and significant effects on business activity.

Ladd’s “period three” surely continues to this day. Agostini and Tulayasathien (2001) examined the effects of corporate income taxes on the location of foreign direct investment in US states. They determined that for “foreign investors, the corporate tax rate is the most relevant tax in their investment decision.” Therefore, they found that foreign direct investment was quite sensitive to states’ corporate tax rates. More recently, Agostini (2007) presented further evidence that foreign direct investment in manufacturing is sensitive to changes in state corporate tax rates, and also showed that the apportionmentApportionment is the determination of the percentage of a business’s profits subject to a given jurisdiction’s corporate income tax or other business tax. US states apportion business profits based on some combination of the percentage of company property, payroll, and sales located within their borders. formula plays a key role in determining the effective tax rate faced by corporations and significantly influences the location of foreign direct investment.

Mark, McGuire, and Papke (2000) found that taxes are a statistically significant factor in private-sector job growth. Specifically, they found that personal property taxes and sales taxes have economically large negative effects on the annual growth of private employment.

Harden and Hoyt (2003) point to Phillips and Gross (1995) as another study contending that taxes impact state economic growth, and they assert that the consensus among recent literature is that state and local taxes negatively affect employment levels. Harden and Hoyt conclude that the corporate income tax has the most significant negative impact on the rate of growth in employment.

Gupta and Hofmann (2003) regressed capital expenditures on a variety of factors, including weights of apportionment formulas, the number of tax incentives, and burden figures. Their model covered 14 years of data and determined that firms tend to locate property in states where they are subject to lower income tax burdens. Furthermore, Gupta and Hofmann suggest that throwback requirements are the most influential on the location of capital investment, followed by apportionment weights and tax rates, and that investment-related incentives have the least impact.

Recent research focuses on the relationship between tax policy and entrepreneurship. Curtis and Decker (2018) study the effects of different tax structures on new firm activity and find that new firm employment is significantly and negatively affected by state corporate income tax rates, but not by individual income or sales tax rates. The authors conclude that young firms are more responsive to changes in state corporate taxes than more mature firms. This finding is in line with the results from a large cross-national study (Djankov et al., 2010), which concludes that a 10 percentage point increase in the effective corporate tax rate reduces entry of new firms by 17.5 percent.

Another strand of research focuses on the tax treatment of capital investment. Chirinko and Wilson (2008) document a growing significance of investment tax credits in state corporate tax codes. They find that capital formation in a state is increased by tax-induced reductions in the price of capital and is reduced by similar reductions in competitor states. Specifically, the authors demonstrate that the number of manufacturing establishments around state borders is higher on the side of the border with the lower price of capital.

In a later paper, Chirinko and Wilson (2023) find that the effects of job creation tax credits are smaller in the short run (meaning these credits are less effective as a countercyclical tool) and more meaningful in the long run (implying they can be effective as an economic development tool). However, Jolley et al. (2015), in their survey of business executives in North Carolina, find that these executives generally prefer tax reductions to selective tax incentives, regardless of whether their firm actually received any incentives from the state. The Index favors broad-based relief over targeted jobs incentives.

Other economists have found that taxes on specific products can produce behavioral results similar to those that were found in these general studies. For example, Fleenor (1998) looked at the effect of excise tax differentials between states on cross-border shopping and the smuggling of cigarettes. Moody and Warcholik (2004) examined the cross-border effects of beer excises. Their results, supported by the literature in both cases, showed significant cross-border shopping and smuggling between low-tax states and high-tax states.

Fleenor found that shopping areas sprouted in counties of low-tax states that shared a border with a high-tax state, and that approximately 13.3 percent of the cigarettes consumed in the United States during FY 1997 were procured via some type of cross-border activity. Similarly, Moody and Warcholik found that in 2000, 19.9 million cases of beer, on net, moved from low- to high-tax states. This amounted to some $40 million in sales and excise tax revenue lost in high-tax states.

Although the literature has largely congealed around a general consensus that taxes are a substantial factor in the decision-making process for businesses, disputes remain, and some scholars are unconvinced.

Based on a substantial review of the literature on business climates and taxes, Wasylenko (1997) concludes that taxes do not appear to have a substantial effect on economic activity among states. However, his conclusion is premised on there being few significant differences in state tax systems. He concedes that high-tax states will lose economic activity to average or low-tax states “as long as the elasticity is negative and significantly different from zero.” Indeed, he approvingly cites a State Policy Reports article that finds that the highest-tax states have acknowledged that high taxes may be responsible for the low rates of job creation in those states.[10]

Wasylenko’s rejoinder is that policymakers routinely overestimate the degree to which tax policy affects business location decisions and that as a result of this misperception, they respond readily to public pressure for jobs and economic growth by proposing lower taxes. According to Wasylenko, other legislative actions are likely to accomplish more positive economic results because in reality, taxes do not drive economic growth.

However, there is ample evidence that states compete for businesses using their tax systems. A notable example comes from Illinois, where in early 2011 lawmakers passed two major tax increases. The individual income tax rate increased from 3 percent to 5 percent, and the corporate income tax rate rose from 7.3 percent to 9.5 percent.[11] The result was that many businesses threatened to leave the state, including some very high-profile Illinois companies such as Sears and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. By the end of the year, lawmakers had cut deals with both firms, totaling $235 million over the next decade, to keep them from leaving the state.[12]

Funderburg et al. (2013) study the effects of state and local business taxes on value added in 15 manufacturing sectors across a subset of states and find that a 10 percent reduction in tax liability on new investment corresponds to a 3.5–5.3 percent increase in value added by the manufacturing sector. These estimates represent the higher end of the range found in prior research (Bartik 1991; Wasylenko 1997).

Giroud and Rauh (2019) use microdata on multistate firms to estimate the impact of state taxes on business activity and find that C corporation employment and establishments have short-run corporate tax elasticities of -0.4 to -0.5, while pass-through entities show elasticities of -0.2 to -0.4. This means that, for each percentage-point increase in the rate, employment decreases by 0.4 to 0.5 percent for C corporations subject to the corporate income tax, and by 0.2 to 0.4 percent within pass-through businesses subject to the individual income tax.

Chow et al. (2022) find that state corporate income taxes significantly affect corporations’ decisions on where to locate their headquarters, an important consideration for both businesses and states. Specifically, they find that a 1 percentage point increase in the corporate income tax rate raises the likelihood of corporations relocating their headquarters out of the state by 16.8 percent, while a corresponding decrease lowers that likelihood by 9.1 percent. This result complements the broader literature (often conducted in a federal or international context) which shows that reducing the effective corporate income tax rate leads to higher capital investment, lower debt (Ohrn 2018), and increased entrepreneurial activity, including that financed by foreign direct investment (Djankov et al. 2010).

A new literature review, Kleven et al. (2020), summarizes recent evidence for tax-driven migration. While the empirical results reviewed in this article are context-specific and do not always show a significant relationship between taxes and migration, there is a general consensus that high-income individuals are particularly sensitive to tax increases, both internationally and within countries. Specifically, inventors, entrepreneurs, sport stars, and billionaires have been shown to be highly mobile within the United States and responsive to major income and estate tax changes (Moretti and Wilson 2017; Akcigit et al. 2022; Moretti and Wilson 2023; Agrawal and Tester 2024).

Rauh and Shyu (2024) analyze Proposition 30 in California, which increased the top marginal income tax rate by three percentage points in 2012, and demonstrate that high earners reported $321,000–$436,000 less in taxable income in the first three years following the reform—about 10 percent of their baseline income of $4.15 million—in response to this major tax increase. They also show that there was a meaningful outmigration effect, which increased with income and was concentrated among top earners. Together, these responses eroded approximately 61 percent of the potential windfall tax revenue from Proposition 30 within two years of the reform.

Some recent contributions to the literature on state taxation criticize business and tax climate studies in general.[13] Authors of such studies contend that comparative reports like the State Tax Competitiveness Index do not take into account those factors that directly impact a state’s business climate. However, a careful examination of these criticisms reveals that the authors believe taxes are unimportant to businesses and therefore dismiss the studies as merely being designed to advocate low taxes.

Peter Fisher’s Grading Places: What Do the Business Climate Rankings Really Tell Us? now published by Good Jobs First, criticizes four indices: The U.S. Business Policy Index published by the Small Business and Entrepreneurship Council, Beacon Hill’s Competitiveness Report, the American Legislative Exchange Council’s Rich States, Poor States, and the previous version of the study. The first edition also critiqued the Cato Institute’s Fiscal Policy Report Card and the Economic Freedom Index by the Pacific Research Institute. In the report’s first edition, published before Fisher summarized his objections: “The underlying problem with the … indexes, of course, is twofold: none of them actually do a very good job of measuring what it is they claim to measure, and they do not, for the most part, set out to measure the right things to begin with” (Fisher 2005). In the second edition, he identified three overarching questions: (1) whether the indices included relevant variables, and only relevant variables; (2) whether these variables measured what they purport to measure; and (3) how the index combines these measures into a single index number (Fisher 2013). Fisher’s primary argument is that if the indexes did what they purported to do, then all five would rank the states similarly.

Fisher’s conclusion holds little weight because the five indices serve such dissimilar purposes, and each group has a different area of expertise. There is no reason to believe that the Tax Foundation’s Index, which depends entirely on state tax laws, would rank the states in the same or similar order as an index that includes crime rates, electricity costs, and health care (the Small Business and Entrepreneurship Council’s Small Business Survival Index), or infant mortality rates and the percentage of adults in the workforce (Beacon Hill’s State Competitiveness Report), or charter schools, tort reform, and minimum wage laws (the Pacific Research Institute’s Economic Freedom Index).

The Tax Foundation’s State Tax Competitiveness Index is an indicator of which states’ tax systems are the most hospitable to economic growth. The Index does not purport to measure economic opportunity or freedom, or even the broad business climate, but rather tax competitiveness, and its variables reflect this focus. We do so not only because the Tax Foundation’s expertise is in taxes, but because every component of the Index is subject to immediate change by state lawmakers. It is by no means clear what the best course of action is for state lawmakers who want to thwart crime, for example, either in the short or long term, but they can change their tax codes now. Contrary to Fisher’s 1970s view that the effects of taxes are “small or non-existent,” our study reflects strong evidence that business decisions are significantly impacted by tax considerations.

Although Fisher does not feel tax climates are important to states’ economic growth, other authors contend the opposite. Bittlingmayer, Eathington, Hall, and Orazem (2005) find in their analysis of several business climate studies that a state’s tax climate does affect its economic growth rate and that several indices are able to predict growth, and that this study’s predecessor “explains growth consistently.” This finding was confirmed by Anderson (2006) in a study for the Michigan House of Representatives, and more recently by Kolko, Neumark, and Mejia (2013), who, in an analysis of the ability of 10 business climate indices to predict economic growth, concluded that this study’s predecessor, the State Business Tax Climate Index, yielded “positive, sizable, and statistically significant estimates for every specification” they measured, and specifically cited the Index as one of two business climate indices (out of 10) with particularly strong and robust evidence of predictive power.
