Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: UK Autumn Budget Prioritizes Short-Term Relief over Long-Term Growth
articles.standfirst: The UK’s 2026 Autumn Budget largely favors short-term relief over growth, highlighting the need for pro-growth reforms such as replacing the Stamp Duty Land Tax with annual property or land taxes.
paragraphs: On 28 October 2026, the British Chancellor John Healey announced the Labour government’s Autumn Budget. While most of the measures are technical or incremental in nature, the increase in taxes on banks coupled with the reduction in capital allowances reinforces a broader trend towards prioritizing short-term revenue generation over policies that encourage investment and support long-term growth.
Perhaps the most economically significant changes in the budget concern business taxation and investment incentives.

The budget reshapes capital allowances by reducing the main writing-down allowance from 14 percent to 12 percent, partially offset by an increase in the first-year allowance from 40 percent to 50 percent.

Last year’s budget already reduced the writing-down allowance (WDA) main rate to 14 percent from 18 percent, reducing the real value of deductions for assets in the main rate pool to 70 percent from 75.9 percent of investment costs.

For leased assets in the main rate pool that receive the first-year allowance, the change would raise the real value of deductions from 79.1 to 80.8 percent of investment costs. In contrast, for main rate pool assets without the first-year allowance—such as assets bought second-hand, leased overseas, or main pool cars—the real value of deductions will decline more significantly, from 70 to 62.2 percent. The overall effect is dominated by the latter, projected to raise an annual average of £871 million in revenue until 2031-32.

Generally, improving capital allowances is one of the most cost-effective taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy tools to encourage capital investment, as it directly reduces the cost of new capital investment simply by pulling deductions forward in time without giving up tax revenue from the returns on past investment.

In contrast, reducing capital allowances gives up capital investment and economic growth in the medium to long term for immediate revenue retention expected for the next three years. The Chancellor should therefore stay patient and consider reverting course, strengthening capital allowances for sustainable economic growth instead of reducing them for short-term fiscal gain.

Another notable measure is the temporary increase in the bank surcharge from 3 percent to 6 percent, increasing the combined corporation tax and bank surcharge rate from 28 percent to 31 percent between January 2027 and March 2028.

While expected to generate around £1 billion of additional revenue, the measure will further increase the tax burden on a sector that already contributes over £12.3 billion annually through the corporation tax, bank surcharge, and bank levy. Higher taxes on banks may provide a short-term boost to public finances, but they also risk reducing the sector’s capacity to support lending, investment, and economic activity, while potentially undermining the UK’s competitiveness as a financial center.

Ideally, the financial sector should face the same rate of corporation tax as other sectors of the economy, allowing Britain to excel in its comparative advantages rather than steering economic activity elsewhere.

From April 2027, mayors will retain a share of local business rates revenues and permanently keep 20 percent of future business rates growth in their areas. In return, part of their funding from central government grants will be reduced.

Devolving property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. revenues to local governments gives them a fiscal incentive to implement pro-growth policies that improve the local business climate. It also gives local governments an automatic mechanism to fund valuable public investments in local infrastructure that capitalize into higher business property values. Retaining a share of local income taxes lets governments compete for local residents.

The budget also foresees a reduced 10 percent Capital Gains Tax (CGT) rate for qualifying disposals by founders or early investors of high-growth, innovative companies, subject to a lifetime limit of £10 million. To qualify, individuals must hold at least 25 percent of the company and meet a complex set of turnover, employment, growth, and innovation thresholds. While low CGT rates can encourage entrepreneurship and venture capital investment, a narrow scope defined by highly specific rules may reduce its effectiveness by creating legal uncertainty and increasing compliance costs.

One notable change is the increase in the Electricity Generator Levy from 45 percent to 55 percent, which will remain in place until March 2028. The levy applies to revenues earned by electricity generators above a specified benchmark price, after accounting for eligible exclusions, exceptional costs, and annual allowances.

While the measure is expected to raise additional revenue from energy producers, it sits somewhat uneasily alongside the government’s temporary reduction in value-added tax (VAT) on domestic electricity bills from 5 percent to 0 percent between October 2026 and July 2027. On the one hand, policymakers are seeking to lower energy costs for households; on the other, they are increasing the tax burden on electricity generation, which may send mixed signals to investors in the energy sector.

The Autumn Budget includes several measures that will directly affect household consumption. One such change is the increase in the Machine Games Duty on higher-stake gaming machines from 20 percent to 25 percent, representing a targeted rise in the taxation of gambling activity and increasing the tax burden on households that participate in this form of leisure spending. By contrast, the budget reduces the overall tax burden on alcohol by expanding the small-producer alcohol duty relief and reducing the alcohol duty for beverages with low alcohol content, incentivizing the industry to shift to lower-strength products and small-scale production.

Alongside these tax changes, the government has announced a one-off £100 council tax rebate for more than 20 million households in council tax bands A to D in 2027. At an estimated fiscal cost of over £2.6 billion, this is one of the largest measures in the budget by expenditure. While the rebate provides short-term support to households facing cost-of-living pressures, it does not address the underlying shortcomings of the council tax system, which remains based on property valuations dating back to 1991. As a result, the measure only offers temporary relief rather than tackling longer-term concerns about the fairness and efficiency of local property taxation.

The budget contains a mixture of positive and negative changes for savers. Most notably, the budget reverses the previously announced reduction in the Cash ISA annual allowance. Instead of reducing the limit from £20,000 to £12,000 for individuals under 65 from April 2027, the government maintains the £20,000 allowance. Additionally, the withdrawal penalty for Lifetime ISA holders purchasing properties above the £450,000 threshold will be reduced from 25 percent to 20 percent starting in October 2026.
However, these positive developments are accompanied by tax increases. From April 2027, tax rates on savings and property income will rise by a further two percentage points across all bands.

From 6 April 2027 to 5 April 2030, a new pension tax allowance removes income tax for pensioners whose total income does not exceed the full new State Pension, at an annual cost of £50 million from 2027-28. It is worth 20 percent of the gap between the State Pension and the personal allowance and is withdrawn at £1 for every £3 of income above the State Pension, weakening work incentives for pensioners.

One of the more encouraging aspects of the budget is its treatment of international trade. The budget suspends tariffs on 72 products from August 2026 and extends suspensions for 361 products through 2027-28. Additional tariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. relief applies to food products, fertilizer, kerosene used for heating oil, and various business inputs.
The import tariff suspensions are projected to relieve consumers by a volume of £60 million and businesses by a volume of £145 million in tariff burdens annually until 2028-29.

However, the government also plans to remove the £135 customs duty relief threshold for commercial transactions and introduce new customs arrangements from October 2028, expected to raise only £215 million in the fiscal year 2028-29, with prospective revenues turning slightly negative by 2030.

The 2026 Autumn Budget prioritizes fiscal consolidation largely through tax increases while simultaneously offering a range of temporary household support measures. Although some policies, like extending tariff suspensions and increasing fiscal devolution, move in a positive direction, they are outweighed by measures that raise the cost of investment and capital formation. This budget avoids addressing several longstanding structural weaknesses in the UK’s tax system. Rather than relying primarily on higher taxes and temporary rebates, the government should focus on spending restraints and pro-growth tax reform. Priorities should include improving capital allowances for buildings and structures, broadening the VAT base while lowering rates where possible. A future budget should also return to the Prime Minister’s own pro-growth ideas, such as replacing the Stamp Duty Land Tax with annual property or land taxes.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

Alex Mengden is an Economist at the Tax Foundation, where he focuses on international tax issues and tax policy in Europe. He holds a BA in philosophy and economics from the University of Bayreuth and an MSc in economics from the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

articles.title: The Stern Review on climate change, 20 years on
articles.standfirst:
20 years ago the Stern Review on the economics of climate change argued that cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions made economic sense. David Miliband and Nicholas Stern offer five lessons from the last 20 years on the political blockages and other challenges that prevent governments from acting on the insight that tackling climate change … Continued
The post The Stern Review on climate change, 20 years on first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: 20 years ago the Stern Review on the economics of climate change argued that cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions made economic sense. David Miliband and Nicholas Stern offer five lessons from the last 20 years on the political blockages and other challenges that prevent governments from acting on the insight that tackling climate change is good for the economy.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

It is 20 years since we both stood with Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, then UK Prime Minister and Chancellor respectively, at the Royal Society in London to launch the Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change. Its central conclusion was that cutting greenhouse gas emissions would be far less expensive than living with rising emissions. Two decades of evidence have only strengthened this finding.

Since 2006, clean technology has advanced remarkably, with great gains in battery capacity, and remarkable falls in the price of solar and wind power. The International Energy Agency reports that nuclear and renewables met 60 per cent of the rise in global energy demand in 2025. Solar and onshore wind now provide the cheapest new source of electricity in many parts of the world, and renewables are set to overtake coal-fired power generation in 2026. Meanwhile the costs of global warming are rising – impacting life and livelihood on every continent.

Yet with rising energy demand, fossil fuel use has kept growing (coal is making something of a comeback in Asia), and so have emissions. Fossil fuels still provide around 80 per cent of global energy supply, spurred in part by enormous subsidies: the IMF puts explicit subsidies at US$725 billion every year, and when implicit subsidies are included (where taxes on fossil fuels are lower than the costs they cause to society), the figure is US$6.7 trillion per year.
Fossil fuels still provide around 80 per cent of global energy supply, spurred in part by enormous subsidies.

The net result is that temperatures (and extreme weather events) keep rising. The target of limiting the rise in global average temperatures to 1.5-degrees Centigrade above pre-industrial levels will not be met. We are already at 1.4 degrees. In fact, every IPCC Assessment Report looks more worrying. Temperature is rising faster than anticipated, at 0.3 degrees Celsius per decade, and so are the risks of crossing major thresholds, such as destabilisation of Greenland and West Antarctica ice sheets or the collapse of the Amazon forest system.

Ironically, many politicians most concerned about migration ignore climate change’s potential to drive even greater numbers of desperate people fleeing more extreme weather, sea level rise, and circumstances that destroy their lives and livelihoods. Of the IRC’s list of countries facing greatest humanitarian risk, three quarters are in the top quartile for climate vulnerability.

Despite the growing evidence of changing climate and its impact, the science and politics are in tension. The physics says that we will only stop temperatures rising and the impacts of climate change increasing when we stabilise concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, in other words, reach net zero globally. The earlier we get there, the lower the temperature at which we stabilise.

However, climate action faces new barriers. The US Administration has renewed its assault on the science. Financial pressures have fuelled a backlash against the perceived costs of climate action in the West, even where action constitutes sound investment that saves resources in the medium term. China’s lead in electrification and its dominance of critical mineral supplies create further friction around a transition to low carbon. With the science clear, politics that is contested, and technology more positive, there are lessons from the last two decades for the next two. It is vital they are learnt.

First, twenty years ago, investing in adaptation and resilience sounded like giving up on mitigation. But as risks have grown, adaptation has become an imperative. It should no longer be the poor cousin in climate action. According to the Global Commission on Adaptation, every $1 invested in adaptation can generate up to $10 in net economic benefits.

Second, energy security has become more urgent. Chokepoints, from Russian gas pipelines to the Strait of Hormuz, are a new focus of geopolitics. The weaponisation of fossil-fuel supply is a strong long-term reason for decarbonization.

Third, China’s remarkable technical progress could and should be a great boon in the drive for low-carbon growth, but China’s industrial dominance in these technologies creates real problems, as concentrated industrial capacity can create dependency, difficulties of resilience in supply chains, and reduce competition. Building capacity for low-carbon technologies such as solar panels and batteries elsewhere, and rapidly, should be a global priority. And trade and industrial policy will be a crucial element of that task.

Fourth, for European countries, which lack the energy independence of the US, a new imperative is greater cross-border energy system interconnectedness alongside a faster shift away from fossil fuels. Mario Draghi has argued persuasively that this is also key to their competitiveness in world markets.

Fifth, AI was only a gleam in the eye twenty years ago. Today, while it is a rising source of energy demand, it promises more efficient grids, better functioning cities, emissions monitoring, materials discovery, and better climate forecasting to support adaptation. Into the 2030s, AI can make the transition faster, smarter, and cheaper.
Twenty years ago, investing in adaptation and resilience sounded like giving up on mitigation. But as risks have grown, adaptation has become an imperative.

The politics of 2026 are very different from those of 2006, and the next two decades will be turbulent. As Jason Bordoff and Meghan O’Sullivan have written: “Moving to a net-zero global economy will require an unprecedented level of global cooperation but will also lead to conflict along the way and ultimately produce winners and losers.”

The difficulty of the politics is no excuse to abandon the rigour, idealism and imagination of the earlier period; we need more of each. In a world that is interconnected but fragmented, and short of unifying leadership, the countries that want to act should support international action more strongly and build new coalitions of the willing, for example, to expand IFI support for the investment that is sorely needed and to build dependable supply chains for processing critical minerals.
Climate action can drive a new growth story. This is the essential insight of the Stern Review that needs to be revived. Green growth is not a contradiction in terms. It is a necessity.

David Miliband is President and CEO of the International Rescue Committee (IRC). From 2007 to 2010, Miliband was the 74th Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs of the United Kingdom, driving advancements in human rights and representing the U.K. throughout the world. In 2006, as Secretary of State for the Environment, he pioneered the world’s first legally binding emissions reduction requirements. He was Member of Parliament for South Shields from 2001 to 2013.

Lord Stern has been Chair of the Grantham Research Institute, London School of Economic, since it was founded in 2008. He is the IG Patel Professor of Economics and Government, Chairman of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, Chair of the Global School of Sustainability, and Head of the India Observatory at the London School of Economics. He was President of the British Academy, July 2013 – 2017, and was elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 2014.

Political betting markets suggest a growing likelihood of US military action, with probabilities exceeding 50% by late November and reaching 73% by year-end. Forecasts anticipate ongoing trade disruptions, particularly affecting economies reliant on the Strait of Hormuz. The potential for renewed hostilities may lead to interruptions in shipping flows, impacting economic recovery in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries.
The report highlights that a new bombing campaign could provoke Iran to retaliate, particularly against high-value targets in the GCC, further complicating the region’s recovery trajectory.

articles.title: Economic Education Includes Addressing Tax Confusion
articles.standfirst: Economics isn’t just a course with supply and demand graphs and a quirky usage of “guns and butter.” It’s a discipline focused on incentives and responses, and we can see its impact all around us, shaping our world and our choices.
paragraphs: Economics isn’t just a course with supply and demand graphs and a quirky usage of “guns and butter.” It’s a discipline focused on incentives and responses, and we can see its impact all around us, shaping our world and our choices. This morning, you may have asked yourself, “should I stop for a coffee on my way to work?” while a lawmaker might have wondered, “should we modify the tax treatment of business income?” Both were economic decisions with broader implications.

Taxes are a cog in that economic machine, influencing small and large forces in the world around us. Increase taxes, for example, and you must reckon with the new incentive structure for hiring, investing, producing, consuming, and more. All these, in turn, have their own micro- and macroeconomic effects.

No matter the tax, people or businesses will respond. While most research demonstrates that if you tax something, you will get less of it, there are ways to minimize negative economic consequences from taxation.

Taxes on the most mobile factors in the economy, such as capital (machinery and investments), are more distortive and have the most negative impact on long-term growth. The inverse is also true, as taxes on factors that can’t easily be moved, like land, are more stable and less distortive. Understanding this can help us see past the ill feelings toward taxes and identify which ones are better than others.

Even the design of a tax can change its economic impact. Tax rates tend to receive the most attention, but the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.—what is taxed—can be just as important. Narrow tax bases can cause people and businesses to make decisions for tax reasons that they might not make otherwise, like saving less money or hiring fewer workers, and require higher rates to raise the same amount of government revenue. For example, a state with a narrow sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. base that has exemptions (like groceries) and sales tax holidays will rely on higher tax rates on taxable goods to generate the same amount of revenue. The resulting price increase can distort consumer decisions on what, or how much, to buy.

Another underappreciated factor that affects the economy is tax illiteracy. If a raise moves you from the 12 percent income tax bracket to the 22 percent and you believe your entire income will be taxed at the higher rate (it will not!), you may forgo a promotion or extra work hours. That decision will impact your spending, saving, and investment decisions too.

Economic and tax education is critical to interacting with our global economy, and you might expect to see educational priorities reflect the weight of the subject matter. Despite a growing number of states mandating financial literacy graduation requirements, some states have repealed requirements for economic education in recent years. But economic literacy and financial literacy go hand in hand.

If more than half of US taxpayers over 18 do not understand basic tax concepts, walking back economic education is quite a puzzling move. Understanding taxation, and economics broadly, helps prepare students for the mundane daily decisions like grabbing a “sweet treat,” inevitable tax questions, and what they can expect from decisions being made at the national level. And those who end up in elected office someday will need to design sound tax policies that generate revenue with minimal economic distortions.

Daniel Bunn is President and CEO of the Tax Foundation. Daniel has been with the organization since 2018 and, prior to becoming President, successfully built its Center for Global Tax Policy, expanding the Tax Foundation’s reach and impact around the world. Prior to joining the Tax Foundation, Daniel worked in the United States Senate at the Joint Economic Committee.

Zoe is the Vice President of Education at the Tax Foundation. She was previously executive director of an issue advocacy organization that advocated for lower taxes, mindful state spending, and better accountability and transparency in government in her home state of Delaware.

articles.title: What Is the US Debt Limit and Why Does It Matter?
articles.standfirst: The debt limit is one of Congress’s few chances to debate unsustainable borrowing, and reforms should create more room for bipartisan deficit reduction, not less.
paragraphs: With total US government debt recently surpassing $40 trillion, the nation’s debt limit is back in the news. Congress most recently increased the debt limit in July 2025, from $36.1 trillion to $41.1 trillion, under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

While the US government has faced several close calls on its debt payments over its 250-year history, a major default would be unprecedented. Congress has raised or suspended the debt limit dozens of times over the past century. But recent fights over when and how to do so have brought the US to the brink of default.

Default should not be an option for policymakers. The economic consequences of the US failing to meet its debt obligations should be too great for lawmakers to even approach the brink. However, the limit remains one of the only brakes on runaway debt and deficits. Any reforms to the process should maintain or increase opportunities for Congress to debate and improve the fiscal health of the nation.

The debt limit is a legal ceiling on how much the US Treasury Department can issue in outstanding obligations. put it another way, it sets a maximum amount for government borrowing. Importantly, the debt limit does not commit Congress to new spending; it allows the US government to pay the bills it has already incurred. Table 1 below describes in brief some fiscal terms that will be used throughout this piece.

While simple in concept, the mechanics of the debt limit are complicated. The current limit is $41.1 trillion, but the government won’t simply default when it appears as if total public debt outstanding is about to hit that mark.

Instead, the Treasury Department can use several so-called “extraordinary measures” that enable it to delay the day the government actually hits the debt limit. The measures include pausing investments and reinvestments in federal employee retirement funds the government manages and suspending the issuance of new debt. The most common extraordinary measures are described in Table 2 below.

Exactly when the US government will next reach the debt limit remains highly uncertain, but one often cited estimate from the Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC) puts that date—the so-called “X Date”—at sometime in 2027. BPC’s estimate incorporates Treasury’s use of extraordinary measures.

The debt limit in its modern form has been around since 1939, though policymakers have acted to limit the government’s borrowing through various ways and means since before the nation was a nation. The 1939 law consolidated a number of different limits into one, combined public debt limit of $45 billion (approximately $1.1 trillion in 2026 dollars). The limit ballooned to $300 billion in 1945 to accommodate World War II debt ($5.7 trillion in 2026 dollars). Since then, Congress has increased, suspended, or modified the limit 118 times.

The debt limit has taken on new importance in the 21st century, as US government debt and deficits ascend to levels never before seen in peacetime. At the turn of the century, the debt limit was just shy of $6.0 trillion ($12.0 trillion in 2026 dollars).

During that time, Congress has had several protracted debates over the debt limit—in 2011, 2013, 2015, 2019, and 2023, for example—that have raised questions over whether the US would default. While the US did not default during those episodes, two of them contributed to credit rating agencies downgrading US government debt from its previous gold-standard AAA rating—S&P in 2011 and Fitch in 2023.

The debt limit is a flawed instrument for improving the US fiscal trajectory. It is also one of the only ones left. In the 1990s, bipartisan budget agreements and a roaring economy lent the US budget surpluses and declining debt. Since then, decades of deficit-financed spending increases and taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. cuts have produced an increasingly unsustainable budget situation.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects that the gap between government spending and revenue will continue to grow in the years ahead. CBO estimates that annual deficits regularly surpass $2 trillion per year, and that debt held by the public will increase from $32 trillion in 2026 to $168 trillion in 2056 (and from 100 percent of GDP to 175 percent over the same period).

While CBO’s forecast does not include any legislative efforts to reduce debt and deficits, it also does not include any major, negative shocks to the nation or its economy (e.g., wars, recessions, pandemics, or other crises). In some sense, then, this outlook actually underscores the potential budgetary and economic peril if Congress fails to act.
Some policymakers have proposed repealing it. Doing so without broader fiscal reforms would be a mistake.

Other policymakers have hinted at potentially letting the US default. Default would be an even greater mistake than repealing the debt limit. A default could lead to a permanent increase in US borrowing costs. Higher borrowing costs would further widen the gap between spending and revenue, and increase the likelihood that economically damaging tax increases are needed to close the gap. A default could also delay Social Security and military payments and rattle global markets that treat Treasury bonds as a risk-free asset.

A middle path might be bipartisan debt limit reform that takes the worst of the brinksmanship off the table while establishing more regular intervals for Congress to debate and enact fiscal reforms. Reps. Bill Huizenga (R-MI) and Scott Peters (D-CA) have proposed one such reform, the Responsible Budgeting Act.
Policymakers could apply Tax Foundation’s four principles of sound tax policy to the debt limit debate:

A $40 trillion total government debt—and rising—guarantees that Congress will soon be discussing the debt limit again. At its worst, the debt limit symbolizes a dysfunctional Washington that has yet to rein in an unsustainable budget trajectory. At its best, it represents one of the last, best brakes on runaway debt and spending. Debt limit reform should be simple, transparent, and neutral on policy direction, and it should create more opportunities to stabilize the fiscal outlook.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

articles.title: Congress Has a Chance to Improve the Taxpayer Experience in 2026
articles.standfirst: The Senate recently passed the Taxpayer Assistance and Service Act, which contains 65 provisions to improve tax administration and the IRS.
paragraphs: “Simple” and “transparent” are not terms typically associated with filing taxes. On the contrary, the annual taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. filing process fills most with anxiety and confusion, costing Americans $536 billion annually. To make this experience a little less stressful, the Senate recently passed the Taxpayer Assistance and Service (TAS) Act, which would ease some burdens for taxpayers and provide valuable data on where complexity arises in the tax code.

The last major congressional effort to address tax administration was the InflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin Reduction Act, which provided $80 billion to the IRS mostly for enforcement and operations support. However, Congress provided little direction to the IRS on how to use the funding, nor did the law directly streamline IRS functions or processes.
After the experience of the COVID-era IRS issues, Congress, the Taxpayer Advocate Service, and taxpayer organizations proposed reforms to improve tax administration, many of which are in the TAS Act.

The Senate-passed TAS Act contains 65 reforms across 10 titles related to IRS modernization, taxpayers’ rights, tax return preparers, and other tax administration topics. While some provisions address specific taxpayer issues, many will improve the experience for the more than 150 million Americans who file taxes every year, while establishing and strengthening important taxpayer protections.

Since 1998, Congress has required the IRS to produce a report on the source of tax complexity, but the IRS has only rarely released it. While data exists on how costly tax compliance is for taxpayers, no data or report exists on which forms or provisions are causing complexity. The TAS Act clarifies congressional intent for the IRS to produce this report and another on the status of the Act’s implementation.

Paper is the enemy of the IRS. Paper returns take more time and resources for the IRS to process than electronic ones, delaying refunds and diverting staff. The TAS Act requires the IRS to accept digital returns and amended returns and then process them electronically. The bill also requires the IRS to create an online dashboard of call wait times and pushes the agency to expand the availability of callback technology. Further, the “Where’s My Refund?” and “Where’s My Amended Return?” tools are expanded and enhanced.

Most, if not all, financial institutions allow customers to create an online account to access their data. The IRS offers online accounts for taxpayers, but they have limited functionality, hindering their effectiveness. The bill improves online accounts at the IRS by expanding the types of tax documents that are viewable and enhancing tax practitioners’ ability to access their clients’ accounts (with client permission).

Taxpayers and tax preparers often face a fundamental imbalance when addressing an issue with the IRS. The agency has a multibillion-dollar budget, sweeping legal powers, and thousands of employees. Taxpayers, on the other hand, juggle busy schedules and face a complex tax code that wasn’t written for them. Tax preparers may have more knowledge of the tax code than their clients, but they also must balance tight deadlines, multiple clients, and a well-resourced IRS.
The TAS Act would strengthen many taxpayer protections Congress has already written into law and enshrine new ones. Among the pro-taxpayer provisions are:

Even the part of the TAS Act that has generated the most discussion in recent weeks—its new requirements for tax preparers—may enhance taxpayer protections, cut down on preparer fraud, and make it easier for taxpayers to identify good preparers from bad.

The TAS Act contains dozens of bipartisan reforms that could simplify tax filing, enhance transparency for taxpayers in dealing with the IRS, and provide more stability in the year-to-year filing process that fills many Americans with dread. The bill won’t solve every problem at the agency, and it’s no substitute for congressional efforts to reform and simplify the code, but it’s a step in the right direction for a better IRS.

articles.title: Pillar Two Implementation in Europe, 2026
articles.standfirst: 22 of the 27 EU Member States have implemented both the income inclusion rule and the qualified domestic minimum top-up tax in 2026.
paragraphs: In recent years, countries have debated significant changes to international tax rules affecting multinational companies. In October 2021, after negotiations at the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD), more than 130 member jurisdictions agreed to an outline for new taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. rules. Pillar Two introduces the global minimum tax with an effective tax rate of 15 percent, increasing tax revenues by an estimated $91 to $155 billion globally, or 6.5 to 8.1 percent of global corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. revenue.

Pillar Two includes three main rules that establish the global minimum tax. The first is a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT), which countries could use to claim the first right to tax profits currently being taxed below the minimum effective rate of 15 percent. The second is an income inclusion rule (IIR), which determines when the foreign income of a company should be included in the taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. of the parent company. When a company’s effective tax rate falls below 15 percent, additional taxes would be owed in its home jurisdiction. The third rule in Pillar Two is the undertaxed profits rule (UTPR), which allows a country to increase taxes on a company if another related entity in a different jurisdiction was being taxed below the 15 percent effective rate. If multiple countries apply a similar top-up tax, the taxable profit would be divided based on the location of tangible assets and employees.

Together, the domestic minimum tax, income inclusion rule, and undertaxed profits rule create a minimum tax both on companies investing abroad and foreign companies investing domestically. They are all tied to the minimum effective rate of at least 15 percent and would apply to each jurisdiction in which a company operates.

The EU Directive on Pillar Two obliges Member States with more than 12 in-scope multinational groups to implement the IIR starting 31 December 2023, and the UTPR starting 31 December 2024. Member States with no more than 12 in-scope multinational groups can elect to defer implementing both rules for six years under Article 50 of the Directive.
Twenty-two of the 27 Member States of the European Union have implemented both the QDMTT, the IIR, and the UTPR by 2026, while five have not.

Five EU Member States can opt for a six-year deferral of Pillar Two implementation, and all of them have done so, with Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Malta deferring all rules until 2029, while Slovakia selectively implemented only a domestic top-up tax in 2024.

By the year 2030, implementation of the Pillar Two Directive would compromise key design features of the distribution-based corporate tax systems in Estonia and Latvia by obliging in-scope companies to distribute sufficient earnings to meet the 15 percent minimum effective tax rate.

Four EU Member States—Cyprus, Poland, Portugal, and Spain—have implemented Pillar Two rules with delay, despite obligations under the EU Directive. In these countries, the rules apply retroactively for 2024.

Among eight major European countries outside of the European Union, only Norway, Turkey, and the United Kingdom have implemented a QDMTT, an IIR, and a UTPR by 2025. Switzerland implemented a QDMTT in 2024 and an IIR in 2025, but has not set forward any plans to implement a UTPR. Iceland is undergoing public consultation to implement a QDMTT and an IIR in 2026, with no statements regarding a UTPR. Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine, the latest candidates for EU accession, have not publicly announced intentions to implement any Pillar Two rules.

In contrast to many European countries, the US has chosen not to implement changes in line with the global tax deal. In June 2025, the G7 announced a political agreement on a global minimum tax “side-by-side” solution that would exclude US-parented groups from Pillar Two’s IIR and UTPR.

Instead, the US has continued to develop its own cross-border tax framework. Recent changes to US international tax rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) produce an outcome similar to Pillar Two, despite the rules themselves being distinct. The newly introduced net CFC tested income (NCTI) acts as a minimum tax of between 12.6 and 14 percent on all foreign income of US companies, using a blended formula instead of country-by-country. Due to less generous foreign tax crediting, the removal of the substance exclusion, lack of loss carryovers, and interest deductibility rules, the US system may be more stringent than Pillar Two.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Alex Mengden is an Economist at the Tax Foundation, where he focuses on international tax issues and tax policy in Europe. He holds a BA in philosophy and economics from the University of Bayreuth and an MSc in economics from the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

articles.title: Your October Round-up
articles.standfirst:
Welcome to October’s round-up! This month, we’re putting the spotlight on workplace mental health tools, a significant topic that we’re seeing a lot of in our pipeline, and asking what it takes for workers to actually use them. With the Budget landing earlier this week, we’ve also pulled out the highlights for founders and investors, … Continued
The post Your October Round-up appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This month, we’re putting the spotlight on workplace mental health tools, a significant topic that we’re seeing a lot of in our pipeline, and asking what it takes for workers to actually use them.
With the Budget landing earlier this week, we’ve also pulled out the highlights for founders and investors, alongside the Resolution Foundation’s overnight analysis.
And as ever, we’ve rounded up the most exciting updates from the WorkerTech world, from demo days to new market reports.
Mind the trust gap: Workplace mental health provision and worker attitudes
An increasing number of employees in the UK are offered mental health support at work. Only a small number use it.
Two new surveys, results of which were released earlier this month give insights into why.

In August and September of this year, Kara Connect, a UK-based wellbeing provider surveyed 2,010 UK employees, and found that while 91% of those employees have access, only 37% would turn to a mental health support tool via their employer. Around a third (32%) worried it would affect their career.

Also released this month was AXA Global Healthcare’s Mind Health Report, which surveyed 19,000 people across 18 countries. It found that while some of the concerns found among UK employees (in Kara Connect’s report) were also present across the world, access was limited. While 84% of those surveyed said they would probably or definitely use at least one form of workplace support if it were available. Only 41% say they have access. 33% of the people surveyed reported concerns that talking about mental health at work would affect job security.
This tells us that there is a design problem at the centre of workplace mental health tools and platforms: trust.

Another piece of evidence that supports our conclusion is found in the Keep Britain Working Review (see section: Culture of Fear), led by Sir Charlie Mayfield, asks employers to share responsibility for health at work. Mayfield has highlighted that a barrier to keeping in work is a widespread culture of fear – employees dealing with early-stage mental health struggles fear that disclosing the same will lead to stigma, discrimination or negative consequences for their career prospects. On the other side, line managers reported being wary of doing the wrong thing in response to such disclosures, and exposure to tribunal action.

Therefore, when it comes to evaluating workplace mental health solutions in our pipeline, we look closely at what workers are being asked to disclose, what the technology is tracking and, crucially, what employers can see.

We also want to see responsible pathways for workplace mental health management; this means just as much of an emphasis on the course of action post disclosure or a flag of worsening mental health as is put on the data collection and evaluation.

As the guidance from Sir Mayfield’s Review starts becoming practice, we expect to see renewed demand for workplace mental health provision tools. Take-up and participation rates will be key to employers assessing a return on investment in such tools, as will the availability of tools and guidance that help line managers support employees that are experiencing mental health strains.

The consequences of ignoring mental health at the workplace may be an early exit, or worklessness. This is especially true for young people, as was discussed in 2024 in research published by the Resolution Foundation, funded by the Health Foundation. The research found that the number of young people workless due to ill health has more than doubled over the past decade, from 93,000 to 190,000, and that people in their early twenties are now more likely to be economically inactive due to mental ill health than people in their forties. Workplace mental health tools that are focused on outcomes in terms of engagement and effective management are poised to succeed in helping solve this issue.

The Chancellor delivered his first Budget on the 28th of October, and as usual the Resolution Foundation’s research team was hard at work producing an in-depth overnight analysis of the measures announced in the budget and what they mean for household incomes for the rest of this Parliament. More on that in the next section.
The Ventures team was on the lookout for announcements or changes affecting founders and startups. Here are a few highlights for the WorkerTech community:

Our overnight analysis of the Budget finds that higher debt interest costs leave the Government with just £14.5 billion of headroom, around three-fifths of its March level. The £4.4 billion cost of living package that was announced is thinly spread and poorly targeted: on average, it is worth less than £15 a year more to households in the poorest half of the income distribution than to those in the richest half.

Typical non-pensioner incomes are set to fall by 3 per cent (£1,050) between 2026-27 and 2028-29. Lastly, the extension of the Local Housing Allowance freeze into 2027-28 means over a million private renting families lose out, with 91 per cent of them in the bottom half of income distribution.

The headline recommendations following the analysis are that future Government cost of living support should be better targeted at lower-income households with high energy needs (rather than thinly spread across the income distribution) and that upcoming reviews of departmental spending and benefits spending will need to be more ambitious if the new Prime Minister and administration’s vision is to be realised.

The real Living Wage (a voluntary hourly pay rate based on what families need to get by) for 2026-27 is £14.10 across the UK and £15.45 in London. Calculated by the Resolution Foundation and overseen by the Living Wage Commission, this year’s rates use a new blended methodology, averaging Minimum Income Standard and relative poverty calculations.

Baltic Ventures’ Demo Day is back Baltic Ventures has welcomed eight new companies onto its accelerator programme, and after 3 months on the programme, they are ready to take to the pitching stage. Baltic Ventures’ mission is to identify and back ambitious and innovative founders outside of London’s startup ecosystem, and this demo day will bring together founders, angels, VCs and ecosystem leaders from across Liverpool City Region and the UK. It’s taking place on November 26th and you can register here.

Ufi Ventures and Tyton Partners release their Q3 2026 VocTech Market Report This latest quarterly report explores how vocational learning and workforce development are changing across the UK, Europe and North America, from evolving skills policy and diverging forecasts of AI’s impact on jobs to where investment is landing. Read the key learnings here. Apply for direct investment from Resolution Ventures We accept applications from WorkerTech ventures on a rolling basis. You can book a slot in our office hours for an initial conversation.

articles.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
articles.standfirst: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt...
paragraphs: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt interest) is forecast to improve by 3 per cent of GDP over the next 5 years, from a deficit of 1.5 per cent in 2025-26 to a surplus of the same size by 2030-31. The IMF singled the UK out this month as one of the few advanced economies where action on the deficit has been taken decisively.

The trouble is that few people outside the Fund expect this squeeze to be delivered. Most of the tightening is scheduled for 2029-30, which could well be the run-up to the next election. This is the familiar pattern of promising fiscal prudence tomorrow, what Charlie Bean once called the “Augustinian approach” to fiscal policy.

None of this is a criticism of the OBR. Its remit requires it to forecast on the basis of the government’s stated policy, so what it publishes is a forecast conditional on the plan being implemented. That is a useful thing, but it’s also not a best guess of what is likely to happen because the stated policies are themselves unlikely to be unbiased.

In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

Figure 1 explains why. It reconstructs one the OBR published in its 2025 Fiscal Risks and Sustainability Report, comparing the OBR’s forecasts for the debt ratio since 2010 with what actually happened. The forecasts are hump-shaped: on average, they show the debt ratio deteriorating for two years and then improving over the later years of the forecast. The outturns are linear: the debt ratio just keeps rising with the forecast horizon. The improvement that every forecast has pencilled in for years three to five has never arrived.
Public sector net debt (as % of GDP), OBR forecasts compared to outturns, 2010-present

What explains this? I can think of three candidate explanations. The first is bad luck: the economy has been hit by a series of adverse shocks over this period. The second is a planning fallacy: planners tend to be overly optimistic about their ability to deliver. The third is that the plans are built to satisfy the fiscal rules and were never meant to be delivered.

To tell these apart, we follow the approach of Beetsma, Giuliodori and Wierts, in a 2009 paper they provocatively titled “Planning to cheat: EU fiscal policy in real time”. The idea in a nutshell is to take the OBR’s forecast errors for borrowing and split them into a part due to government decisions on taxes and spending and a part due to everything else, above all macroeconomic news. Helpfully, the OBR’s own publications make this possible in a way that would be more difficult in most other countries. We use two of its datasets: every official forecast, so we know what was planned each year; and every revision between one forecast and the next, which the OBR itself splits into the effect of policy decisions announced in the interval, classification changes, and underlying changes to the economy and debt interest. The policy estimates include both the direct cost of measures and their indirect effects on the forecast through the economy, such as higher receipts when spending raises GDP.

For each forecast and each year of its horizon, we add up the policy revisions made in every later forecast for that year. Since each forecast reports its revisions relative to the one before, the sum is the total effect on that year’s borrowing of all the decisions taken after the plan was published. An example hopefully helps fix the intuition. Take the March 2021 forecast for borrowing in 2023-24. The six forecasts that followed attributed revisions to 2023-24 of £11bn, £1bn, £31bn, £19bn, £8bn and £0.3bn to policy, £70bn in all or 2.5 per cent of GDP. Over the same period, the economic outlook improved, which is why the outturn missed the forecast by only 1.4 per cent of GDP in the end. In other words, the method measures how much each plan was undone by later decisions, and differentiates this from how much the economy helped or hurt.

Table 1 shows the results, with the forecasts split into those made between June 2010 and March 2014 and those made from December 2014 onwards (excluding Covid years). In the first period, borrowing came in about 1 per cent of GDP above plan by year 3, and this entirely reflected macro news. Evidently, this was a period where the coalition government held to its plans and the economy fell short. In the second, borrowing has come in fully 2 per cent of GDP above plan by year 3, and three-quarters of that is accounted for by policy decisions taken after the forecast was made. These decisions raised borrowing in the third year of every one of the 24 forecasts since December 2014. So this latter period is not explained away by bad luck.
Notes: Per cent of GDP. Target years 2020-21 to 2022-23 excluded; windows complete to 2026-27, with 2026-27 measured against the October 2026 forecast.

Which decisions explain these slippages? The OBR’s policy measures database records every measure since 2010 by the tax or spending line it affects, so the slippage can be attributed accordingly. Figure 2 does that for the third year of each forecast since December 2014.

The direct cost of the measures announced after each forecast added 1.8 per cent of GDP to year-3 borrowing on average (their indirect effects, mainly the extra receipts that higher spending generates, bring that down to the 1.5 in Table 1). Of the 1.8 per cent, 1.5pp is departmental spending and it is positive in all 15 forecasts. A further 0.2 is the devolved and local authority spending that follows from it via the Barnett formula. Welfare measure net to almost nothing. Fuel duty contributes 0.1, small but present in all 15, because the planned rise is cancelled every time. Tax measures as a whole net to zero at year 3, though by year 5 tax rises outweigh cuts.

The departmental slippage comes in two forms. Spending Reviews give departments budgets for a fixed number of years, currently to 2028-29. Beyond that the forecast rests on a Treasury assumption about total spending growth. Our results say that it is when the next Review replaces that placeholder with settlements that the total comes out higher. In particular, where a forecast’s third year lay beyond the Review period, later departmental decisions added a median 2 per cent of GDP to borrowing, and two-thirds of that arrived at the Review itself. Where the third year already had settled budgets, the additions were smaller and more varied.

So to summarise: of the three explanations we started with, borrowing slippages since 2014 have not in the main been driven by bad macroeconomic news, although there certainly has been plenty of that. They instead reflect departmental spending outstripping forecasts, primarily in the years beyond the planning horizon of the Spending Review. Whether the assumption for those years reflects a planning fallacy of the kind that afflicts most long-range plans, or the incentives the fiscal rules create to pencil in restraint where it costs least, is not settled.

The credible path takes the OBR’s forecast and subtracts from it the typical amount by which later decisions have undone past plans. Concretely, we take the median policy slippage at each horizon from the second panel of Table 1, nothing in the year of the forecast, 0.1 per cent of GDP in year 1, 0.6 in year 2, 1.5 in year 3, 1.6 in year 4 and 1.8 in year 5, and subtract it from the planned primary balance. The band around the result is the interquartile range of the same record. There is no estimation involved—this is just the plan minus what slippage normally occurs.

One point to note before we discuss the results. We focus here solely on slippages from policy decisions, not from macro news. Macro forecasts will also be wrong, and the assumptions underpinning them can be optimistic. For example, the OBR has been criticised for a trend growth path strong than many outside forecasters assume. But the OBR was set up precisely to make those expert, independent judgements, and they are matters on which reasonable people disagree. We are looking instead for the places where a systematic bias is plausible, and Table 1 says that since 2014 that has been in the policy assumptions.

In making these translations we assume that 85 per cent of the slippage lands on the current budget rather than on capital, which is its historical share, and that the extra debt is financed at 4.5 per cent.

To be clear, this is a conditional forecast of how the plan is likely to proceed: it assumes the policy process of the past decade continues, and in particular that next year’s Spending Review raises departmental budgets for 2028-29 to 2030-31 well above the figures the OBR’s forecasts are built on.

That does not seem like a bad assumption. Inflation has run higher than expected since the current settlements were fixed in June 2025, so the OBR now puts the departmental limits at £7bn a year less in real terms than when they were set, and it estimates that unprotected departments would need £11bn more by 2031-32 simply to avoid real cuts from 2028-29. On top of that sits the defence commitment, social care and whatever the Milburn and Timms reviews recommend. None of this is in the credible path above. It rests purely on historical slippage alone.

But the same arithmetic describes a big opportunity. The 2027 Review is the first moment since 2014 at which a government could settle the target year’s budgets at a level in the forecast, and if it did, the gap in the charts above would mostly close. In other words, we would update our priors on the credible path significantly were this to happen.

The prize here would be lower gilt yields. NIESR’s Laubach-style regression results suggest that each percentage point of projected deficit adds 15-20 basis points on the 10-year gilt yield. So a plan that credible delivers 1.5-2 points of primary surplus relative to the credible path could be expected to take 25 to 40 basis points off gilt yields, worth over £10bn each year in debt interest—with wider effects for the whole economy. That would be a credibility dividend worth buying.

articles.title: Budget 2026 special
articles.standfirst:
Afternoon all, While Wednesday’s Budget might have been a more modest affair than we’ve become accustomed to, RF staff were still crunching the numbers late into the night, soundtracked by Treasury officials cheering on the Chancellor for downing a pint getting through his first Budget. Instead of taking Friday a little easier, we’re still here … Continued
The post Budget 2026 special appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: While Wednesday’s Budget might have been a more modest affair than we’ve become accustomed to, RF staff were still crunching the numbers late into the night, soundtracked by Treasury officials cheering on the Chancellor for downing a pint getting through his first Budget. Instead of taking Friday a little easier, we’re still here to bring you bonus content.

Overall, this scattergun Budget did not rise to the scale of the challenges facing Britain. We need more than £100 to the wrong people in the face of another energy price shock, and a forecast for falling living standards over the rest of the Parliament. Read on for five brand new scary charts fit for Halloween: from why things have already got worse, to why it (actually) isn’t all about economic growth.

That said, there were things to welcome this week. A sensible decision on minimum wage, worthwhile reform in closing the gap between tax rates on savings and property income with those on wages, and money to help the PuFiNs fly.
The stage is set for the true reckoning of priorities in 2027 – but first, sleep.

One of the Chancellor’s big choices was to use some of his insurance policy (letting the current budget that he has promised to balance fall from £24bn to £15bn). If things turn out better than expected this will prove a wise move. So far, however, it looks like the Chancellor’s chips are down. The OBR took economic data up to mid-August into account in its forecast. By Budget day, gas prices were far above the OBR’s central forecast and looked dangerously close to its “severe” shock scenario, while oil had climbed two-thirds of the way there. On energy prices, the OBR’s downside scenario is starting to look like the central case (though at our event this week Haskel explained that how long high prices are sustained for will be crucial). In that scenario, inflation tops 5 per cent next year. But the Government does get a sliver of good news. Although the severe scenario does show higher borrowing overall, that’s entirely down to a one percentage point rise in gilt yields that has not yet materialised. So while households are facing something like the severe scenario, the Treasury (for now at least) is not.

One bit of good news the OBR didn’t have time to incorporate was the continued resilience of the UK economy in July and August. And there were 34 pages of the red book dedicated to a plethora of measures aimed to continue to boost economic growth. My favourite was topping up the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank by a combined £20.4 billion (as we’ve been calling for). But at the same time, the Government’s ambitious plans for higher investment have again been chipped away at. Capital departmental spending (CDEL) is now set to fall to 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2029-30, down from 4.3 per cent in the March forecast. The exception is defence investment, thanks to the Defence Investment Plan. Take that out, and we’re actually planning to invest less than we did in 2023-24: CDEL excluding defence has lost over £5 billion since the March forecast. While it has other important aims, defence CDEL is less likely to boost economic growth than other categories like transport or energy, both of which are set to shrink.

Despite there being very little about social security in this Budget, welfare spending dominated the headlines the following day. Two ongoing reviews may prove more memorable than this Budget: Milburn on young people and Timms on disability benefits. For the decade following the pandemic, almost all of the rise in welfare spending is from two sources – benefits for pensioners (£37 billion) and working-age health and disability benefits (another £37 billion). The Prime Minister deserves credit for his boldness on moving away from the triple lock which in the long run will put the first on a more sustainable trajectory; even if on Wednesday the OBR scored the princely sum of zero for savings from it in the first year. The combined response to Milburn and Timms will presumably aim to address the second. The total spend on young people neither earning nor learning runs to around £4 billion, while working-age disability spending in England and Wales stands at nearly £28 billion. Milburn may be more of a headline grabber, but addressing the drivers of higher ill-health and disability across all age-groups remains highly consequential for the public finances as well as living standards.

Families are on track to pay much higher energy bills this year than last. The left panel below shows how unevenly that increase is set to land: up £217 in 2026-27 for the typical household (compared with 2025-26). But there is as much variation between households with the same income as between households of different income. Within every income bracket many households face very large rises, with around one-in-five of the poorest households facing increases of more than £300. This is why help needs to reach those with both low incomes and high energy use.

The Chancellor’s main response, a £100 Household Energy Payment for homes in Council Tax bands A to D, does neither. As the right panel shows, eligibility barely varies across the bottom three quintiles and remains high even at the top, where three-in-five households qualify. A £100 bung to everyone means giving it to many people who don’t need it – either because they are on high incomes, fixed rate tariffs, or have low energy needs. This scatter-gun approach will provide little comfort for many of the one-in-six of the poorest families who already tell us they can’t afford to heat their homes.

The most disappointing thing about this Budget was what it told us about the long-run prospects for living standards. Real household disposable income per person is set to grow by just 0.1 per cent a year on average between 2019 and 2029, compared with 0.9 per cent between 2007 and 2019 and 2.4 per cent in the decade to 2007. TOTC readers will no doubt be familiar with the role economic growth (the blue bars) played in our post financial crisis disappointment. That it’s become relatively more expensive to buy things from the rest of the world (the yellow bars) also matters. But the 2020s squeeze on living standards has a new source (the red bar in the chart below): net taxes and benefits, which added to income growth after the financial crisis, are now a drag on it.

This is not really a story of consolidation – borrowing in 2029-30 is forecast to be little lower than it was before the pandemic. Over this period, taxes are up to pay for higher spending, with health spending, in particular, 1 percentage point higher as a share of the economy. Especially painful is spending an extra 2.4 per cent of GDP on debt interest.

This final chart sums up the dilemma the Chancellor has put off but cannot avoid in 2027. If we cannot afford the public services and defence we want without a bigger red bar – will he choose to disappoint on those or to squeeze household incomes even further?

articles.title: What does the abolition of the gas standing charge mean for households?
articles.standfirst:
This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack. While the £100 Household Energy Payment grabbed most of the headlines, another energy bill change announced on Wednesday has got less attention. But John Healey’s request for Ofgem to abolish the standing charge on household gas bills by the end of 2027 will also affect … Continued
The post What does the abolition of the gas standing charge mean for households? appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.

While the £100 Household Energy Payment grabbed most of the headlines, another energy bill change announced on Wednesday has got less attention. But John Healey’s request for Ofgem to abolish the standing charge on household gas bills by the end of 2027 will also affect future bills. And because it’s a regulatory change, the Treasury leaves it out of its distributional analysis. So here we’ve tried to fill that gap and understand who will win – and lose – from this switch.

The standing charge, £108 a year for the typical billpayer, is paid by every gas-connected household however little gas it uses. Suppliers will recover it through higher unit rates instead, so the change costs the Exchequer nothing, and efforts to reduce the disparity between gas and electricity costs will – in a small way – help to make the case for more heat pumps in homes.

But it is not free: it moves around £600 million a year from households that use more gas to those that use less, with no regard to their incomes. In effect, it adds to what we at RF have dubbed the “shadow tax and benefit system hidden within energy bills”, with the transfer set by a regulator rather than in a Budget.

Still, upfront, there is a lot to like about it. Standing charges make up a much bigger share of low energy users’ bills than higher users: at today’s prices the charge is an eighth of a typical gas bill, but more for those who use less gas. Prepayment customers who self-disconnect also keep building up standing charges as debt, which abolition would end. The catch is that gas unit rates would rise by around 10 per cent – at a time when they are at record highs with little chance of falling back to earth.

Not all households will benefit. We estimate that 13.3 million (48 per cent) of households in Britain would be better off, by £46 a year on average, and 9.9 million (36 per cent) would be worse off, by £61 – the losses are larger because the same sum falls on fewer households. The other 4.5 million (16 per cent) are not on the gas grid so will be unaffected. But for the typical household the change is small: the median gas-connected household would gain just £13 a year, less than 1 per cent of a typical energy bill in 2026-27.[1]

There are winners and losers in every income group: which side a household lands on depends on how much gas it uses, not on how much it earns. The pattern by income is very mildly progressive (Figure 1). Half (50 per cent) of households in the poorer half of the income distribution would be better off, compared with 46 per cent in the richer half. The picture is similar at the ends of the distribution – 47 per cent of the poorest fifth would gain, against 44 per cent of the richest fifth.
Figure 1: The spread of winners and losers from abolishing the gas standing charge is relatively flat across the income distribution

The bigger divide is by household size, which we show in Figure 2. Larger households use more gas, so would lose out more: 54 per cent of households with two children and 58 per cent of those with three or more would be worse off, paying £20 and £35 a year more on average, respectively. By contrast, nearly two-thirds (65 per cent) of single pensioners would be better off, saving £28 a year on average.
Figure 2: Most households with two or more children would be worse off from abolishing the gas standing charge

The timing of payments changes too. January to March accounts for 43 per cent of a year’s household gas use. Turning a flat daily charge into a higher unit rate pushes more of the bill into winter, by moving a daily charge into one concentrated in times when consumption is high.

For a household using Ofgem’s typical 9,500 kWh a year, payments between October and March would rise by around £20, and those between April and September would fall by around £30. Prepayment customers, who pay as they go, would see more of their bill land in the months when money is tightest – and all would become more exposed to the cost of a cold winter.

The Government has promised “targeted mitigation” for households that lose out but has not said what it will be. Our analysis has shown that it should focus on lower-income families with higher energy use, such as those with children. The difficulty is that the Government still has no tool to find them – even four years into an energy bill squeeze. The benefit system, through which help like the Warm Home Discount is passported, reaches only around a quarter of households and misses most of those in the poorer half of the income distribution.

A social tariff, on the other hand, could shield those for whom higher gas prices pose a welfare risk, allowing the benefits of abolishing the standing charge to be banked while mitigating the risks at the sharp end – as well as helping families struggling with the high cost of energy today. Without it, every reform of this kind – including the overhaul of electricity standing charges promised for next year – will be yet another untargeted transfer between billpayers.
Jonathan Marshall is a Principal Economist at the Resolution Foundation. You can follow him on Bluesky here.
[1] Based on a typical consumption level of 9,500 kWh of gas per year.
