articles.title: The fiscal devolution roadmap is the radical reform in an otherwise quiet budget
articles.standfirst:
The fiscal devolution roadmap is the radical reform in an otherwise quiet budget ellie.slee.lamb Fri, 30/10/2026 - 16:29 This document may not have grabbed headlines but could bring about real change. 5 Comment Thomas Pope Institute for Government Yes Public finances Devolution Budget Public spending Labour Burnham government HM Treasury
No

The fiscal devolution roadmap, published alongside the budget, detailed plans to fund mayoral strategic authorities (MSAs) through a share of income tax rather than grants, and allowing mayors to retain some of the proceeds of growth.

This was not headline grabbing news. For one thing, we already knew the roadmap was coming: it was first announced by Rachel Reeves at her Mais lecture in March, when she proposed income tax retention. The new regime will also not be implemented until April 2028, and some important details are still to be confirmed. And the impact on people will not be obvious when the change comes in either. Mayors will not have control over income tax rates, so this is about how funding flows to mayors rather than how much tax people pay.

Nonetheless, the roadmap is significant. It promises a fundamental change in mayoral funding that suggests the Treasury is not (at least yet) reining in the prime minister’s devolution ambitions. As the Treasury fills out the details of its plans, through consultation and in the upcoming devolution white paper, it should ensure it delivers on the potential upsides from fiscal devolution while developing a wider institutional system that sets mayors up to succeed.

The roadmap sets out an ambitious new settlement for mayors across the country

The Treasury plans for almost all mayoral grants to be replaced by a share of income tax receipts, with areas able to retain more revenue if their places grow more quickly. This is a big change. Currently, mayors receive grants from central government, with often onerous requirements about how they should be spent. Even the most advanced mayoralties that receive ‘integrated settlements’ – intended to be flexible grants – in practice are constrained by having to meet specific targets set by government departments. And grants are only confirmed for a couple of years, making it hard for mayors to make long-term commitments.

The roadmap is more ambitious than we might have expected – especially if Reeves were still in post – in two ways.

The first is in scale and scope. One key question we posed for the roadmap was how willing the government would be to roll out fiscal devolution to new mayors as well as the established premiers. Making fiscal devolution available to all mayoralties rather than only the most advanced, is a change in approach from previous administrations. To date, new powers or flexibilities have tended to be rolled out to a couple of places – often trailblazers like Greater Manchester and the West Midlands – first, with other places trickling in behind them in subsequent years. This government is going further and faster, and announced new MSAs alongside the budget yesterday.

Second is that the roadmap is ambitious in the level of autonomy it promises for mayors. A more cautious government might have proposed that central government would retain substantial control over how these revenues were spent. Instead the roadmap commits to mayors having choice over which policy areas the money should be spent on, and proposes that accountability for this spending should mainly be to local institutions and people rather than central government and parliament.

This represents a fundamental change in the relationship between central government and mayors, and will mean a real transfer of control and responsibility from ministers to mayors over those policy areas – like skills and local transport – that the government devolves to mayors. 

The government still has important choices to make 

The roadmap laid out the structure of the system, which reflects careful design choices so far, but further details will determine exactly how the system works in practice. One important choice is how far the system will allow divergence between places growing quickly and those lagging behind. The roadmap confirms that places will keep a percentage of the growth they achieve above the national average for a long period – 10 or 15 years – but not what that percentage will be. 

Likewise, it proposes a floor below which places will not be allowed to fall below, proposed at 95% of assessed need but subject to consultation. These parameters will determine, on the one hand, how big a growth incentive the system will give to mayors, and on the other how far the system will permit inequality in funding between better and worse performing areas.

A wider set of choices will also matter for whether this is an effective, functioning system. Rolling out these freedoms to all mayors will require capacity and capability to develop quickly, especially in newer institutions. In this context the Treasury’s commitment to additional capacity funding is especially. Likewise, effective local accountability requires well-functioning local scrutiny: something the devolution white paper later this year should answer.

The roadmap’s radicalism must not get lost in the fine print

In the past, for example on integrated settlements, ministers’ initial radicalism has been watered down as officials have got further into the weeds and political interest has waned. One of the big possible upsides of fiscal devolution is greater long-term certainty about funding that is not tied to biennial spending reviews, potentially allowing borrowing against future revenues for long-term investments. Whether mayors really do have that assurance depends on how the system updates funding over time. The Treasury must ensure these fine-print details do not undermine the purpose of the reforms.

The fiscal devolution roadmap is an impressive document – both in the careful choices about system design made so far and its radicalism. The next stage is just as important to ensure the final outcome is a workable and more effective system than what we have now.

articles.title: Abolishing a public body in practice
articles.standfirst:
Abolishing a public body in practice ellie.slee.lamb Fri, 30/10/2026 - 15:21 Lessons from the Closure Report for the National Citizen Service (NCS) 4 Comment Matthew Gill Institute for Government Yes National Citizen Service (NCS) Public bodies Public spending Labour Burnham government Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
Closure report for the NCS
No

The National Citizen Service (NCS) was a programme of experiences for young people in England, designed to promote social cohesion, engagement and mobility. Set up in 2011, its institutional history has been complex – reflecting the competing demands of financial and operational accountability to government alongside the need for creativity and independence to enthuse young people. Lessons from how its governance has changed over the years formed a case study in our report on How to set up a public body.1 Gill M and Bishop M How to set up a public body, Institute for Government, 20 November 2024, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/how-to-set-up-a-public-body

When that report was published in November 2024, the government had just announced the NCS’s abolition. Subsequently, its leadership team used the Institute’s report How to abolish a public body (2023)2 Dalton G, Amos N and Gill M, How to abolish a public body: Ten lessons from previous restructures, Institute for Government, 8 March 2023, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/abolish-public-bodies  to inform their handling of the closure process, and to document lessons learned afterwards.

Here, we summarise the key lessons from the closure. We also publish the NCS’s own closure report, which contains more detail to support those involved in future abolitions; this is found at the foot of this page.

Three key lessons are foregrounded by the NCS experience

The closure report, written by the NCS team involved, identifies three key lessons from the closure. All of these were anticipated in the Institute’s prior work, but come into sharper focus in light of their experience:

1) Strategic planning

At the time abolition was announced, it was not intended for the functions of the NCS to be directly replaced. A National Youth Strategy was published over a year later, in December 2025,3 Department for Culture, Media and Sport, Youth Matters: Your National Youth Strategy, GOV.UK, 10 December 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/youth-matters-your-national-youth-strategy  and the government has since set out to procure delivery partners to support local authorities in providing youth support4 Department for Culture, Media and Sport, ‘Young Futures Hubs and Transformation Programme’, 8 July 2026, GOV.UK, www.gov.uk/guidance/young-futures-hubs-and-transformation-programme  and to administer a £416.8m Youth Matters Fund.5 Department for Culture, Media and Sport, ‘Youth Matters Fund: delivery partner competition’, 10 July 2025, GOV.UK, www.gov.uk/government/publications/youth-matters-fund-delivery-partner-competition  These partners might – or might not – have benefitted from a continuation of NCS Trust systems and expertise. But we will never know, because clear future plans were not developed before existing programmes were axed.

The apparent lack of a detailed business case for the abolition,6 Gill M and Dalton G, When should public bodies exist?: Rewriting the ‘three tests’ for when government does things at arm’s length, Institute for Government, 12 July 2023, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/public-bodies-tests  alongside failure to consider the interconnectedness of the NCS with the wider youth support ecosystem, also resulted in unintended consequences – including, for example, the failure of valued partner organisations. Without proper analysis in advance, it is possible to miss the respects in which a public body functions not only as a delivery programme in its own right, but an anchor or co-ordinating institution essential to its wider field.

2) Workforce transition

A combination of parliamentary protocol, short timelines and cross-government value for money requirements made it very difficult to give staff either advance notice of the abolition or enhanced redundancy settlements. As a result, there was limited opportunity to consider how public assets could be mothballed or transferred (including, for instance, delivery expertise, digital systems and research evidence). The ability to communicate with staff more transparently and to recognise their contributions could have improved staff retention and engagement in the remaining time for which they were needed.

3) Decision-making structures and processes

Once the wind-down commenced, NCS and staff at the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) swiftly established the legislative requirements of closure, the accountability structures to be maintained throughout transition, and effective collaboration processes.7 National Citizen Service, Joint Statement by the NCS Trust Board and DCMS, GOV.UK, 8 July 2025, www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-citizen-service-trust-minutes-of-the-june-2025-board-meeting-and-joint-statement  They achieved this despite a lack of clear government guidance or access to an experienced transition team. 

It was a fortunate coincidence that the interim CEO of the NCS had prior wind-down experience. As our research identified, public body abolitions are large transformation programmes requiring specialist expertise – and prior experience – to be brought in from the start. Building an appropriate transition team quickly should be a key plank of any abolition plan.

Effective abolitions take time as well as expertise

The closure report concludes with a table detailing the various consequences of insufficient time being available to plan an orderly wind-down of NCS activities. While many of these points are NCS-specific, some of the themes – including for example the lack of time to fully evaluate whether any systems would be of value to maintain for government more widely, or to work out how to achieve best value when exiting contracts – illustrate why timescales for future abolitions should be informed by operational as well as political realities.

The centre of government should support public body abolitions better

The closure report assesses the NCS closure process against each of more general lessons set out by the Institute in How to abolish a public body. This leads to some granular recommendations, for instance, on what the Cabinet Office should include in the more detailed guidance we recommended that it develop in relation to public body abolitions. 

A properly resourced central team in the Cabinet Office or elsewhere should be given the capacity to develop such guidance. Until that happens, the NCS closure report shows once again that public body closures require careful strategic and operational planning for their system-wide impact and the smooth transition of any ongoing functions. Those tasked with these important projects should refer to it – alongside our own reports.

articles.title: What does budget 2026 mean for business and growth?
articles.standfirst:
What does budget 2026 mean for business and growth? ellie.slee.lamb Fri, 30/10/2026 - 11:12 It’s the age-old question. 4 Comment Giles Wilkes Institute for Government Yes Public finances Budget Public spending Labour Burnham government HM Treasury
No

It is a frustrating question to answer, because the truth about the economy, and most of the things that might have some bearing upon it, is that the former is very, very big, and the things are generally quite small. 

Those of us who think professionally about ‘government’ need to be reminded, from time to time, that it is in many ways much smaller than people realise.1 https://freethinkecon.wordpress.com/2010/01/06/the-government-is-smaller-than-you-think/  Yes, the state taxes a fair bit and spreads the revenues around. But it does not generate as much of GDP as the over-cited tax/GDP ratio would suggest. A great deal of what it does is redistribute incomes, rather than direct activity.

The budget sent few shockwaves across the economy

Its influence is vast, of course, but it mostly comes to bear over the medium to long term. In principle, sudden changes in tax and spending might rapidly heat up or freeze activity, but A. this does not happen often and B. it is usually the Bank of England that really holds the whip-hand over aggregate spending. Finally, C. if you are thinking about Wednesday’s budget, it takes only the briefest glance at various tables in the OBR’s Economic and Fiscal Outlook (e.g. A.10)2 https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6ae1f7b839d29f3f9b9b3f36/economic-and-fiscal-outlook-october-2026-web-accessible.pdf  to see that its direct effect on spending is likely to be slight.  

Therefore, the usual answer applies: in terms of immediate outcomes, John Healey’s budget3 https://www.gov.uk/government/news/government-slashes-red-tape-and-tariffs-to-give-businesses-breathing-space  means nothing. I doubt any professional forecasters are changing their numbers. But even when the budget contains something as large and stinky as 2024’s employer NICs rise, it can be hard to detect the influence on actual economic aggregates. Only about one budget in 20 has that kind of effect; in my professional lifetime, 100% of such events were delivered by Kwasi Kwarteng (though this is hard to prove, because the mini budget was largely unwound a month later). 

Related content

Budget 2026

John Healey’s underwhelming budget punts big decisions into 2027

John Healey's packed budget was big in size but small in ambition. He and Andy Burnham will need to make difficult political arguments and economic decisions in 2027.

Read the comment

The long-term effects

However, the question is not meaningless. Chapter 4 in John Healey’s first budget – titled “Good Growth in Every Postcode” – contains over 30 pages and 160 paragraphs of various growth measures. The point is that they will show their effect over the years or decades. They include many (mostly pre-announced) policies on energy, interesting new ideas for accelerating the delivery of data centres, some easing up of rules on high-talent immigration, the reprioritisation of climate-related spending towards defence, a more muscular and political approach to delivering infrastructure, and more money for the PuFins (public financial institutions). The government is also recreating the Better Regulation Executive and delivered savings administrative red tape that it measured at £800m.1 You can find a nice assessment of it in Anna Valero’s blog: https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/politicsandpolicy/the-2026-budget-buys-stability-and-points-in-the-right-direction-on-growth/?123

On the negative side of the ledger, the chancellor raised some money by making capital allowances less generous. Defence capital, which is rising, is not generally as good for growth as other kinds of investment, which is not. The IfG’s perpetual call for a tax reform strategy has gone unheeded, again (fear not, we will not give up). The bullet is yet to be bitten on welfare reform, and as my colleague Tom Pope has pointed out, most of the difficult decisions have been punted forward into 2027. We do not know for certain how Healey will make his spending review work, so any uncertainty hanging over business was not fully dispelled. 

I will not attempt to weigh up both sides of the ledger and say which of them won: supply side measures take years to show an effect, and cannot be teased apart. 

Has 40 years of neoliberalism been brought to an end?

What we do know is that Andy Burnham’s government has some big long-term ambitions, in various states of definition. Devolution is pretty well understood; reindustrialisation vaguer and looser; the end of neoliberalism has a lot of work to do. None of them were meant to be achieved in a single fiscal moment. Progress is going to be observed gradually, if at all. 

John Healey’s first budget was a holding exercise, intended to prepare the ground for more challenging work ahead. On its own terms it worked. It was not meant to fire the starting gun on an investment boom, suddenly “unleash” the economy, or whatever your favourite, misleading metaphor for boosting growth might be. Anyone expecting otherwise who now feels disappointed should blame themselves, not the chancellor. Growth doesn’t come from headline grabbing budgets. It never has.

Healey’s budget: Policies today, problems tomorrow

Nick Garland, a former speechwriter to ex-chancellor Rachel Reeves, joins the podcast team to explore the significance of Healey’s big day.

articles.title: The top Latin American cities in 2026
articles.standfirst: Discussion of the world’s major cities often overlooks the role and dynamics of Latin America. Yet, to ignore the region would be to ignore around a quarter of the world’s land mass and almost a 10th of its population.
paragraphs: Discussion of the world’s major cities often overlooks the role and dynamics of Latin America. Yet, to ignore the region would be to ignore around a quarter of the world’s land mass and almost a 10th of its population.

In the 2026 edition of the Global Cities Index, Latin American cities are at the forefront of our analysis. Not only has the region seen some the largest increases in their ranking relative to last year, but we have also introduced a new ‘Cities to Watch’ section for the region allowing our analysts to highlight the top five city-economies they are most excited about and think investors should take notice of. The five we covered—Brasília, Lima, Medellín, Monterrey, and Santiago—are a group of cities with diverse drivers, united by their productivity-led expansion as they progress up the value chain.

In terms of the overall rankings for the region, Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, takes top spot in the region and 138th overall (Chart 1). The city has the region’s second largest economy and has a deep skills base centred around strong universities and the many corporate headquarters. Second up is Chile’s Santiago, boasting similar credentials but higher housing costs and weaker Environmental scores cost it the top spot. Rounding off the top three is rapidly developing Lima as a combination of rural-urban migration, infrastructure investment, and rising trade volumes positions Peru’s capital as a key regional leader.

The megacities of São Paulo and Mexico City also rank highly, supported by their large GDP size and elevated scores in the Human Capital category. In fact, the Human Capital category is an area of relative outperformance across the region, with cities benefitting from good universities and high levels of educational attainment. The strength of Human Capital in driving Latin American cities’ performance in the index is perhaps best illustrated by the fact that nine of the 10 cities topping the overall rank for the region also top the Human Capital score, with only Medellín breaking into the top, as Costa Rica’s San José falls out.

The region’s poorest-performing category is Quality of Life, which may sound odd when one thinks of the golden beaches of Rio de Janeiro or the cosmopolitan streets of Santiago and Buenos Aires. However, the region has high levels of inequality, severe poverty, and some of the highest crime rates in the world (Chart 3). Cities as far afield as Port-au-Prince in Haiti, Guatemala City, and Fortaleza in Brazil are emblematic of this reality.

While it would be easy to say that reducing crime will shoot Latin American cities up the rankings, it is much more nuanced than that. This is because of the strong link crime has with other socioeconomic factors, like poverty and inequality, explaining the poor performance of Latin American cities across each of these metrics. Instead, the region needs broad-based interventions to stem to the drivers of crime, which in turn means stronger economic performance as much as it does stronger law enforcement.

Looking ahead, the region is set to see several of its cities climb the rankings and become more prominent in the index. Chief among them is Lima. GDP growth in the city will significantly outpace all other major Latin American cities and, over the next decade, will average 3.2% per annum, more than double the rate of São Paulo and rivalling the growth expected in some of Europe’s and the Middle East’s most dynamic cities. Moreover, this will open up substantial consumer market opportunities—having already surpassed Rio de Janeiro in 2021, Lima is projected to have higher average disposable income than both São Paulo and Bogotá by 2050—despite having a level just 82% and 93%, respectively, of the two today.

Slightly further south, Arequipa, Peru’s second-largest city and one of the world’s leading copper producers, is also set to rise in the rankings. Industry accounts for close to two-fifths of the city’s output, and this specialisation has supported one of the fastest rates of economic expansion among Latin American cities over the past two decades, averaging 5.1% per year. Supported by a strong investment pipeline and sustained demand for copper as electrification advances, we expect Arequipa’s largest gains to come in its Economic score, lifting it into the top 10 Latin American cities in our index over the next decade.

Panama City and Georgetown (Guyana) are also set to climb the rankings, reflecting their roles as both capital city economies and centres of national economic activity. Panama City will remain among Latin America’s top-performing cities, supported by deep human capital, high income per person, and its strategic location at the Pacific mouth of the Panama Canal. Georgetown, by contrast, stands out more for its vast natural resources. It is already Latin America’s fastest-growing city economy, with average annual growth of 12.6% over the past two decades. Offshore oil discoveries and rising infrastructure spending are at the centre of this, driving strong employment growth and higher incomes. These dynamics should support further progress over the coming decade, even if income disparities remain among the highest in our Global Cities Index.

Weaker momentum across some of the region’s more established urban centres will see them lose ground in our index over the coming decade. Rio de Janeiro is one such example, with growth set to remain subpar and substantially weaker than in other vital cultural epicentres, such as Buenos Aires and Santiago. A mature urban economy, softer demographic trends, and limited productivity gains are likely to constrain its performance. A similarly weak outlook applies to Cancún, where the same tourism reliance that drives its global appeal also leaves the city with a less stable economic footing than its more diversified city peers.
To explore the full rankings and see how other cities perform, visit the 2026 Global Cities Index site.

articles.title: Bank of Japan will continue rate hikes to keep inflation at the target
articles.standfirst: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) delivered a ‘hawkish pause’ today, keeping its policy rate at 1.25%. This was widely expected and doesn’t alter our near-term forecast. The bank said underlying inflation has already reached the 2% inflation target and stressed that more rate hikes are needed to prevent inflation overshooting. We maintain our call that the BoJ will hike in December and April to a terminal rate of 1.75%.
paragraphs: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) delivered a ‘hawkish pause’ today, keeping its policy rate at 1.25%. This was widely expected and doesn’t alter our near-term forecast. The bank said underlying inflation has already reached the 2% inflation target and stressed that more rate hikes are needed to prevent inflation overshooting. We maintain our call that the BoJ will hike in December and April to a terminal rate of 1.75%.

According to its Quarterly Outlook Report, the economy has been developing in line with the projections set out in the previous report and underlying inflation has reached a level consistent with the 2% inflation target. Governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated that the focus of monetary policy has shifted from raising inflation to 2% to keeping it at the target, given the risks are now tilted to the upside.

Although the BoJ’s favourite indicators for underlying inflation have reached the 2% target, a key driver has been the successful pass-through of a series of external inflation shocks from the supply-side, instead of the wage-driven demand growth that the government and BoJ have pursued. Domestic demand has been resilient to rate hikes and the terms-of-trade shock, but has lacked momentum.

We expect the inflationary shock from higher energy prices and past yen depreciation will gradually fade and that inflation will stabilise around 2% in late 2027. However, if the supply-side shock lasts for longer than we expect, the BoJ may need to hike to 2% by July, just before the terms of the two most hawkish board members end, despite rising pressure from the government.

The central bank decided to increase the annual sales amount of its holdings of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on the open market from 330 billion yen to 860 billion yen starting in 2027. This will shorten the time required to complete the sales from approximately 112 years to 43 years.

articles.title: New Research Finds That Revenue-Maximizing Top Tax Rate Likely Lower Than Previous Estimates
articles.standfirst: A new paper shows raising top income tax rates on the current tax base may not yield as much revenue as previously estimated, due to opportunities to shift income to different tax bases within the tax code.
paragraphs: Not all taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. hikes bring in more revenue. Setting the rate too high might not yield as much as a lower tax rate would, because tax rates influence how much people work and how much businesses invest—both activities that affect the income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.. Economists and policymakers, therefore, are keen on determining the “Goldilocks rate.” A new research paper sheds some light on this question, finding that the income tax rate that maximizes revenue may actually be lower than previously estimated.

An influential policy paper in the “optimal tax theory” literature was published by economists Peter Diamond and Emmanuel Saez in 2011, “The Case for a Progressive Tax.” That paper sought to identify the “peak” of the Laffer curve—the marginal tax rateThe marginal tax rate is the amount of additional tax paid for every additional dollar earned as income. The average tax rate is the total tax paid divided by total income earned. A 10 percent marginal tax rate means that 10 cents of every next dollar earned would be taken as tax. at which tax revenue is maximized.

Building on earlier theoretical work from Saez, the 2011 paper estimated a top revenue-maximizing tax rate of 73 percent in the US. The findings of that paper were frequently misunderstood by policymakers and commentators, including by some who thought that the paper’s findings meant the top tax rate should be set at that rate.

To start, the top revenue-maximizing rate estimated in the paper was inclusive of all taxes at the federal, state, and local levels, including all payroll taxes and sales taxes. That is, the paper did not estimate that revenue would be maximized if the top individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source rate (35 percent at the time) was increased to 73 percent.

A second, and critically overlooked, contributor to the 73 percent figure was the assumption of a tax base that is broader than our system was at the time (and still is). The authors estimated that using the existing, narrower tax base, with numerous deductions and credits, would yield a top revenue-maximizing rate of 54 percent, or 48 percent for just the top federal income tax rate. For context, that rate is not much higher than the combined federal and state income tax rates faced by high-income taxpayers in states such as New York and California.

Diamond and Saez’s 2011 paper was certainly not the last word on this topic. Many papers published since have taken different approaches, producing a range of total government revenue-maximizing tax rates from all sources between 46 percent and 73 percent.

In a new paper building on this work, economists Rachel Moore, Brandon Pecoraro, and David Splinter argue that these papers used tax bases that were either too broad or too narrow, often missing important behavioral adjustments. Given our current tax system, they find that the Laffer curves are flatter than Saez and other authors estimate, implying that the revenue gains from increasing top tax rates are smaller than what those previous estimates suggest.

Policymakers are largely interested in how the change in the top ordinary income tax rate would impact revenue, but a large share of income at the top actually falls outside this tax base. For example, while the ordinary income tax base includes some capital income—such as short-term capital gains and pass-through businessA pass-through business is a sole proprietorship, partnership, or S corporation that is not subject to the corporate income tax; instead, this business reports its income on the individual income tax returns of the owners and is taxed at individual income tax rates. profits—other types of capital income, such as long-term capital gains and qualified dividends, are taxed at lower rates. The ordinary income tax base is reduced further by deductions and credits for various kinds of investment.

The authors improve upon previous studies by constructing different tax bases and using detailed administrative data covering high-income taxpayers to estimate behavioral responses along the Laffer curve. The model allows them to capture different margins of adjustment in response to changes in tax rates. For example, corporations may switch organizational forms to noncorporate structures if tax rates on pass-through business income fall. Similarly, individual income taxpayers may increase tax-deductible activities, such as charitable giving, when their tax rates rise.

Accounting for these additional margins, the authors find that the revenue losses from federal rate increases roughly double compared to previous estimates that use only one tax base. Using a single broad tax base yields a revenue-maximizing federal income tax rate of 55 percent. That revenue-maximizing rate falls to 48 percent when using multiple bases and accounting for all possible behavioral responses (the “true” base), yielding an additional $43 billion in revenue at that rate, or 0.2 percent of GDP.

Taking into consideration all taxes at the federal, state, and local levels, the top federal income tax that maximizes revenue falls even further. The top federal individual income tax rate that would maximize total government revenue from all sources is 39 percent, with an increase to that rate yielding $1 billion in additional total tax revenue. At that rate, the losses to state and local revenue almost fully offset the federal revenue gains. A rate of 39 percent is also very close to the current top federal income tax rate of 37 percent.

Overall, this new paper shows raising top income tax rates on the current tax base may not yield as much revenue as previously estimated, due to opportunities to shift income to different tax bases within the tax code. Policymakers should keep this in mind when thinking about increasing tax rates on high-income taxpayers without making other reforms to the tax code.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Alex Durante is a Senior Economist at the Tax Foundation, working on federal tax policy and model development. Alex worked as a research assistant at the Federal Reserve Board and served as a staff economist on the Council of Economic Advisers.

articles.title: Property Tax Relief on the Ballot: Three Approaches, One Clear Winner
articles.standfirst: This November, states across the country are asking voters to consider changes to their state constitutions to address the burden of rising property taxes.
paragraphs: In November, voters across the country will not only choose who will represent them in elected office, but also whether to approve certain changes to their state constitutions and statutes, including a variety of proposed tax policy changes. Rising property taxes have dominated discussions in many state capitols and among homeowners and business owners. While some states have addressed rising property taxes through legislation, others have turned to the ballot box.

This November, 12 property tax measures are on the ballot across 7 states. The most consequential are proposals to substantially raise homestead exemptions or tighten assessment limits, proposals that would shift property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. burdens in economically distortionary ways. Alternatively, North Carolina voters will consider a levy limit that would limit property tax revenue growth in a structurally sound way.

Assessment limits cap the amount by which a property’s taxable assessed value can increase annually. Oklahoma State Question 847 would tighten the state’s current assessment limit by reducing the annual cap on fair cash value increases for homestead property and agricultural land from 3 percent to 1.75 percent and lower the cap for other property from 5 to 4 percent.

The measure would also modify Oklahoma’s property tax relief provisions for homeowners over the age of 65. Oklahoma’s constitution currently freezes the fair cash value of a homestead for qualifying seniors whose income does not exceed the local median income. State Question 847 would replace this with a tiered, income-based structure, allowing seniors with incomes up to 180 percent of the median to receive a special assessment limit ranging from 0.35 percent to 1.4 percent. Higher-income seniors would receive the standard 1.75 percent limit.

Assessment limits are often created to protect established property owners from rising taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. bills that could price them out of their homes, but they come with numerous unintended consequences.

First, they create a “lock-in” effect, where homeowners may be reluctant to move or improve their property because taxable value resets when a property is sold or substantially improved. This reduces housing mobility and makes it less likely that growing families or older homeowners will relocate to homes that better meet their needs.

Second, assessment limits cause similarly situated properties to have vastly different assessed values based solely on when they were purchased. Because newer property owners are more likely to have taxable values that reflect current market conditions, more of the property tax burden gets shifted onto them.

By widening the gap between market and assessed values—especially for homestead, seniors’, and agricultural properties—Oklahoma State Question 847 would shift more of Oklahoma’s property tax burdens onto non-favored properties, including commercial and industrial properties, rental properties, and second homes.

Homestead exemptions reduce property taxes on primary residences by excluding a portion of the property’s value from taxation. Two states are asking voters to massively expand their existing homestead exemptions.
Florida’s Amendment 3 would substantially increase the state’s homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes.

Under current law, Florida homeowners who qualify are exempt from all property taxes on the first $25,000 of assessed value. A second inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin-adjusted exemption of $25,000 applies to assessed value beginning at $50,000 but does not apply to school district property taxes.

Florida Amendment 3 would maintain the existing $25,000 homestead exemption for school district property taxes. For all other property taxes, the amendment would increase the homestead exemption to $150,000 beginning in 2027, and to $250,000 beginning in 2028. Amendment 3 would also direct the legislature to establish a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities to increase the exemption, if they choose, to any higher level, up to the exclusion of all homestead property value.

While Florida Amendment 3 has received significant attention in recent months, Wyoming Initiative 1 should not be overlooked. This measure would add an additional homestead exemption for certain property owners to its two existing homestead exemptions.

In 2024, lawmakers adopted a long-term homeowner exemption, which now stands at 50 percent of the first $3 million in market value on primary residences of owners or spouses 65 or older, who have paid Wyoming residential property taxes for at least 25 years and who live in the home at least eight months per year.

In 2025, lawmakers adopted a 25 percent exemption on the first $1 million in market value (of both land and structures) for owner-occupants of single-family residential housing who reside in the home at least eight months per year. Those claiming the 50 percent long-term homeowner exemption may not simultaneously claim the 25 percent exemption.

Initiative 1 would create a third homestead exemption that would exempt an additional 50 percent of a home’s value (excluding the underlying land), with no value cap, for owners who have been Wyoming residents for at least one year and who lived in the home for at least six months during the preceding year. Eligible homeowners could claim both the 25 percent exemption and the new 50 percent exemption.

While both Florida Amendment 3 and Wyoming Initiative 1 would provide substantial relief to qualifying homeowners, neither would reduce the cost of providing local government services. As a result, the tax burden would ultimately get shifted onto non-favored properties, including commercial and industrial properties. Moreover, because commercial apartment buildings and multi-family dwellings that are not owner-occupied would not qualify for the exemption, the increased tax burden would likely be passed along to many renters. Furthermore, two similarly situated properties could face significantly different tax bills solely due to differences in property classification and the owners’ residency statuses, undermining the principle of tax neutrality.

Conversely, if approved by voters, the North Carolina Property Tax Levy Limit Amendment would require the North Carolina General Assembly to enact a property tax levy limit for local governments. The amendment would supplement North Carolina’s existing statutory property tax rate limit of $1.50 per $100 of assessed value.

Property values have risen significantly in recent years, outpacing inflation. In jurisdictions that have failed to adjust millages downward, property owners have experienced significant increases in their property tax bills. In North Carolina, property values rose substantially faster than inflation-adjusted property tax collections between 2018 and 2023. While some jurisdictions offset valuation increases with lower rates, others chose to capture the revenue windfall generated by higher property values.

North Carolina’s current rate limit constrains tax rates but does not directly limit total property tax collections. Valuation increases can generate significant additional revenue if rates are left unchanged or are reduced only slightly.
Levy limits are the most effective approach for constraining the growth of property tax collections, and they are a reform that each of the states mentioned here could benefit from.

Unlike assessment limits and expanded homestead exemptions, which create significant economic distortions, levy limits constrain property tax collections growth in a neutral, economically efficient manner. They directly control the growth in overall property tax collections by serving as a kind of allowance for government spending. When property values rise such that maintaining a static millage rate would increase property tax collections from existing property beyond a certain level, levy limits require that millage rates be adjusted downward, preventing unlegislated tax increases. Well-designed levy limits permit a reasonable amount of revenue growth, often incorporating adjustments for inflation and new construction.

This approach provides revenue stability for local governments while preserving the relationship between property value and property tax liability. Unlike assessment limits and homestead exemptions, levy limits do not disincentivize moving, improvements to property, or new construction.

In 2026, Iowa lawmakers enacted Senate File 2472, establishing a well-structured 2 percent property tax levy limit for cities and counties, with an allowance for new construction and improvements. Local government officials may adjust millage rates within the overall levy limit, provided they remain within Iowa’s current rate caps. Local governments may exceed the limit with voter approval at a special election.

If voters approve North Carolina’s amendment, lawmakers would have the opportunity in 2027 to follow in Iowa’s footsteps, designing a levy limit that works well for the state. A levy limit would be a structurally sound, long-term reform that preserves the property tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates., provides local governments with a stable and reliable revenue source, and avoids the distortionary policies that shift tax burdens rather than reducing them. Among the property tax relief options appearing on ballots this year, North Carolina’s proposed levy limit stands out as the most effective and economically neutral approach.

articles.title: A “Token Tax” Could Kill the Promise of AI
articles.standfirst: If we want to ensure that AI raises economic growth, we shouldn’t be pursuing tax policies that are stuck in the past and represent some of the worst ideas from the early internet age.
paragraphs: Lawmakers want to taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. artificial intelligence, but the playbook they’re pulling from increasingly resembles a relic of the past.

When it comes to taxing innovation, it’s wise not to reinvent the wheel. But if we want to ensure that AI raises economic growth, we shouldn’t be pursuing tax policies that are stuck in the past and represent some of the worst ideas from the early internet age.

There is no shortage of proposals coming out of Congress to tackle the purported threats AI poses. From Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-VT) AI Sovereign Wealth Fund to Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s (D-MA) call for an excise tax on data centers, there is among some policymakers a fear that if AI becomes a dominant part of our economy, the tax code must have a say in its direction.
This is a preview of our full op-ed originally published in City Journal.

Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

articles.title: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
articles.standfirst: Properties where someone has died in tragic circumstances can have big reductions in price.
paragraphs: The previous occupant of Ryua's apartment, pictured here, sadly took their own life
From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.
"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.
"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."
While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.
"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.
Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.
Ryua says that she shares her Tokyo apartment with a ghost

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.
Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.
For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state. For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."
The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.
But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

The 69-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.
Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.
"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."
Diane Tincher says she got a 50% reduction on her home in rural Japan

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.
It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.
Diane Tincher got a huge discount on her home in rural Japan
Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap.
Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

articles.title: It’s good to be flexible
articles.standfirst:
This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.  Yesterday the Chancellor told us what the minimum wage rates will be from April 2027 (well, strictly speaking he told the Times on Tuesday…). All rates – both adult and youth – will go up by 3.9 per cent. The adult rate goes to £13.21, … Continued
The post It’s good to be flexible appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.

Yesterday the Chancellor told us what the minimum wage rates will be from April 2027 (well, strictly speaking he told the Times on Tuesday…). All rates – both adult and youth – will go up by 3.9 per cent. The adult rate goes to £13.21, a 50p increase, worth £1,040 a year for someone working 40 hours a week. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) expects inflation in Q2 next year to be 3.6 per cent; if this comes to pass, then minimum wage earners will see their pay go up slightly in real terms.

There was some chatter online in the form of “oh look, another chunky minimum wage increase”. But in fact, the Low Pay Commission (LPC) was conservative in its recommendations this year, making full use of its new freedom to be flexible in the face of labour market conditions. Some people doubted it would, because it’s not in the LPC’s recent institutional memory to do so: since 2015 the adult minimum wage has been set by following government-set targets for increases, rather than trading off pay gains for workers against employment risks. But it did, and, in my view, came to a sensible decision.

Calling the increases ‘conservative’ might sound peculiar, given that the 3.9 per cent increase in the adult rate is bigger than the 3.7 per cent increase the LPC estimated would be needed back in April for an ‘on-course rate’ (i.e. to stick to the two-thirds of median hourly wages bit of its remit). But it’s true, because new data published last week1 showed median hourly pay growth of 5.9 per cent in the year to April 2026 (see the chart below). Had it stuck doggedly to that part of its remit, this would have led to a 5.7 per cent National Living Wage (NLW) increase. As you can see in the chart, such a figure would have been way ahead of current average earnings growth (3.7 per cent in the three months to August 20262) and even further ahead of where pay growth is expected to be next year (the median forecast for 2027 among external forecasters is 3.3 per cent).

Surely, you might say, the LPC would have been mad to have done that? Maybe. But it’s more or less what happened back in 2025. The 2024 pay data came in stronger than expected (because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) had introduced a new methodology that meant more high earners in its Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings sample), and the LPC’s rigid remit meant this fed straight into the 2025 NLW uprating in a mechanical way. (It was doubly unfortunate that this accidentally big uprating came alongside the hike to employer National Insurance contributions …). The Government learned from that episode and relaxed the LPC’s remit: the ‘two-thirds of median pay’ benchmark for bite of the NLW is now a “key reference point”, not an unbending requirement[MB1] .

There’s a similar story of newfound flexibility on the youth rates. The Government’s policy is that the higher youth rate (which currently applies to 18-20-year-olds) should converge with the adult rate. The LPC had initially interpreted the Government as wanting convergence to happen within the Parliament (i.e. by 2029), which meant closing a 25 per cent gap in five years. This led to bumper increases in the youth rate, seen pretty clearly in the chart below.

If the LPC had done something similar this year – continued closing the gap to the adult rate, with a target of 2029 – then the 18-20-year-old rate would have increased by roughly 10 per cent. But the Government has responded to flashing alarm bells in the youth labour market by relaxing (or clarifying) this part of the LPC’s remit too. The LPC was told explicitly it could choose the pace of the youth-adult convergence (i.e. ‘don’t fixate on 2029’) and that it should prioritise young people’s employment prospects.

I thought this might lead to some convergence, albeit less than in recent years, resulting in a youth uprating just above the adult uprating. But the LPC paused convergence altogether. I think this was a good call. As I set out last week, we can’t say for sure that minimum wage increases are to blame for a deteriorating youth labour market, but we also can’t say that they are not, and it’s not worth taking the risk.

So overall, the LPC and Government have both shown a new flexibility when it comes to minimum wage setting, and that’s to be applauded. If labour market conditions improve, there may be scope for bigger upratings in 2028. At our recent event, Arin Dube said he thought a bite of 70 per cent or higher might be possible. Equally, if the labour market continues to struggle, caution would be the right approach again.

articles.title: The 2026 Budget buys stability and points in the right direction on growth
articles.standfirst:
The 2026 Budget builds on the back of strong economic growth in the first half of the year. The overall direction of travel is clear and positive, writes Anna Valero, but the challenges of protecting investment and economic growth remain, especially in an environment of continued global economic storms and spending pressures. Enjoying this post? Then … Continued
The post The 2026 Budget buys stability and points in the right direction on growth first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: The 2026 Budget builds on the back of strong economic growth in the first half of the year. The overall direction of travel is clear and positive, writes Anna Valero, but the challenges of protecting investment and economic growth remain, especially in an environment of continued global economic storms and spending pressures.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

The Chancellor’s first Budget had to do three things at once in a challenging and uncertain context: maintain a credible fiscal buffer against future shocks, support households struggling with a prolonged cost of living crisis, and nurture the green shoots of growth that have emerged despite global headwinds (or, more like storms – as the Chancellor put it).

On the first two, the OBR confirmed that the Chancellor is forecast to meet the fiscal rules by 2029-30 with headroom of £15bn against the stability rule (rising to £22bn in 2030-31) which seems reasonable given the context and market expectations; and a package of household support has been set out to provide “breathing space” (though this could have been better targeted). The harder test is the third. Increasing the quantity and quality of public investment, measures to boost business investment, and a successful programme of devolution will be crucial for shaping prosperity.

Growth is what generates the tax receipts to stabilise public finances and raise living standards. The UK economy has shown resilience, with growth ranking top of the G7 in the first half of the year. Recent productivity data restatements imply that our post financial crisis slowdown was less bad than previously thought, but there’s still significant slowdown that must be addressed. The uptick in productivity (per worker) that we have seen since Q3 2024 suggests that this is possible if business investment is encouraged and confidence maintained.
The UK economy has shown resilience, with growth ranking top of the G7 in the first half of the year.

The OBR has upgraded GDP growth projection for this year (from 1.1 per cent to 1.2 per cent). This comes with a downgrade for next year and upgrades later in the forecast period. Business investment is forecast to be 0.5 per cent higher in 2030 than in the March forecast, slightly raising capital deepening and trend productivity. While not mentioned in the speech, the Prime Minister’s recent interest in getting closer to the EU could materially improve the growth outlook – the OBR’s assumption is that Brexit will reduce the level of UK productivity by 4 per cent over 15 years.

The Budget has protected public sector net investment – historically public sector investment has been low and volatile. But quality matters as well as quantity – well designed public investments that catalyse private capital are needed. The (further) £20.4 billion boost to the Public Finance Institutions, enabled by the previous Chancellor’s change to the fiscal rules, is crucial here and will channel more support towards renewable energy, defence, AI and other areas.

The AI package (confirmed at £700 million) which will help the UK to benefit from the opportunities of AI, while managing the risks and shaping adjustment, puts more resource behind the Prime Minister’s ambition to take a lead on these themes during the UK’s G20 presidency. And the Data Centre Covenant is a positive step for ensuring that this type of infrastructure investment benefits communities. On the green transition, the Energy Wealth Fund announced alongside the Jackdaw decision will enable extra tax revenues to be channelled towards clean energy projects, improving energy affordability and resilience and generating sustainable growth.

The main risk is reprioritisation away from areas that were identified as being important for growth and in line with the Modern Industrial Strategy of 2025 (that is already generating positive outcomes), with departments finding savings to be able to fund the Defence Investment Plan.

The absence of new broad-based taxes on business is positive for investment. The anticipated increase to the banks corporation tax surcharge is temporary and smaller than that expected, with these and some other taxes (e.g. on gambling) paying for reliefs. But the more interesting question is whether new targeted reliefs address real market failures that prevent investment in productive, resilient assets. New reliefs for entrepreneurs and to business rates for retail and hospitality businesses are welcome but are not a substitute for deeper reform consistently called for by the IFS and others. Moreover, the key barriers for high-growth firms are at the scale up phase, where pensions reform, catalytic capital and bolder action on procurement and regulation (mentioned by the Chancellor) are likely to matter more. Skills shortages are another barrier consistently highlighted by businesses, and further measures to incentivise investment should be explored.

High energy costs are a problem for UK businesses, particularly energy intensive ones. A key challenge is to ensure that short-term support does not dampen incentives to invest in cheaper, more resilient, clean alternatives. Here, the Chancellor began with an emphasis on longer term energy reforms – including breaking the link between gas prices and the costs of electricity, and pledges to limit policy costs in bills. Such reforms will support electrification as well as reduce costs, and are accompanied by other more immediate support.

The forthcoming 10-year plan, the outcomes of the Milburn and Timms reviews that will inform much-needed welfare reform and associated savings, and next year’s Spending Review will determine whether this direction or travel delivers the desired outcomes.

Non-fiscal measures to reduce the costs of regulation had already been announced before Budget, but the announcement to bring the Better Regulation Executive back was new. This language matters – much regulation exists for a reason, and indeed, new technologies, transitions and risks call for new regulations to shape investment. What matters is that the regulation is designed and implemented effectively, provides certainty and supports innovation.

Large and persistent regional disparities must be addressed, both to improve living standards and to improve national growth performance. In a highly centralised economy, well-designed fiscal devolution can align incentives for growth locally, generate income streams for leaders to borrow against, and give regional leaders – armed with local knowledge – complementary levers that work together for growth. The new fiscal devolution roadmap sets out new steps on business rates retention and a share of income tax assigned to mayors from 2028 (when new powers for visitor levies also come into effect). Building capacity, balancing incentives for growth with equalisation for places losing out, and improving coordination between national and regional policymakers on place-based decision-making will be important for success.

The Budget gives a clear direction of travel: stability and breathing space first, setting up some big decisions ahead. The forthcoming 10-year plan, the outcomes of the Milburn and Timms reviews that will inform much-needed welfare reform and associated savings, and next year’s Spending Review will determine whether this direction delivers the desired outcomes. The last Spending Review involved difficult decisions and prioritisation, and higher inflation erodes the value of settlements. The central challenge will be protecting investment and pro-growth reforms while competing pressures, including defence and any continued global economic storms, mount.

Anna Valero is a Professor in Practice at the LSE’s Centre for Economic Performance and Global School of Sustainability; Director of the CEP’s Growth Programme and Deputy Director of the Programme on Innovation and Diffusion. Her research focuses on the drivers of productivity and innovation in firms and regions, and in particular on informing policies for environmentally sustainable and inclusive growth. Anna was a member of the Council of Economic Advisers to the Chancellor of the Exchequer in 2024-25 advising on growth, and Industrial Strategy Adviser in 2025-2026. She has held a number of other advisory roles for the UK government and policy institutions.

articles.title: Budget 2026 – continuity with Reeves
articles.standfirst:
John Healey’s 2026 Budget follows the fiscal foundations set down by Rachel Reeves, writes John Van Reenen. But while stability has been preserved, many tough decisions including welfare reform and funding increasing healthcare and defence spending have been postponed. Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles. The … Continued
The post Budget 2026 – continuity with Reeves first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: John Healey’s 2026 Budget follows the fiscal foundations set down by Rachel Reeves, writes John Van Reenen. But while stability has been preserved, many tough decisions including welfare reform and funding increasing healthcare and defence spending have been postponed.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

The global backdrop to John Healey’s first Budget was Made in America, crafted by President Trump. Earlier this year, inflation was projected to be heading back to the 2 per cent target, but the Iran War torpedoed that with a huge spike in energy prices. Market jitters over the high and growing US deficit has pushed up bond yields everywhere, and this has added significantly to the cost of servicing UK debt – to the tune of £14bn.

But there is some good news. UK growth has been resilient this year, and productivity growth – the fundamental determinant of living standards in the long term – is looking up. Our research shows that since Labour was elected, output per worker growth has been 1.6 per cent, per annum, compared to 0.3 per cent in the previous decade. Moreover, the ONS now reckons that productivity per hour was twice as fast since the 2008-9 global financial crisis than previously thought. This is still about half of the pre-crisis average, but the UK now looks much less of an outlier.

The Budget has followed the fiscal foundations laid down by Rachel Reeves. The Chancellor kept to the strong framework laid down in 2024. Day-to-day spending has to be balanced in three years, by the end of this parliament. The previous government had targeted five years away, far too distant to be credible.

I believe that there is an unhealthy obsession about the precise “headroom” against this Stability Rule. Nevertheless, the fall from £24bn to £15bn is in line with expectations and uses Reeves’ buffer to do its job of insuring against uncertain times.
The Budget has followed the fiscal foundations laid down by Rachel Reeves.

The Budget has giveaways of 0.25 per cent of GDP 2026/27, most eye-catchingly the £2.6bn in £100 payments to households to help with their energy bills. These giveaways were balanced by tax rises: a temporary 3 per cent increase in the Bank Surcharge (raising £1bn next year) and 2 per cent more on savings and property taxes (£1bn p.a.).

Earlier this month, IMF ​Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said “The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively.” This fiscal consolidation is possible only through the difficult decision to significantly raise taxes in Labour’s first two budgets. Healey’s tax rises amount to £6.5bn in 2030/31 compared to the £66bn. The past Chancellor took the hit for these politically unpopular decisions.

There has been much glib commentary on the need to radically reduce public spending. But this ignores the fact that the current plans from the 2025 Budget already incorporated tight spending limits over the next three years. This is further sharpened by the increase in inflation because departmental spending plans are set in cash terms, so their real value is eroded when inflation rises. Since the Chancellor has not increased the envelope to compensate for this, it means tough times ahead.
The challenge will be to keep to these plans. The multi-year Spending Review next year that determines the splits between departments will crystallize these trade-offs.

Although the OBR upgraded this year to 1.2 per cent GDP growth, it downgraded next year’s to 1.0 per cent. The better news on UK productivity growth does not (yet) seem reflected in its forecasts, perhaps unsurprisingly as it downgraded long-run productivity growth only last autumn.

Andy Burnham is betting big on decentralisation to boost growth by allowing more local control over taxes such as business rates (20 per cent next year and all by the end of the decade). I welcome this as it will give local leaders more “skin in the game”. But it also requires the government to allow places who use these revenues wisely and do better to pull away from those who do not – even if this generates some regional inequality. And the momentum on national strategic priorities such as the Oxford-Cambridge corridor and Heathrow expansion must not be lost.

Reeves’ net debt rule sensibly made allowance for the assets of public financial institutions, such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as liabilities. This has created space for the extra £20bn announced today to help business investments in infrastructure such as energy, AI and defence.
Ending the triple lock is a great move, but we must return to reforming disability benefits.

The Better Regulation Executive is an opportunity to bolster the positive planning reforms and push back against excessively costly ones. Increasing housing supply through existing deregulation (e.g., Planning and Infrastructure Act) is better than the new ‘Your First home Scheme’ which spends £4.7bn on boosting demand.
Perhaps inevitably, this was a “steady as she goes” Budget. It means many crunch decisions have been postponed until next year.

First, welfare needs to be tackled. Ending the triple lock is a great move, but we must return to reforming disability benefits. The Timms and Milburn reviews must be the basis for more radical reform, not reversals and prevarication.

Second, the baroque structure of UK tax needs serious reform. There are too many cliff-edges and regulatory taxes on growth that keep firms small such as the high threshold for VAT registration. Property taxation is a mess.

Third, defence was why Healey ejected Keir Starmer’s. Defence spending increases must be made a growth rich as possible and not come from cuts to other public capital investment. Public R&D, in particular, needs increasing in the military and elsewhere.

Finally, how are we to pay for health over the long-term? Demographics and other forces mean that healthcare costs as a share of GDP will inevitably rise further. The creation of an NHS for social care will add to these costs.

The scale of defence and health spending makes it inevitable that these will require increases in general taxation. It follows that the main parties cannot continue with their refusal to countenance increases in the rates of income tax, VAT or employees’ National Insurance. It is better to face this reality than to be forced to act when the crisis comes.

John Van Reenen OBE is the Ronald Coase Chair in Economics and School Professor in the Department of Economics at London School of Economics. He is also an associate and former director of the Centre for Economic Performance at LSE. He was Chair of the Council of Economic Advisers to the Chancellor, 2024-2025.

articles.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
articles.standfirst: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council...
paragraphs: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged.

Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.

The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 100 basis points since February, to around 5.3 per cent. As explained in this blog, some of that rise can be traced to the war in the Middle East and would presumably unwind if there were a resolution. But over half of it likely reflects other factors, including heavy government borrowing worldwide and the AI investment boom, which have pushed up global long-term real interest rates. These are forces that could exert a persistent effect on gilt yields.

The DMO’s financing remit for 2026-27 has been modestly revised up today by £7.4 billion, taking planned gilt issuance to £250.6 billion. This means taking on additional debt at what could prove to be a persistently higher cost of borrowing.
Successive economic shocks this century have ratcheted up the debt-to-GDP ratio. After both the global financial crisis and the pandemic, debt stabilised at a higher level.

But for fiscal policy to act as a shock absorber, the government needs to have adequate capacity to step in and act when the next shock hits the economy. A consistently high debt ratio limits this ability. Therefore, the minimal test of credibility of for today’s budget was whether the Chancellor was willing to stop the debt rising even further.

The OBR forecasts that policies announced in this budget will lead to increased borrowing over the next three years of £12.4 billion, which will then be followed by a reduction of £7 billion on average in the years after. Based on the forecast paths laid out by the OBR today we can see that our minimal test of credibility was not met with Public Sector Net Debt peaking at around 97 per cent of GDP in 2028-29 before falling only slightly to 96 per cent of GDP in 2031-32, higher than the ratio in August this year of 94 per cent.
Today’s Budget comes against a fragile global backdrop as the risk of adverse shocks appears to have increased over the past year. Bond markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop

UK ten-year gilt yields remain the highest in the G7, leaving the public finances exposed to shifts in market sentiment. In our judgement, this strengthens the case for building fiscal buffers. The Chancellor’s decision to reduce headroom by £9 billion therefore leaves the government vulnerable to future shocks.

This is underscored by the path for debt interest now being higher than was set out in March 2026. By the end of the decade UK debt interest is expected to rise to around £150 billion annually – more than the government currently spends on education.

A credible fiscal strategy could help to reduce debt interest. Even modest fiscal restraint could deliver a credibility dividend of 10-20 basis points off gilt rates (worth around £1-2 billion a year by the end of the parliament).

Today’s Budget measures do not attempt to place the debt-to-GDP ratio on a sustained downward path in the medium term. Difficult decisions have, once again, been deferred, leaving the integrity of public finances contingent on good fortune. But hoping for the best is not a credible basis for managing the public finances. This approach leaves the UK government more exposed to renewed market scrutiny in the months ahead.
The longer the Chancellor delays the necessary adjustment, the larger, and more difficult, these adjustments will be.
