articles.title: Inflation Could Climb Above 5% in Early 2027
articles.standfirst: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month.  Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4...
paragraphs: Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5 per cent in September from 3.1 per cent the previous month. Monthly price growth between August and September in 2026 was high at 0.4 per cent compared to 0 per cent in 2025, leading to the increase of 0.4 percentage points in annual inflation.

The monthly inflation of 0.4 per cent corresponds to an annualised rate of 4.9 per cent and flows on from the high monthly inflation of 0.5 per cent in August. This suggests that the continuing energy supply issues caused by the American war on Iran are feeding into general price inflation. These effects are likely to escalate until a resolution to the conflict is found. Under our preferred forecast scenarios, inflation looks set to reach
The Bank of England will face pressure to tighten policy as inflation continues to increase.
If we look at the broad categories of inflation over the last 12 months, we see:

Services inflation this month is pretty much in line with wage data reflecting a cooling labour market: the latest ONS figures on wage increases excluding bonuses, covering June to August 2026, came in at 3.7 per cent.
The biggest contributors to the change in headline inflation between August and September were:

However, these overall contributions combine the “base effects” of inflation dropping out from the previous year with the new inflation “dropping in”. We need to unwrap these to get the true picture. Figure 1 (below) shows the sectoral contributions to overall inflation, with the previous year’s monthly inflation dropping out (blue) and the current month’s new inflation dropping in (brown). The overall impact is the sum of the two, shown by the burgundy line.

Focusing on the new monthly inflation (brown), eight sectors registered an increase in prices this month, with two registering falls (interestingly these two were Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). The blue dropouts from the previous year are negative or close to zero in eight sectors, and positive in two (also Transport and Food and Non-Alcoholic Beverages). Overall, the burgundy line, showing the total effect for each sector, is significantly negative in one sector, and significantly positive in three sectors, as listed above.

We can look ahead over the next 12 months to see how inflation might evolve as the recent inflation “drops out” as we move forward month by month. Each month, the new inflation enters the annual figure and the old inflation from the same month in the previous year “drops out”. We depict the following scenarios for future inflation dropping in:

The Iran war makes the future path of inflation highly uncertain. In my initial blog, The Possible Effects on UK Inflation in 2026 of the US-Iran Conflict, published on 23 March, I contrasted the possible effects of two scenarios, a “good scenario” with a short conflict that left most of the energy infrastructure in the Gulf intact and an “ugly” scenario with a prolonged conflict in which most of the infrastructure is destroyed. With the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and now the additional closure of the Bab-el-Mandeb, we seem to be heading into the “ugly” scenario, with a major inflationary spike. In addition, the direct conflict between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah (the Houthis) has led to the destruction of significant pipelines and refineries in Saudi Arabia. Unless the conflicts are resolved soon, there is likely to be more inflation coming our way and also negative impacts on output and employment across much of the world as we move into 2027.

I have therefore revived our old friend from 2022, the “sanctions” scenario, now renamed the “Hormuz” scenario. This and the very high scenario seem to be most relevant at present, and we also depict the high and medium scenarios for reference. The low scenario seems unlikely to be relevant so we have not depicted it.

If we look at the very high and Hormuz scenarios, inflation might be at 4.2-4.7 per cent in December 2026. Even the medium and high scenarios suggest that inflation will be at 3.4-3.7 per cent by December. So, under all scenarios, inflation looks set to rise in the final quarter of 2026.
For further analysis of inflation in the United Kingdom, see:
Seasonal Adjustment of CPI and CPIH, Huw Dixon and Monica George Michail. NIESR Policy Paper 45, May 2025

articles.title: The Return of the Energy Shock
articles.standfirst: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of...
paragraphs: In this blog we present updated forecasts from our Multi-Recurrent Neural Network (MRN) model, extending the outlook from September 2026 to August 2027.1 This is our fourth MRN update of the year, following the February, May and July 2026 blogs. Three things have changed since July:

The July blog made a testable claim: our recommended Intermediate Energy MRN projected 3.0 per cent for June 2026, easing to 2.7 per cent by August, before rising to a 4.5 per cent peak in February 2027. The outturns were 2.6 per cent in June and 3.1 per cent in August. The model was 0.4 percentage points too high in June and 0.4 points too low in August, and the sign of the error flipped exactly as the geopolitics did. In June the peace announcement was pulling energy prices down faster than the model’s training data allowed for; by August the collapse of that deal was pushing them up faster. We flagged the first possibility explicitly in July (“a June print materially below this range would suggest the peace-deal energy price fall is passing through faster than the model anticipates”). We did not anticipate the second, and nor, on the evidence of its July Report, did the Bank of England, whose central projection assumed oil prices would drift from $76 to $71, and inflation would peak at 3.2 per cent in the fourth quarter of 2026. Two lessons follow. The first is that the MRN carries no oil price assumption at all; it extrapolates from the energy history it has seen. So its twelve-month path is best read as an unconditional projection of where the data were pointing at end-August. The Bank’s and NIESR’s forecasts are conditional on an assumed path for oil prices. Part of the gap between us is therefore a difference in what is being forecast, not only in how; the fair test is whether the unconditional path keeps moving the right way when the world moves, as it did between June and August. The second is that readers of our May blog will recall that the then-current MRN had inflation “well beyond 5 per cent in early 2027”; the July update, trained during the brief peace, pulled that back to 4.5 per cent. The present round returns to the May reading.

Figure 1 shows the current forecast of two classes of MRN model: the Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which uses CPI level and month-on-month change, ONS UK energy CPI, the monthly Brent average and, new in this round, Bank Rate; and the Intermediate Energy MRN, which adds real GDP, PPI, the 10-year gilt yield and the sterling effective exchange rate to that set. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects annual CPI inflation of 3.7 per cent in September 2026, 4.1 per cent in November, 4.4 per cent in December, and then a step up to 5.4 per cent in January 2027, holding at 5.4 per cent in February and March before easing to 4.3–4.4 per cent in April–May and drifting back up to 4.9 per cent by July and August 2027. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN follows a similar path but peaks later and higher, at 5.7 per cent in June 2027. The Average MRN peaks at 5.3 per cent in February and does not fall below 4.5 per cent at any point in the forecast window. The quarterly averages are 3.9, 5.2 and 4.8 per cent for the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first two quarters of 2027, respectively.

We must state two things about this path clearly. The first is that the peak has moved up by almost a full percentage point since July, from 4.5 per cent to 5.4 per cent, while its timing has stayed put in the first quarter of 2027. That revision is almost entirely the energy channel doing what it is designed to do: the price of Brent crude oil is 50 per cent higher than when the July models were trained, UK wholesale gas prices have risen 78 per cent since the Bank’s July Report, and the Ofgem energy price cap has gone from £1,477 in Q2 to £1,663 in Q3 and £1,723 for October–December, with Cornwall Insight now forecasting £1,999, a 16 per cent rise, for January 2027. The second is that part of the January step is arithmetic rather than economics. The CPI fell by 0.5 per cent month-on-month in January 2026; so, roughly half a point of the first quarter peak is that base effect. It is real, in the sense that the headline rate will print it, but it does not imply a fresh burst of price pressure in that month.

This is the first round in which we forecast the policy rate, and the two classes disagree in a way we think is informative rather than embarrassing. The Simple Energy + MPC MRN, which sees inflation, energy and the rate itself, but nothing of the real economy, has Bank Rate rising from 3.75 per cent to 4.0 per cent by February 2027 and 4.5 per cent by June. The Intermediate Energy MRN, which also sees GDP, producer prices, gilt yields and sterling, has it falling to 3.5 per cent by November, 3.25 per cent by January and 3.0 per cent by March, before settling at 3.25 per cent. The average of the two dips to 3.5 per cent through the winter, touches 3.25 per cent in March, and is back at 3.75 per cent by June 2027.

Read the two classes as the two sides of the Monetary Policy Committee’s own argument. At its 17 September meeting the Committee held at 3.75 per cent by six votes to three, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voting for an immediate quarter-point increase on the grounds that slack “may have already peaked” and that raising rates is “a better risk-management strategy when faced with uncertainty about inflation dynamics and second-round effects”. The six who held pointed to “very limited evidence of emerging second-round effects” and to slack “still evident in a range of indicators”, with Alan Taylor arguing that policy “should respond to evidence of propagation rather than mechanically to volatile ticks in headline energy prices”. The Simple class, which has no measure of slack and reacts to headline energy, is the hawkish minority’s direction of travel. The Intermediate class, which can see weak activity and the restrictiveness of financial conditions, is the majority’s. We do not claim the network understands this debate; we claim that the two feature sets encode the two positions, and that is exactly why we report both rather than only the average.

The September 2026 inflation number from the ONS is due on 21 October and is the first direct test of these forecasts. The Intermediate Energy MRN projects 3.7 per cent, the Simple Energy + MPC MRN 3.9 per cent and the Average 3.8 per cent, all well above August’s 3.1 per cent, reflecting the motor-fuel surge the Bank has already documented. A September number in the 3.6–3.9 per cent range would validate the near-term path; something nearer 3.3 per cent would suggest the VAT cut and the G7 reserve release are biting faster than the model allows. The second test is the 6 November MPC decision: the Simple MRN class implies the hawks gain ground, the Intermediate MRN class implies the first cut arrives by November, and the two cannot both be right. The third is the Ofgem announcement for January 2027, due in late November, which will fix the single biggest input into our peak in the first quarter of 2027. The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook and the NIESR Autumn Economic Outlook both appear before our next update, and we will report how the MRN stands against their revised paths.

1 The modelling approach is described in Binner, J. M., Kelly, L. J. and Tepper, J. A. (2025) ‘Professional Forecasters vs. Shallow Neural Network Ensembles: Assessing Inflation Prediction Accuracy’, Journal of Risk and Financial Management, 18(4), 173 (MRN methodology). https://doi.org/10.3390/jrfm18040173.

articles.title: Has Fiscal Policy Adjusted To A World Of Higher Interest Rates?
articles.standfirst: As all good economists know, fiscal sustainability comes down to the gap between the interest rate the government pays on its debt and the growth rate of the economy, r...
paragraphs: As all good economists know, fiscal sustainability comes down to the gap between the interest rate the government pays on its debt and the growth rate of the economy, r minus g. Think of this as a race. If r is lower than g, debt (the IOUs we’ve written in the past) will grow more slowly than the economy, exerting a downward force on debt as a share of GDP. In this world, government spending on schools, hospitals, defence and so on can exceed tax revenues indefinitely without the debt ratio rising—as long as the deficit isn’t too big. But when r is above g, the converse will be true, and the debt ratio will rise unless the government runs a primary surplus big enough to cover the gap.

The big change in the global financial system over the past few years has been the big increase in r. While the gap between r and g has worked in the government’s favour in the years since the global financial crisis, this has flipped recently with r exceeding g on new borrowing; importantly, the gap between r and g has widened further just this past year.

In this week’s blog, I look at what this means for the UK’s public finances and for our ability to keep the debt ratio stable over the medium term. My argument in a nutshell is this. The government’s plans already contain a £100 billion planned consolidation, roughly of the scale needed to stabilise debt at the interest rates prevailing in February. But much of it is back-loaded to around the next election, and is unlikely to be delivered. If the rise in rates since February persists, debt interest will be around £15 billion a year higher by the end of the decade than the OBR assumed, which means more tightening on top. This has the feel of a slow-motion car crash: each year, cheap debt issued when rates were low is refinanced at today’s rates.

The mood music ahead of the Budget later this month is that the Chancellor will instead allow borrowing to rise modestly relative to plan to cushion the effects of the Iran war. Some of that is justified—some limited energy cost relief for the most vulnerable households, for example. But borrowing to absorb a shock only makes sense if the shock is temporary. We can’t know for certain whether higher rates are here to stay, but there are good reasons to think they might be, and the costs of getting it wrong are skewed. That points to planning for rates staying high.

The 10-year gilt yield is now 5.3 per cent, its highest level since 2007 (Figure 1). The real yield, which strips out compensation for inflation, is 2.0 per cent, the highest since 2008. For most of the decade after the GFC, the real yield was negative, reaching minus 3 per cent in 2020 and 2021. That was when much of today’s debt stock was issued, and as it matures, it is refinanced at today’s rates.

Since the end of February, around the time of the OBR’s last forecast, the 10-year yield has risen by about a percentage point (Figure 2). At the short end, much of the rise reflects inflation compensation: 55 basis points of the 120-basis point rise at five years. At the long end, it’s almost all real: 60 of the 68 basis points at thirty years. This is just telling us that markets expect the energy shock to pass, but they are pricing in a more persistent increase in real rates.

The cleanest way to see this is via the 5-year rate 5-years ahead. This is the real rate financial markets are pricing for 2031-36. It’s useful because it looks through the near-term repricing of Bank Rate and inflation. Since February, it has risen by 75 basis points in the UK and almost 100 basis points in the US, taking both back to, or above, where they were before the financial crisis.

In all, real rates have risen by around 5 percentage points since the end of 2021. Most of that came in 2022 and 2023, after the first energy shock and the Liz Truss mini-Budget. There was a further lurch upwards of around 100 basis points from mid-2024, and yet another since February.

The benign reading of higher real rates is that they reflect stronger expected growth, in which case r minus g might not have moved much. There’s some support for this in the UK. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in the three months to August, the eighth consecutive three-month rise, and was 1.8 per cent higher than a year earlier, comfortably above most estimates of trend growth. Last month, the ONS also revised up post-crisis productivity growth from 0.7 to 1.3 per cent a year. But that revision came from lower estimates of hours worked rather than higher output, so GDP is unchanged and the implications for future growth are unclear.

GDP growth so far this year is running close to our pre-war NIESR February forecast of 1.4 per cent, significantly stronger than the forecast we made once the war had begun. Is that telling us that the underlying growth capacity is stronger than we thought, perhaps because the AI capex boom is lifting growth everywhere? Or that the effects of the war have been smaller than feared, or have yet to be felt in full (inflation in the UK won’t peak until the new year).
The truth is, it’s too early to tell. The safer assumption for now is that g has barely moved, so the rise in r has widened the gap one for one.

On paper, the government’s plans already contain a large consolidation. The OBR’s March forecast, based on those plans, has the primary balance moving from a deficit of 1.5 per cent of GDP last year to a surplus of 1.5 per cent by 2030-31 (Figure 4). That is a tightening of 3 per cent of GDP, or around £100 billion per year by the end of the forecast. At the interest rates prevailing in February, this was enough to stabilise the debt ratio and then have debt falling, from 96.3 per cent to 95.1 per cent by 2030-31.

The key question is whether this path is credible. I doubt it. It has the classic shape of jam today, belt-tightening tomorrow, which Charlie Bean once called the Augustinian approach to fiscal policy. The timing makes it harder still. Around half of the tightening is scheduled to happen in 2028-29, and 2029-30, ahead of the next general election (which must happen by August 2029). Economists know this as the time-inconsistency problem, after Kydland and Prescott. We want to convince people that we’ll do something painful in future, whether going on a diet or saving more next year for retirement, but when the future arrives those plans no longer look so appealing and we renege. The problem is that the people we’re trying to convince understand that incentive and don’t believe us in the first place.

Figure 5 shows the problem in practice. It plots every OBR forecast of the primary balance since 2010 against what actually happened. Almost every forecast shows the primary balance rising into surplus within five years. The outturn has not been in surplus once over this period, the last being in 2001-02.
This time inconsistency may also help to explain why UK borrowing costs have stayed high relative to other countries’, even with a material consolidation pencilled in.

As we saw earlier, interest rates have moved a lot since the OBR’s last forecast. On our rough calculations, if they stay at today’s levels, debt interest will be £15 billion a year higher by 2030-31 than the OBR assumed in March. Will the Budget tighten policy to reflect this? It doesn’t appear so. The runway has instead been laid for a Budget with less “headroom” against the fiscal rules, which simply means more borrowing relative to plan.

Whether that is the right call depends on whether the rise in rates is temporary or permanent. The logic comes from Bob Hall’s famous 1978 paper on the consumption Euler equation (Hall shared this year’s Nobel prize with Michael Woodford). A household that smooths its consumption should respond only to news about its permanent income. Faced with a temporary hit, it borrows and keeps spending; faced with a permanent one, it cuts back. Robert Barro applied the same logic to government a year later: debt should absorb temporary shocks, while taxes and spending should adjust to permanent ones. Borrowing to help the most vulnerable through a temporary energy price spike passes this test. Borrowing to absorb a permanent rise in the cost of debt does not; it simply postpones the adjustment and makes it bigger.

So is the rise in rates permanent? We can’t know for sure. But the evidence in the first section points to a large persistent component. The rise at the long end of the gilt curve is almost entirely in real rates; the real rate markets expect in five to ten years’ time has risen by around 75 basis points and almost 100 in the US, which points to a global shift rather than something specific to the UK. Our recent Market Anatomy report sets out the evidence in more detail and finds that two-thirds of the move looks like a lasting rise in global real rates.

There are two ways to make decisions under this kind of uncertainty. The first is Bayesian: treat a share of the shock as permanent, in proportion to how persistent such shocks have been in the past, and update as the data come in. Real interest rates have historically been very persistent, and forward rates already embody markets’ best guess of the persistent component. On that approach, policy should respond to most of the move now.

The second is robust control: ask which outcome would be worst and set policy to avoid it. Here the costs of getting it wrong are lopsided. If the government tightens and rates fall back, it can loosen again later. If it borrows more and rates stay high, it risks a loss of confidence in the public finances that is hard to reverse, as France has found and as the UK learned in 2022. Robust control points to planning for rates staying high.

Both approaches point the same way. The rise in rates since February is not a reason to run down headroom; if anything, it is a reason to rebuild it. Borrowing more now also shifts the burden of adjustment onto younger and future taxpayers, who will inherit the higher debt interest bill.

articles.title: What Might the UK Budget Mean for the Devolved Governments?
articles.standfirst: John Healey’s first Budget as Chancellor will, understandably, be judged mainly on the UK government’s fiscal position: meeting the fiscal rules, who bears the burden of tax and spending changes,...
paragraphs: John Healey’s first Budget as Chancellor will, understandably, be judged mainly on the UK government’s fiscal position: meeting the fiscal rules, who bears the burden of tax and spending changes, and the reaction of increasingly captious gilt markets. But for a Chancellor who has pledged to “move power and money out of Westminster”, one question deserves more attention than it usually gets: how do Westminster’s funding decisions reach the nations that already have devolved budgets?

The answer is neither uniform nor straightforward. Spending, tax and benefit decisions reach the devolved budgets through different channels and to different degrees, so the net effect is rarely obvious from headline announcements. That matters more than usual this year, with all three devolved administrations facing a difficult 2027–28. What their finance ministers expect from the Budget on 28 October will depend as much on where changes are announced as on how large they are.

The devolved governments’ funding is mainly set at UK spending reviews. These fix departmental budgets for several years, and the Barnett formula turns those plans into a block grant for each administration. The grants are not recalculated from scratch at each Budget. Funding carries forward from the last fiscal year, and any change to UK spending flows through the same formula.

As a result, when a Chancellor changes spending, each nation gets roughly a population share of any increase or cut in services that are devolved to it, called a Barnett Consequential. What flows through depends on what is devolved. Health and schools are devolved in all three nations, policing and justice only in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and immigration and defence in none. As a result, UK government departments made up 39 per cent of identifiable public service expenditure in Wales in 2024-25, 30 per cent in Scotland and just 5 per cent in Northern Ireland.

Budget announcements are priced differently in each nation. The Barnett formula gives new funding as an equal amount per head, not as an equal percentage increase. Per-head spending in each nation started above England’s level, so the same cash amount translates to a smaller percentage increase. Over time, this ‘Barnett squeeze’ pulls funding per head towards English levels, which does not necessarily reflect each nation’s baseline needs or its urban–rural mix. To slow that erosion, Wales receives at least 105 per cent of its population share of new UK spending, and Northern Ireland currently receives 124 per cent.

On paper, the devolved governments enter this Budget in reasonable shape. Large real-terms expansions in the Autumn Budget 2024 and Spending Review 2025 settlements have fed through to the block grants, and in-year top-ups to English spending in 2026, such as the funding to clear local authorities’ SEND deficits, have produced large consequentials. But that expansion is front-loaded. Following the 2025 Spending Review, growth in UK day-to-day departmental spending slows from 2.4 per cent in real terms in 2025–26 to 1.0 per cent a year from 2027-28. The squeeze is sharper for the devolved governments, whose funding from the UK government is expected to fall by 0.7 per cent in real terms in the two years to 2028–29, according to the latest Treasury data.

One way to see what this means for the economy is the Hutchins Centre’s Fiscal Impact Measure (FIM), which NIESR has applied to track the direct contribution of fiscal policy forecasts to UK GDP growth. Because devolved governments control spending far more than taxes and benefits, I use only its government purchases component: the growth of real government consumption and investment relative to potential output1. When the two grow in line, the measure is neutral. Faster growth adds to demand, and slower growth subtracts from it.

The FIM shows that Scotland’s fiscal boost came earlier and is fading sooner than that for the United Kingdom as a whole. Government purchases added 0.58 percentage points to Scottish growth in 2024–25, against 0.17 for UK growth, helped by greater use of devolved borrowing powers and a rising share of government spending by the Scottish Government. The Scottish measure has since fallen below the UK average (0.27 against 0.49 percentage points in 2026–27). It is forecast to turn negative from 2028–29 and stay negative through 2030–31, even as the UK measure recovers. This reflects the tightening needed to absorb mounting pressures. An ageing population is increasing demand for health and social care, and Scotland’s more generous social security system costs around £0.8-1.1 billion a year more than its block grant adjustments provide. To accommodate this, the Scottish Government plans real-terms growth of around 2.4 per cent a year for health and social care, funded by cuts averaging 1.7 per cent across most other portfolios.

Wales faces a similar squeeze under a new government. Plaid Cymru won 43 of the 96 seats in May and leads a minority government that must negotiate its budget through the Senedd. Its first full budget, for 2027–28, faces funding that is effectively flat in real terms, with the core block grant set to fall. That leaves little room for commitments such as Plaid’s childcare expansion, costed at around £400 million a year once fully rolled out. With the draft Welsh budget due on 17 November, any consequentials announced on 28 October will feed almost directly into those choices.

Stormont’s difficulties are more immediate. It has yet to agree a budget for the current year, and departments have been limited to 95 per cent of last year’s funding since April. The Executive has so far refused to accept the UK government’s offer of £450 million in 2026–27 and £400 million in each of the following two years. Behind the dispute lies the question of need. The interim fiscal framework sets Northern Ireland’s relative need at 124 per cent of English spending per head, but Gerald Holtham’s 2025 review put it at 128 per cent, and the Treasury has agreed to consider a review if independent evidence points elsewhere. Executive ministers say parity with Scotland or Wales would require £1–3.5 billion a year in additional funding. That review, more than any one-off settlement, will decide whether Stormont’s funding keeps pace with its needs.

First, further top-ups to English spending. This year’s write-off of 90 per cent of English councils’ historic SEND deficits was worth around £5 billion. However, the OBR forecasts that councils will add a further £4.9 billion in 2027–28 alone, when the statutory override ends and councils must recognise them on their balance sheets. A second write-off is therefore possible, and it would again bring consequentials.

Second, how outstanding defence increases are paid for. The £15 billion Defence Investment Plan is funded mainly by cuts to other department spending, with £4.7 billion still to be found on Budget day. The devolved governments already expect to absorb a share of the announced savings, via the announced 1 per cent cut to UK departmental capital budgets. Of rumoured further cuts, those to carbon capture and hydrogen are mostly reserved and would not touch Scottish and Welsh block grants, but others such as cuts to the Boiler Upgrade Scheme will likely reduce Scottish and Northern Irish budgets. Where the remaining £4.7 billion cuts fall will decide how much devolved budgets shrink.

Third, the Chancellor’s promise to move money out of Westminster. The fiscal devolution roadmap due on Budget Day is expected to set out English mayors’ share of business rates from 2027, with a share of income tax to follow from 2028. All else being equal, replacing central grants with retained taxes would shrink the spending on which Barnett is based, so devolved administrations will be checking whether the Treasury adjusts their block grants to compensate.

Finally, some things are unlikely to change. The first is Northern Ireland’s settlement. The UK government has said its offer will not be improved, and the Northern Ireland Secretary has warned he will set a budget himself if the Executive does not. Even if a deal is confirmed on the day, it is unlikely to match what Northern Ireland ministers have asked for. The second is social security. With the recommendations from the Timms review of PIP yet to report, major reforms to disability benefits, which drive Scotland’s largest block grant adjustments, look unlikely before a later fiscal event. The third is tax. With the government’s commitment not to raise income tax, National Insurance or VAT still in place, large policy changes to the taxes behind Scotland’s and Wales’s block grant adjustments are unlikely.

Spending decisions are only one of the routes by which a Budget reaches the devolved governments. For those with significant devolved tax powers, Scotland above all, the forecast that comes with the Budget matters more. Each block grant is reduced by an adjustment reflecting the revenue, or the social security spending, that the UK government has given up through devolution. These adjustments rest on OBR forecasts that are revised at every fiscal event. They are reconciled against outturn years later, sometimes with large corrections.

For example, the reconciliation of Scottish income tax for 2024–25 will cut Scotland’s 2027–28 budget by £720.5 million. That is above the roughly £670 million the Scottish Government can borrow each year to cover forecast errors. Most of the cut (£512 million) comes from a larger block grant adjustment, as income tax receipts elsewhere in the United Kingdom outperformed the OBR’s forecast and the remainder (£209 million) comes from Scottish receipts falling short of the Scottish Fiscal Commission’s (SFC) forecast. In past reconciliations these forecast errors have largely offset each other, with an SFC estimated correlation of −0.86. However, this is the first time in the last five budgets that they have compounded.

A strong OBR forecast for UK income tax on 28 October would be good news for the Treasury, but it could signal a larger block grant adjustment, and a tighter budget, for Holyrood and, to a lesser extent, the Senedd. Devolved governments will have to absorb any forecast revisions into their plans while forming their own view of how plausible those forecasts are.

The headline figures on 28 October will be only a partial guide to what the Budget means for Holyrood, Cardiff Bay and Stormont. Each enters 2027–28 in a somewhat tighter position, as this year’s one-off funding falls away and UK spending growth slows. For Wales, the consequentials announced on the day will matter most, feeding straight into a draft budget three weeks later. For Scotland, the forecast revisions behind its tax adjustments may matter as much. And for Northern Ireland, the question remains whether there will be a settlement at all.
1 Forecast FIM is available at the UK-level through the OBR and at the Scottish level through the Scottish Fiscal Commission. Welsh and Northern Irish forecast data is not readily accessible.

articles.title: Raising Revenue: Taxing the Wealthy?
articles.standfirst: The case of wealth taxes Wealth in the United Kingdom has grown far faster than incomes over recent decades, yet the tax system still heavily taxes income over wealth. Income...
paragraphs: The United Kingdom faces record borrowing costs, and while public debt sits at 95 per cent of GDP and spending is set to rise, the Chancellor needs to raise revenue. After pledging not to tax working people, the focus will likely turn to taxing the wealthy.

Wealth in the United Kingdom has grown far faster than incomes over recent decades, yet the tax system still heavily taxes income over wealth. Income taxes are targeted because they are easy to measure and taxed at source; however, a wealth tax, defined as an annual levy on an individual’s worth, is difficult to measure. While such a tax can help redistribute wealth and reduce inequalities, in practice, valuing total assets such as homes, shares, pensions and businesses can prove very difficult. As such, pure annual wealth taxes are rare, found in only a handful of OECD countries such as Norway and Switzerland.

They also have economic implications; the Mirrlees Review notes that a 1 per cent annual wealth tax lowers the reward for saving, yet charges investors earning exceptional returns no more than those with the same wealth earning ordinary ones. The United Kingdom therefore has no annual net wealth tax; instead, it targets assets predominantly held by the wealthy, including capital gains tax (CGT), inheritance tax (IHT), stamp duty land tax (SDLT), council tax and, from 2028, a “mansion tax”.

Ahead of the 28 October Budget, Chancellor John Healey faces a difficult backdrop. Public sector net debt stands at 94 per cent of GDP, and borrowing is already £8.1bn above forecast. Debt interest now costs around £110bn a year, more than the defence budget, as 10-year gilt yields hit their highest level in nearly two decades. With public finances under pressure, the Chancellor must bring down borrowing while raising defence spending, supporting welfare and easing rising household energy bills. With little room to borrow more, the Budget will need to raise revenues.

Two taxes dominate speculation: a rise in CGT and a lower threshold for the new mansion tax. Both promise money from the wealthy without breaking the manifesto pledge not to raise taxes on working people, namely income tax, National Insurance and VAT, which together make up 60 per cent of tax revenues.

CGT affects less than one per cent of the population and contributes around 1.3 per cent of total receipts, yet it is the lever politicians often reach for first, with policy swinging between taxing gains like income and lower flat rates. Raising rates or aligning them with income tax at up to 45 per cent looks like a clear way to make wealth pay its share. But unlike income, gains are highly elastic as investors can choose when to sell and when to hold. If investors anticipate a rate rise, they can rush to sell assets at the lower rate, as was seen in the run-up to the 2024 Budget, which triggered an 82 per cent increase in realised gains (which then rose a smaller-than-expected 24%), leading to a one-off record of £24.2bn in receipts. In the longer run, the behaviour can flip, as investors “lock-in” and hold assets for longer than intended or productive, reducing the flow of revenue. Higher rates can also push highly mobile investors and business owners to relocate to countries with more favourable tax rates, removing the tax base entirely. The true impact on revenue is unclear, but HMRC estimates show that by 2028-29 an extra percentage point on the higher rate would have minimal impact, while a 10-percentage point rise would reduce receipts by around £3.6bn a year.

Property taxes, however, are inelastic. Since they are in fixed supply, the charge cannot be avoided by selling or moving abroad. Hence, the mansion tax, an annual surcharge on homes worth over £2m, is more predictable and efficient than CGT, but few homes are liable, and it is expected to raise just £430m a year. Lowering the threshold to £1.5m would roughly double the number of homes liable but would still do little to cover proposed additional spending and bring down borrowing.

While this sits with the wealthy, those who are asset-rich and cash poor, or highly leveraged, may feel impacted disproportionately, particularly in London, where liable homes are concentrated after decades of house-price growth.

These adverse impacts will be compounded as the surcharge sits on top of an outdated council tax, and they do not stop with owners, as landlords may pass the cost on to renters. Perception is a risk too, as the mansion tax announcements showed; tax-related backlash can reach far beyond those paying, so the Chancellor must weigh revenue against fallout.

Rather than tweaking rates, the Chancellor could reform how wealth is taxed. The Mirrlees Review, offers a better route to a “progressive, neutral” system, where similar activities are taxed alike. Given many people hold money in assets rather than income because gains are taxed less, taxing gains at income tax rates, but only above a risk-free return such as gilt yields, would remove that incentive without discouraging investment. Also, ending CGT’s exemption at death would ease lock-in and ensure gains passed on at death are taxed.

Reforming property taxation may offer a stronger case, given the current system’s inefficiencies. Despite decades of rising house prices and a shortage of homes, council tax in England still rests on 1991 valuations, so lower-income households pay a larger share of their income than wealthier ones. Stamp duty, meanwhile, penalises buyers upfront and discourages moving. Replacing both with a single tax on current property values, or a land value tax, could raise revenue more efficiently, falling hardest on the most valuable homes and drawing on an inelastic base. While this would take time to implement and raise little additional revenue at first, it is economically efficient and, as research suggests, land tax comes with a growth boost after shifting taxes from labour and capital onto land. As a NIESR blog by Mark Cliffe suggests, to prelude this, new high-value council tax bands from 2028 could fund a temporary stamp duty holiday for downsizers, incentivising better use of under-occupied homes. Further still,NIESR’s modelling suggests that if a large sum is needed quickly, a rise in income tax would do the least damage to GDP, even though that would break the manifesto pledge and fall on workers rather than wealth.

Overall, wealth should be taxed to reduce inequality, but tweaking rates will do little to reduce borrowing materially. Although harder to implement and slower to pay off, reforming the base, would raise more and distort less, offering a fairer and more lasting way to make the wealthy pay their share.

articles.title: Ahead of a presidential election, France first needs to help itself on debt
articles.standfirst: When could market stress justify European Central Bank intervention over French debt and what must France do first for such support to be defensible?
paragraphs: After decades of declining global borrowing costs, long-term government bond yields across the developed world are rising. Underlying this trend are ageing populations and deteriorating fiscal trajectories, the exit from near-zero long yields in Japan, a pressing need for rearmament spending in Europe and, increasingly, the private financing demands of the artificial-intelligence investment boom.

Of all the sovereigns facing rising rates, France may face the biggest challenge. Today’s bond market is exposing a French economic problem that has been building for years. France has lost economic ground relative to Germany since about 2010, in a context of Germany’s own weak performance. More strikingly, France has lost ground relative to Italy since 2020 (Figure 1). France must grapple with structurally higher long-term interest rates in the context of a very weak fiscal starting point and a longstanding growth problem.

Until now, French government bonds have enjoyed something close to a mini-exorbitant privilege, with yields just a little higher than Germany and in any case too big to fail. Public debt climbed from around the Maastricht-compatible 60 percent of GDP at the birth of the euro to 120 percent today, without governments being forced to confront the sustainability of public debt and the French social model.
Figure 1: General government debt in France, Germany and Italy (% of GDP)

However, French public expenditure is about 57 percent of GDP, among the highest in the advanced world. Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large. Disposable income of those aged over 65 is 94 percent of the population-wide average, compared with an OECD average of 87 percent, with four-fifths of the income of this group coming from public transfers (OECD, 2025). Labour-market exit happens at 62 years on average compared to 64 across the OECD. France’s expected 2026 primary deficit, at 2.5 percent of GDP, is among the larger in the euro area (European Commission, 2026).

The French-German spread indicates how much of the bond repricing is specific to France relative to Germany, but the outright yield is the market variable that matters most for debt dynamics. It determines the marginal rate at which France refinances itself and, over time, the effective interest cost on the debt stock. The government now projects the debt-interest bill to rise from €79.2 billion in 2026 to €91.2 billion in 20271. With gross financing needs running into hundreds of billions of euros per year, a persistently higher clearing yield will gradually raise debt-service costs and make an already difficult fiscal adjustment harder.

That does not mean demand for French debt is about to disappear. France has one of the world’s deepest sovereign bond markets and its debt auctions continue to clear. The more plausible danger is an orderly but persistent repricing. Higher yields worsen future interest costs; weaker fiscal arithmetic encourages investors to demand larger risk premiums; and the consolidation needed to stabilise the debt can itself weigh on growth. What begins as a justified repricing can, beyond some point, become non-linear and self-reinforcing.

French voters are increasingly concerned about the public debt, but concern should not be confused with support for the measures required to bring it down2. The proposed 2027 budget illustrates the difficulty. An overall adjustment of €54 billion is envisaged3, though this would lower the deficit only from 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 to 5.0 percent in 2027, while public debt is still projected to rise from 119.3 to 121.7 percent of GDP (Direction générale du Trésor, 2026).

Measures including restraint on pension indexation are politically explosive. Leader of France’s Rassemblement national (RN), Marine Le Pen, should she win the April 2027 presidential election, would therefore face an awkward choice: oppose spending restraint and appeal to economically populist voters, or demonstrate to markets that an RN-led France would take fiscal sustainability seriously. In response to market pressure, she has promised €140 billion of net savings by 2032 and a return to primary balance within 18 months of taking office. But whether savings on that scale can be credibly delivered is uncertain, particularly while she continues to defend retirement at 62. She has also called for discussions with the European Central Bank to ease French borrowing costs once France has regained control of its public finances4.
By contrast, centre-right presidential contender Edouard Philippe has proposed to raise the normal retirement age to 65 and make private pension saving compulsory5.

These competing positions illustrate a broader political problem. Market pressure may increase the value of fiscal credibility, but if voters see pension cuts or other savings as being dictated by ‘the markets’, Brussels or Frankfurt, the same pressure could strengthen the political extremes.

The deeper problem is that France may not possess the political machinery for a durable fiscal reset. The present government lacks a parliamentary majority and, ahead of the presidential election, can at best begin the adjustment rather than complete it. A broad national coalition capable of sustaining a major fiscal reset looks unlikely without much more severe market stress and political duress; the new president could again face a fragmented National Assembly. That leaves two distinct risks: a crisis before the election, when the government has little capacity to respond, and a crisis after if the new political settlement proves incapable of producing a governing majority for adjustment.
In either case, a sufficiently sharp rise in yields would bring the ECB into the argument.

The euro area is far better equipped for sovereign stress than it was in 2010-12, when concerns about government solvency spilled into banks and fragmented financing conditions across the currency union. Banks are now better capitalised, and the ECB has additional tools. But what the ECB can legitimately do in terms of bond purchases is narrow. Outright Monetary Transactions, under which the ECB could purchase short-term sovereign bonds, would require a European Stability Mechanism programme and associated conditionality for France6. A French request for such a programme before the election is politically hard to imagine unless the crisis becomes extreme.

That leaves the more-recent Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) and other minor tweaks in current ECB policy and operations at the Governing Council’s disposal. The ECB could for instance decide to pause or slow the shrinking of its balance sheet in the face of rising yields across the euro area, similarly to the Bank of England for British government debt7.

A broad tightening of financial conditions across the euro area could also elicit a general monetary-policy response, including slower balance-sheet reduction (Pradhan, 2026). But that is different from targeted support for France. It would be a response to tighter monetary conditions across the currency union, not to a France-specific fiscal risk premium.

If market pressure on France itself were to intensify, the TPI would be more relevant. It can in principle be deployed without a predetermined quantitative limit, but was created to counter “unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics” that threaten monetary-policy transmission and are not justified by country fundamentals8.

That distinction goes to the heart of the problem. Suppose investors demand a higher yield from France because the country continues to run large deficits, debt is approaching 120 percent of GDP and still rising, trend growth is weak and parliament is unwilling to agree a credible adjustment. Why should that repricing be considered unwarranted? A wider French-German spread is not in itself evidence that monetary transmission has broken down. Some of it may simply represent investors putting a price on fiscal choices that the French political system has so far been unwilling to confront.

France’s current Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP) does not by itself rule out TPI. Under the ECB’s framework, a country subject to an EDP can still meet the fiscal-framework criterion provided it has not been assessed as having failed to take effective corrective action. The ECB Governing Council would also consider debt-sustainability assessments by the European Commission, the European Stability Mechanism, the International Monetary Fund and the ECB itself. These assessments are inputs into the ECB’s decision, not automatic triggers. Formal eligibility is therefore only part of the problem.

The harder question is when a fundamentally justified repricing becomes an unwarranted and disorderly market move. Because TPI was designed to prevent fragmentation, the clearest case for intervention may arise when pressure that begins in France starts to push financing conditions elsewhere away from what is justified by those countries’ own fundamentals. That transition can be non-linear: liquidity deteriorates, risk premia overshoot and other sovereign markets are dragged along. There is no observable line telling the Governing Council precisely when the first process becomes the second.

Nor can the ECB plausibly defend France against the global component of higher yields. If German, Japanese and United States long yields are rising because global term premia, fiscal supply and inflation uncertainty have increased, the ECB cannot exempt France from that repricing without changing monetary conditions for the euro area as a whole. Thus, the relevance of the outright yield. France’s problem is the interaction between a weak fiscal position and a higher global level of long-term interest rates, not merely a widening spread.

An unconditional TPI intervention would therefore be dangerous. It would risk replacing years of market forbearance with central-bank forbearance, weakening the incentive for France to reform. Repeated use of the ECB balance sheet to suppress a warranted fiscal risk premium would also blur the boundary between protecting monetary transmission and shielding governments from market discipline.

It would also create an obvious legitimacy problem. During the sovereign crisis, adjustment and conditionality were demanded from smaller euro-area countries. A perception that France could obtain an effectively unconditional ECB backstop, despite failing to make comparable efforts could be politically explosive elsewhere. The political controversy left by the scale of sovereign-bond purchases during the previous decade heightens that sensitivity. Thus heavy ECB purchases before the election, without a corresponding French adjustment, would quickly become part of the political fight in France rather than being seen simply as a technical effort to preserve monetary-policy transmission.

France first needs to help itself, taking enough domestic action to change the nature of the ECB’s problem: a credible budget, pension reform, binding medium-term expenditure restraint or some broader political agreement that shows that Paris will accept responsibility for stabilising the debt trajectory.

Only then would ECB intervention become easier to defend. If France has credibly begun the adjustment and markets nevertheless move into a disorderly overshoot, or if French stress contaminates other sovereign markets without justification, TPI can plausibly be presented as protecting monetary transmission, rather than protecting French politicians from their own decisions.

France may need to experience more market pressure before its political system is willing to accept reforms it has postponed for years. Much greater stress may be what ultimately makes a broader governing agreement feasible. But there is also a limit to how much pressure Europe can safely tolerate. If yields rise too far or too quickly, weaker growth, higher future debt-service costs, financial spillovers and political radicalisation could turn a necessary repricing into a systemic euro-area crisis.

The challenge is to find the narrow space between too little pressure to produce reform and too much to contain safely. France has spent much of the euro era benefiting from the assumption that it occupies a special position in the monetary union. Weak growth and deteriorating public finances have coexisted with exceptionally favourable financing for far too long. France cannot control the rising tide of global interest rates but can control whether it is seen by investors as a country already credibly adjusting its public finances, or one still waiting for the ECB to make the problem disappear.

articles.title: The Bank of England Should Not Stop Paying Interest On Banks’ Reserves: Here Is Why
articles.standfirst: As the Chancellor looks to find additional sources of revenue in his upcoming Budget, some commentators (e.g., Gerald Holtham) and politicians (e.g., Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice, both of Reform...
paragraphs: As the Chancellor looks to find additional sources of revenue in his upcoming Budget, some commentators (e.g., Gerald Holtham) and politicians (e.g., Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice, both of Reform UK) have suggested that stopping the payment of interest on bank reserves might be a way of doing this. But is this really a sensible thing to do? The Bank of England thinks not and previous work by NIESR suggests not. In what follows, I run through the arguments underlying this view.

It is first worth recalling how we got here. The Bank of England moved from a system of ‘scarce reserves’, where the banks were kept short of reserves and so had to borrow from the Bank at its policy rate, to a system of remunerated reserve balances with reserve averaging in 2006. This change better enabled the Bank to stabilise the interbank interest rate around its policy rate, making monetary policy more effective. But, although the banks chose the level of reserves in this system, it became clear during the global financial crisis that this level of reserves was too low.

In 2009, in response to the global financial crisis, the Bank started buying up government bonds financed by the creation of reserves, a process known as quantitative easing. This led to a much larger level of reserves than the banks would willingly hold. The quid pro quo for this was that the Bank of England were paying interest on these reserves, compensating the banks for interest they would otherwise have lost. This point was made by Bill Allen in this article in Central Banking, who argued that this meant that the Bank of England was able to buy gilts at a cheaper price than would have been the case had they not been paying interest on reserves. Given that, to stop paying interest on reserves now would be an act of bad faith. This point was made even more strongly by Tim Young in this letter to the Financial Times.
But, leaving aside this issue, there are other reasons why stopping the Bank of England from paying interest on reserves would be a bad idea.

First, commercial banks would have a strong incentive to minimise their holdings of reserves. This could leave the banks potentially short of liquid assets to cover unexpected payment outflows, making them less resilient to shocks. And this problem was a key reason for moving from a system of ‘scarce reserves’ to ‘ample reserves’ in the first place. To the extent that liquidity regulation requires banks to hold a given level of reserves, the banks would be led to recoup the cost of holding these reserves from their customers, via lower deposit rates and/or higher charges. Indeed, this has happened in the Euro Area since the ECB stopped paying interest on reserves. As a result, there would be no net gain for society: there may be (short-term) fiscal savings but these would be offset by higher costs for consumers.

Second, the Bank of England would find it harder to carry out monetary policy. By setting the interest rate on reserves, the Bank can directly control the marginal cost of funding for banks. In turn, this will feed through to interest rates throughout the economy, allowing monetary policy changes to affect real decisions. In a world in which no interest is paid on reserves, the Bank would only be able to affect interest rates by ensuring that banks needed to borrow reserves from it. And this would mean creating a shortage of reserves, with the additional risks to financial stability that this would entail. One answer to this critique is that the Bank could adopt a ‘tiered’ structure for reserves where it pays interest on reserves up to a certain level. Although this could be done, as Bill Allen said in this article in Central Banking, it would have to be done very carefully and would still be subject to the other criticisms in this note.

Third, to stop paying interest on reserves while forcing banks to hold them for liquidity purposes effectively represents a tax on the banks, who would have to pay interest on the funds they borrow to finance their reserve balances. While the government can, of course, feel free to tax the banks above and beyond what they tax other companies, it would seem much better to be open about this and apply a direct tax on banks rather than tax them by stealth.

Finally, and perhaps most worryingly, if the government were to instruct the Bank of England to stop paying interest on reserves, this would bring into question the Bank’s independence. Given such an instruction would be motivated by short-term pressure on the public finances, rather than a more reasoned examination of how the financial system functions, this would be a clear case of political interference in the Bank’s operations. And if the Bank of England were seen as subject to political interference, monetary policy credibility could well be lost leading to a rise in inflation expectations. In turn, this would imply higher inflation on average, making it harder for the Bank to bring inflation down without lowering output and raising unemployment, and making us all worse off.
